2.text: The decrease in Germany in 2022 was mainly linked to the new EU Portal for road transport posting declarations, which became the obligatory prior declaration tool from 2 February 2022, so posted drivers were no longer reported in the national prior declaration tool [p1008][p977]. Germany’s reported postings fell by 34% compared with 2021, but excluding road freight transport they increased by 17% [p959].

6.text: The S80/S50 ratio was slightly below its 2010 level by 2023, after income inequality declined from its 2014–15 peak with fluctuations [p698]. During the pandemic, the wealth share of the top 10% decreased while the bottom 50%’s share rose [p91], though median net wealth grew over 20% for all income quintiles in 2017–2021 and the top quintile gained most in absolute terms, by EUR 50,000 (PPS) [p93]. In 2023, higher income deciles were affected to a greater extent in many Member States [p795].

9.text: Variation is mainly linked to countries’ current renewable capacity/share: Member States with higher installed capacity today tend to have lower re-training expenses per person because additional job creation is lower, while “catching-up” countries face higher needs [p22][p138]. For example, Belgium, Ireland and Italy need about 1 job per thousand people in the labour force by 2030, with re-training costs of EUR 10 (Italy) to EUR 13 (Belgium) per person in the labour force in 2030, whereas Portugal and Sweden, with higher renewable shares (59% and 78%), have job creation close to 0.4 per thousand [p22][p138]. Costs are also scaled to Member States by service-worker wages using Eurostat labour cost levels, so a country at 80% of the EU average wage has training costs reduced by 20% [p18].

14.text: Strong gender segregation persists in digital and green occupations: women make up just 28% of green-task jobs and are underrepresented in ICT, while green occupations with increased demand are more male-dominated [p876]. Care responsibilities keep 7.7 million women outside the EU labour market versus only 450,000 men, and women’s STEM skills gap hinders participation in emerging green and digital industries [p931]. The green transition’s job displacement and creation are concentrated in traditionally male-dominated sectors such as mining, engineering, construction and energy, and the “AI workforce” is small and male-dominated [p931][p878].

19.text: The approach is to ensure human-centric technologies serve workers’ needs and values rather than dictate how they work, involving workers early in the design and application of new technologies and promoting physical and mental well-being, including the effects of AI and virtual worlds [p953]. It also emphasises humane work design, workers’ participation in technology implementation, and reassessing the value attributed to human work while addressing mental stress and skills shortages [p926]. For platform work, it stresses regulatory needs, transparency and human oversight of algorithmic management to protect workers’ rights [p937].

20.text: Determinants include age (older workers make fewer sectoral transitions), gender composition (women remain underrepresented in “transforming sectors,” though no significant male–female difference in sectoral transitions is observed), and sector-specific factors such as higher trade-union density and male dominance in energy-intensive industries, which are linked to lower flows out of employment [p24][p25]. Training participation also matters: energy records the highest training rates, while mining and construction lag, and only 10.9% of energy-intensive-industry workers received training in 2023 versus 12.7% economy-wide [p25][p14]. Workforce dynamics are further shaped by seasonality, cyclicality, digitisation, decarbonisation, climate/COVID-19 shocks, job upgrading, geography, skill compatibility, and labour-market rigidity [p8].

21.text: In the EU in 2022, tertiary-educated adults had much higher adult learning participation than those with lower education. Using AES data including guided-on-the-job training, participation was 65.7% for tertiary-educated adults versus 25.1% for those with lower secondary education or less [p76]. Excluding guided-on-the-job training, the high-qualified participation rate was 58.9% versus 18.4% for the low-qualified, meaning high-qualified adults were more than three times as likely to participate [p653][p596].

22.text: Between 2021 and 2022, inflows of EU movers rose from 859 000 to 976 000 (+14%), while their net mobility increased by 21%, from 296 000 to 358 000 [p443][p449]. Third-country nationals showed a much larger increase: inflows reached 3 324 000 in 2022, a 133% increase, and net mobility rose from 556 000 in 2021 to 2 456 000 in 2022 [p446][p449].

23.text: Digital-intensive future-oriented occupations show better employment conditions: job strain is lowest in occupations with higher digital skills intensity (16%) [p887], earnings predictability is highest there and in AI-exposed occupations [p906], and digitally intensive jobs are more secure than the EU average, with a majority on permanent contracts and over 90% full-time, compared with EU part-time work at 17.7% in 2021 [p884]. By contrast, green in-demand future-oriented jobs have high job strain—34% in less digitally intensive green jobs with increased demand—and only 50% of workers in green in-demand jobs can accurately predict earnings in the next three months [p887][p906]. Green-transition occupations also report long working hours, and about one in four workers in green in-demand and new/emerging/enhanced green occupations fear undesirable change; job insecurity is lower in all future-oriented occupations except green in-demand jobs with labour shortages [p887].

25.text: The pages do not provide a single Central-vs-Western aggregate, but they show the Ukraine conflict sharply boosted TCN inflows especially in Czechia: TCNs were 94% of 2022 inflows there, and the Ukrainian inflow rose from 32,000 in 2021 to 308,000 in 2022, shifting Czechia’s net mobility from -24,000 to 202,000 [p453][p455]. By contrast, high TCN shares in Slovenia (83%) and Croatia (77%) were described as longer-term trends not significantly driven by the Ukrainian conflict [p453]. Western destinations also saw TCN-share increases—Germany +28 pps, Ireland +24, Portugal +24—but Germany and Poland did not report specific Ukrainian data, limiting direct comparison [p453][p444].

26.text: The high share of female EU movers in part-time work in countries such as Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%) may be explained by inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493]. Male EU movers’ part-time rates in those countries are much lower—12% in Switzerland, 14% in Austria and 9% in Germany [p493].

31.text: Strong nominal wage growth (6.1% in 2023 and 5.0% in Q2-2024 in the EU) combined with easing inflation turned real wage growth positive again in Q3-2023, reaching 2.4% year-on-year in Q2-2024 (1.8% in the euro area) [p530][p715]. Despite this rebound, real wages in 2024 were still forecast to be 1.1% below their 2019 level in the EU [p715].

These country shifts are mixed relative to the EU-wide pattern that the younger mover cohort shrank by 3 pps and the oldest expanded by 3 pps between 2018 and 2023, with EU movers ageing somewhat faster [p460]. The provided pages do not contain evidence on how these specific shifts affect broader EU labour-mobility patterns.

However, women remain underrepresented in occupations with the highest exposure to AI, and at a more granular level gender segregation can be found in certain jobs with higher AI exposure [p878][p905]. Both female and male workers experience approximately the same level of higher occupational exposure to AI, while sectors such as health, finance, and statistics are likely to see significant AI impacts [p905].

By contrast, Eastern European Member States showed much stronger wage growth: nominal growth exceeded 11% in Bulgaria, Croatia, Latvia, Hungary, Poland and Romania [p788], while real wage growth was expected to exceed 5% in Bulgaria, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland and Romania [p791].

43.text: The pages do not give occupation-level gender percentages or a complete list; they list examples. For green high-demand shortage jobs (LST-LSF-GD; 12 occupations, mostly craft), examples are bus/tram drivers, carpenters, welders, electrical mechanics, and heavy truck/lorry drivers [p872]; for green new/emerging enhanced shortage jobs (LST-LSF-GNE; 13 occupations), examples are building electricians, plumbers/pipe fitters, civil engineers, heavy truck drivers, and motor vehicle mechanics/repairers [p872]. These groups are male-dominated: most future-oriented occupations have >50% men, and about 80% in these green shortage groups report fewer than half female colleagues, with about 36% reporting no/nearly no women colleagues [p877].

46.text: EU labour-market resilience reflected improved matching efficiency, expected GDP growth, a shrinking working-age population and persistent labour/skills shortages that can push firms to retain workers [p764]. Labour supply also rose, with non-EU nationals contributing 1.24 million to the 2023 total labour-force increase of almost 2 million, helping alleviate shortages [p704]. Firms retained more workers than needed, and the COVID-19 policy response helped prevent unemployment scarring, while low long-term unemployment indicates improved matching [p704].

48.text: The 2024 EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages covers five policy domains: activation of under-represented people in the labour market; support for skills, training and education; improving working conditions; enhancing fair intra-EU mobility; and attracting talent from outside the EU [p635]. It also includes measures such as the EU Talent Pool, the European Skills Agenda, individual learning accounts and micro-credentials, and increasing participation of older workers, women and young people not in education, employment or training [p771].

86.text: In 2023, 36% of female EU movers worked part-time versus 8% of male EU movers, a 28-pp gap [p475][p493]. For EU movers specifically, the report attributes high female part-time employment to inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493]. It also notes the highest female mover part-time rates in Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%), compared with much lower male mover rates of 12%, 14% and 9% [p493]. A broader analysis links women’s part-time prevalence to difficulties combining paid work with family responsibilities, unpaid care work, lack of child/long-term care services, and gendered earner/caretaker attitudes [p850].

89.text: Future EU labour-force trends are shaped by population ageing and a shrinking working-age population, with EU labour supply expected to decline by 0.3% per year until 2070 [p726]; by 2030, the active population aged 55–64 is projected to rise by 6 million and those aged 65–68 by 2.8 million [p737]. Participation is projected to rise from 79.4% in 2022 to 82.7% in 2070 for ages 20–64, with older women’s participation from 59.1% to 72.6% and older workers’ employment from 62.3% to 72.3% [p818], while migration and convergence to Sweden’s participation levels could substantially offset ageing effects [p1012]. Proposed interventions include pension reforms raising statutory retirement ages, restricting early retirement and allowing flexible retirement [p737], tailored activation, flexible work and reasonable accommodations, inclusive training via Individual Learning Accounts and anti-discrimination enforcement [p737], plus the EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages, EU Talent Pool, European Skills Agenda, micro-credentials, intra-EU mobility and attracting non-EU talent [p771].

104.text: The workshop highlighted people with disabilities, unpaid care workers and regional vulnerabilities, as well as precarious workers, self-employed individuals and those facing discrimination, as vulnerable groups in the twin transitions [p926]. People with disabilities face a much lower EU employment rate, 50.6% versus 74.8% for people without disabilities [p928]. Women bear disproportionate unpaid care responsibilities, with 7.7 million women in the EU outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men [p931]. Workers in energy-intensive/fossil-fuel-dependent industries and the regions depending on them are also flagged [p933].

Housing allowances and social housing are found to reduce poverty in the short term and to narrow divergence in poverty risks across countries [p152][p81]. The pages do not provide a comparable long-term regional-disparity estimate for housing investment.

108.text: The pages do not report a 20–34 band, but they show higher underemployment among younger part-time workers: the predicted probability is 0.363 for ages 20–29 versus 0.182 for ages 55–64 [p856]. Younger part-time workers are also about 8 pp more likely to be underemployed than prime-aged workers [p851].

110.text: Yes. The report states that as labour demand increased over the last decade, underemployment “steadily declined both in relative and absolute terms” in the EU [p847]. In 2013, around 30% of part-time workers were underemployed, compared with less than 20% by 2023, and the number of underemployed part-time workers immediately available to work longer hours fell from over 8 million to about 5 million [p847].

111.text: Declared care workers are entitled to additional compensation, overtime pay, and paid leave under labour rights, while undeclared care workers lack legal protection and social protection in case of unemployment or illness [p193][p177]. Because undeclared care workers receive pay without official documentation and neither income tax nor social insurance contributions are fully paid, they are not eligible for related social insurance benefits [p161]. Care workers are also more likely to have temporary contracts and to be undeclared, depriving them of legal guarantees and social protection [p177].

114.text: No. Real wage growth reached 2.4% year-on-year in Q2-2024, but real wages in the EU remained below pre-pandemic levels on average in 2024 [p530][p639]. They were still forecast to be 1.1% below their 2019 level in the EU in 2024 [p715].

119.text: EU movers’ EU-wide median income was higher than nationals’ in 2022 (EUR 20 714 vs EUR 19 506), even though nationals’ median income grew faster (2.6% annually vs 1.9% for movers) [p524]. This apparent paradox reflects the migration pattern: EU movers tend to go to Member States with rather high income levels, raising their EU-wide median despite typically earning less than nationals within each Member State [p524].

123.text: Workers in energy-intensive industries (EII) are relatively male-dominated and show greater labour-market stability: from 2014 to 2023 in the EU27, a higher share remained in employment year-to-year and fewer moved into inactivity or unemployment than in the total economy [p13]. This lower mobility may reflect higher trade-union density and the male-dominated workforce’s lower transitions into inactivity due to care responsibilities [p13][p25]. However, only 10.9% of EII workers received training in 2023, below the 12.7% economy-wide average, which risks hampering reskilling for the green transition [p25]. Women remain underrepresented in “transforming sectors,” including just 14% of mining workers in 2022 and 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023 [p6].

124.text: In Spain, France and Italy, TCNs had higher fixed-term contract shares than nationals in 2022—34% vs 20%, 26% vs 14%, and 23% vs 16%, respectively [p412]. This reinforces TCNs’ more precarious contractual position EU-wide, where TCNs had the highest fixed-term share in 2023 (24% vs 11% for nationals) [p475][p485]. Since fixed-term rates are declining across groups but TCNs remain furthest from stable employment, these country gaps can slow overall labour-market integration [p474][p485].

129.text: Principle 17 of the European Pillar of Social Rights specifically supports the inclusion of people with disabilities in the labour market and society, including through supportive services and workplace adaptation [p929]. It is also identified as the principle on inclusion of persons with disabilities in the employment guidelines [p645].

133.text: EU-LFS 2021 data show AI-exposed occupations are broadly gender-balanced, with women holding 52% of current jobs, but women remain underrepresented in the occupations with the highest AI exposure, which may make them more vulnerable to the digital transition and less able to benefit from AI [p878]. Although female and male workers experience approximately the same level of higher occupational exposure to AI, gender segregation persists in certain high-AI-exposure jobs and in sectors such as health, finance, and statistics [p905]. Women are also at higher risk of being left behind in the digital transition and have greater need for digital-skills education and training, so equipping women to benefit from AI is important for an inclusive transformation [p907].

137.text: Shifting the EU workforce toward higher education is simulated to raise long-run GDP per capita by 0.3 pp after 50 years and 0.15 pp after 25 years for a 1 pp increase in the high-skilled share [p1016]. The projected 2020–2045 increase of 14.15 pp in the high-skilled share would imply lower-bound GDP gains of 4.24 pp by 2095 and 2.12 pp by 2070 [p1016]. Education also raises individual wages—an average return of 7.3% per additional year in Europe, and 9.8% for females versus 7.9% for males [p1015]—while increasing basic skills by 25 PISA points could add 0.5 pp to average annual EU GDP growth in the long term [p130]. In labour-supply terms, the “Education” scenario projects the EU labour force falling by 15.6 pp, or 33.2 million people, by 2070, a smaller decline than under the standard scenario [p1012].

138.text: In the EU, 44% of people aged 55–64 had at least basic digital skills, compared with 64% of those aged 25–54; among older people, the Netherlands and Finland were above 70%, while Romania was only 14% [p828]. In 2022, 29.9% of 55–64-year-olds participated in learning, versus 49.5% of 25–34-year-olds, and participation rose by 2.5 pps for older people versus 3.7 pps for young adults since 2016 [p654]. Older people complete fewer hours of education and training than younger people, though they tend to be better matched to their jobs [p840].

139.text: Yes. The pages state that unequal digitalisation across businesses can feed the existing digital divide and workplace inequalities [p924], and that digitalisation can self-reinforce social exclusion and create new categories of vulnerable workers [p924]. They also note that rising AI uptake increases labour-market polarisation, with unskilled workers more exposed while the skilled workforce benefits [p925]. Cross-country differences in basic digital skills are sizeable, ranging from 28% to 83% [p99].

142.text: The report frames the twin transitions as compounding existing vulnerabilities through skills mismatch, digital exclusion, gig-economy job security and displacement of traditional industries toward greener sectors [p928]. For workers with disabilities, EU employment is only 50.6% versus 74.8% for people without disabilities; telework may help some with physical disabilities, but digitalisation creates barriers for visual or auditory impairments and green manual roles may be less accessible, while invisible disabilities are often unrecognised [p928][p929]. Digital inaccessibility can also hinder task performance, workplace communication and career advancement [p929]. The transitions are gendered too: almost 92% of women are regular carers versus 68% of men (81% versus 48% daily), 7.7 million women are outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men, and women make up just 28% of green-task jobs while being overrepresented in tasks and sectors more exposed to automation [p929][p931][p876].

177.text: Targeted policies should go beyond skills to include active support for quality employment and education (including underrepresented groups), hiring incentives in greener sectors, fair tax-benefit and social protection systems, and better working conditions [p26]. The Council Recommendation guides Member States to adopt policy packages on quality employment in the green economy, skills and training, social protection, and access to essential services, aligned with just-transition investment needs [p138]. 16.text: Gender segregation persists in future-oriented technical/digital occupations: higher-digital-skills-intensity and certain green jobs are largely male-dominated, while critical labour-shortage/care occupations have a higher share of women [p905]; ICT occupations are the most digitally intensive but underrepresent women and older workers [p876]. This can constrain long-term adaptability because women perform more tasks prone to automation and are at higher risk of being left behind in the digital transition, requiring more digital education and training [p876][p907]. Training access is also uneven: most workers in occupations of interest have not recently trained, although higher-AI/higher-digital-intensity occupations report the highest training shares [p907], while in transforming sectors energy has the highest training rates and mining/construction are below average, with energy-intensive industries at only 10.9% trained in 2023 versus 12.7% for the whole EU economy [p25].

17.text: Gender disparities are likely to shape labour-market outcomes in the green transition because women are underrepresented in the “transforming sectors”: they were only 14% of mining workers in 2022 and 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023, while women made up just 28% of green-task jobs [p6][p876]. Since expected job losses are concentrated in male-dominated mining but employment gains are also expected in male-represented construction and waste management, women may benefit less unless their employment in clean energy expands [p6]. Sector-to-sector transition rates show no significant difference between men and women, but training is below average in mining and construction, and only 10.9% of energy-intensive-industry workers received training in 2023 versus 12.7% economy-wide [p24][p25]. Care responsibilities also constrain participation, with 7.7 million women in the EU outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men [p931].

Current initiatives reflect this split: green work includes a toolkit due early 2025 and a Sweden-led taxonomy working group, while third-country work stresses labour-market intelligence, multilingual single-source information, qualification recognition, fair/ethical recruitment and capacity-building [p1033][p1034]; the 2025 Work Programme continues both green-transition support and fair recruitment of third-country nationals [p1047].

77.text: Higher training completion among older people is associated with higher unemployment-to-employment transitions: Denmark, where older people complete about 20% more training hours than EU 25–64, has the highest transition rate at more than 30%, and Germany, the Netherlands and Austria also combine high training with relatively high job-finding [p828]. In contrast, Member States with low training levels—Bulgaria, Greece, Romania and Slovakia—have older people’s transition rates below 10% per quarter [p828]. In 2022, more than half of older people participated in training in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Sweden, while less than 15% did so in Bulgaria, Greece, Poland and Romania [p827]. The report concludes that education and training policies are among the most effective tools for promoting older workers’ employment, especially when combined with search assistance and counselling [p828].

84.text: Based on EU-SILC data, minimum wage non-compliance affects more than 8% of the workforce in Germany, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Lithuania, Hungary, Portugal and Sweden [p797]. The workers most affected are young people, unskilled workers, women, workers in smaller firms and part-time workers; they are generally younger, less educated, more likely female, on fixed-term or part-time contracts, and employed by smaller firms [p797]. Non-compliance is also relatively higher in agriculture, construction and services than in manufacturing [p797].

85.text: Labour-market transitions support the green transition by moving workers out of shrinking sectors and into expanding ones, which helps avoid worsening labour shortages in affected sectors and enables smoother sectoral adjustment [p46]. Skills investment is central: wind and solar deployment is estimated to require about 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU, with EUR 1.1–1.4 billion in associated skills investment by 2030 [p25]. However, training gaps remain—only 10.9% of workers in energy-intensive industries received training in 2023 versus 12.7% economy-wide—so upskilling and reskilling are urgently needed, especially in construction, energy production/distribution, and transport [p25].

90.text: Gender and household status strongly shape underemployment among EU part-time workers: women are significantly less likely than men to be underemployed (by 8 pp or more), and people living with partners are less likely than singles (by 8 pp or more), differences not explained by occupational or sectoral patterns [p851]. Descriptively, 18% of women part-time workers are underemployed, including 16% of mothers of young children, while 15% of part-timers with partners are underemployed versus 26% of those without partners [p850]. In regressions, women with small children and women living with partners are 16 pp and 9 pp less likely to be underemployed than women without children or partners, whereas for men children or a partner have no large effects [p852]. These patterns reflect gendered work/care roles and working-time constraints—women’s lower underemployment can mask caring responsibilities and limited ability to consider longer hours, while male part-time work is less often preferred and more than a quarter of male part-timers want longer hours [p850][p852][p853].

91.text: Digital transformation creates labour-market risks through unequal digitalisation across European businesses and a digital divide that can hinder innovation, reduce productivity, feed workplace inequalities, and self-reinforce social exclusion and privileged positions [p924]. Platform work and AI-driven algorithmic management create unequal and exploitative dynamics, low wages, lack of social protection for vulnerable groups, wider platform–worker power imbalances, surveillance, reduced bargaining power, and “invisible” AI workers [p925]. In the EU platform economy, more than 28 million people worked through digital labour platforms in 2020, 5.5 million were estimated to be incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earned less than the minimum wage [p552]. AI and automation can replace routine jobs and affect high-skilled workers, while unskilled workers are more exposed and the skilled workforce benefits, increasing polarisation [p552][p925]; women may be disproportionately affected due to overrepresentation in AI-exposed sectors and more automatable tasks, and make up just 28% of green-task jobs [p876].

93.text: EU movers face lower risks and material hardship than third-country nationals: in 2022, AROPE was 27% for EU movers versus 46% for TCNs [p508], SMSD was 8% versus 16% [p509], and housing cost overburden was 19% versus 26% [p383]. The report notes that TCNs here include all non-EU countries, including EFTA countries, due to SILC data limitations [p508]. Country-level differences may also reflect movers’ characteristics such as education, skills, or employment sectors interacting with national conditions [p510].

94.text: Benchlearning supports PES modernisation by systematically comparing PES organisational set-ups and outcomes against an “ideal PES,” combining quantitative performance data with qualitative self-review, peer review and expert review [p1045]. In 2024 the 4th cycle launched with 15 assessments covering Lithuania, Bulgaria, Latvia, Croatia, Austria, Portugal, Hungary, Germany, Greece, Czechia, Estonia, The Netherlands, Malta, Ireland and Cyprus [p1045]. The findings show PES progress especially in ecosystem management, while quality management and channel strategy were most challenging; success factors included up-to-date strategies, learning from crises and uptake of technology such as e-services and automated skills-based matching [p1046]. Iceland’s example shows recommendations led to mutual learning, coaching and study visits, helping it strengthen services such as quality management [p1046].

95.text: In the EU in 2023, the employment rate for people with tertiary education was 86.3%, and the gap between high- and low-educated persons aged 25-64 was 28.0 pps, implying a low-skilled rate of about 58.3% [p618]. For persons aged 25-54, the employment rate was 64.1% for lower education and 89.7% for tertiary education [p73].

96.text: Limited mobility in energy-intensive industries is attributed to higher trade union density and a male-dominated workforce less affected by transitions into inactivity due to caring responsibilities [p12][p25]. These sectors also show high labour-market stability and are relatively well-paid, with wage premiums reported in some cases [p13].

97.text: PES career guidance has shifted toward digital and green competencies: 48% of PES report digital skills, 32% green skills, and 51% both as changes in guidance focus over the last five years [p1058]. This mirrors labour-market change, with EU ICT specialists rising by 59.3% since 2013 to over 9.5 million in 2023, while 4 in 10 adults and one-third of workers lack basic digital skills [p638]. The green transition is also reshaping demand, with the green-economy workforce share rising from 2.2% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2021 [p638]. Training patterns reinforce this: occupations with higher AI exposure and high digital-skills intensity have lower shares of workers reporting no recent training [p904], and policies stress upskilling/reskilling and digital skills for the twin transition [p806].

98.text: Factors include strong gender segregation and male dominance of “transforming” and green occupations [p876][p6], women’s disproportionate care responsibilities—7.7 million women in the EU were outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men [p931], and women’s STEM skills gap [p931]. This leaves women underrepresented in green energy: they were only 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023 and 14% of mining workers in 2022 [p6], and just 28% of green-task jobs [p876]. Within renewables, women made up 40% of solar PV versus 21% of wind, while oil and gas had 22% [p6].

99.text: In 2023, the older-worker (55–64) employment rate rose by 1.7 pp to 63.9%, a much stronger increase than the 0.4 pp rise to 35.2% for young workers (15–24) [p72]. Older workers remained the main driver of labour-force growth from 2019 to 2023, adding about 1.2 million people yearly, while the youth labour force began growing from 2021 and reached 19.3 million in 2023 [p753]. Youth employment nevertheless returned to pre-2008 levels in 2023, with a 35.2% employment rate and a record-low NEET rate of 11.2% [p618].

103.text: The green transition is concentrated in “transforming sectors” such as mining and quarrying, manufacturing, energy, water/waste, construction and transportation [p24][p2]. From 2018–2019 there was a net inflow of workers into all transforming sectors except mining and extraction in the EU, while older workers make fewer sectoral transitions and women remain underrepresented, at only 26.7% of energy-industry workers in 2023 and 14% in mining [p24]. Contrary to expectations, energy-intensive industries show fewer transitions to non-employment than other sectors, but training lags: only 10.9% of their workers received training in 2023 versus 12.7% economy-wide [p24][p25]. Delivering EU Green Deal renewable targets would require about 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers and EUR 1.1–1.4 billion in skills investment by 2030 [p25][p12].

105.text: In Portugal, domestic-service workers are under a special regime outside the Labour Code, and unemployment benefits require a full-time monthly written contract registered with social security; most work for several employers and opt for the lower-contribution “agreed regime,” so many lack unemployment protection [p177][p269]. Portugal also has shorter termination notice periods than for other workers—7 days for contracts under 6 months, 15 days for 6 months to 2 years, and 30 days for over 2 years [p278]. In Hungary, employees (including simplified employment) and self-employed domestic workers generally have access to all insurance-based benefits and labour protection, but those under Act XC of 2010 do not have labour protection and may only get basic healthcare if they pay for it themselves [p269][p275]. Shortfalls remain in Hungary through no collective agreements covering domestic workers and carers being unmonitored, with no access to workers’ representation or collective bargaining [p261][p177].

However, a hypothetical extreme positive scenario that simultaneously exploits the entire potential of labour-force activation could offset the projected adverse decline [p1022], and the most optimistic scenario—moving to Swedish participation rates—could almost fully offset the effects of ageing [p1017]. The Draghi report’s projection of a workforce shrinking by close to 2 million workers each year by 2040 is cited on [p1023].

109.text: Austria and France were among five countries with falling absolute regional income disparities (convergence) [p105], and show catching-up beta coefficients of -0.02 for Austria (2014–2021) and -0.01 for France (2014–2021) [p106]. By contrast, Czechia and Sweden were among four countries with rising absolute disparities (divergence) [p105]; Czechia’s standard deviation rose by 20% between 2007 and 2022 [p105], and neither Czechia nor Sweden shows robust evidence of catching-up [p106]. The difference is linked to metropolitan vs non-metropolitan income growth: in converging countries metropolitan regions had slower median income growth than non-metropolitan ones, e.g. slow growth in Austrian major metropolitan regions [p106], whereas in Sweden Stockholm had among the highest median income growth and non-metropolitan Södermanland and Kronoberg the lowest [p106]. For Czechia, absolute dispersion increased but less than the cross-regional average of median incomes, implying a decline in relative income dispersion [p106].

113.text: Individual learning accounts enable people to accumulate funds for labour-market-relevant training, and evidence from the Netherlands and Austria suggests they can boost training participation and learning intentions among older adults [p838]. The EU treats ILAs as flagship actions that can increase adult participation in education and training and improve skills–job matching [p771]. They are intended to give individuals a personal budget for labour-market-relevant training and develop the national training offer, with 2 of 31 PES supporting access and 13 of 31 designing pilots or planning introduction [p1031]. ILAs can also make learning more accessible to underperforming groups when combined with top-ups, career guidance and targeted outreach [p654].

116.text: Voucher systems show stronger evidence of reducing undeclared domestic work: France’s CESU system was associated with informal employment falling from about 50% in 1996 to 20% in 2015 [p187], and 2021 research found Belgium’s service vouchers halved undeclared work in the covered activities [p188]. Tax incentives are more mixed: Germany’s had little effect, while Spain’s 2011 introduction increased declared domestic workers over the following two years before plateauing [p287]. On equity, tax incentives are regressive—German relief rises with household taxable income, and Sweden’s top income decile received 40% of total tax deductions [p287]—while vouchers and tax incentives may mainly benefit higher-income households and have limited formalisation impact among lower-income groups [p194]. Coverage varies: Belgium’s vouchers grew from 62,000 workers in 2006 to 150,000 by 2014, serving about one million users [p188], and France’s HR CESU distributed EUR 400 million in 2020 through 20,300 companies for 809,000 workers [p187]; vouchers could also be extended to more professions, as in Belgium [p311].

For digitalisation, it should ensure human-centric technologies serve workers’ needs, involve workers in technology design and application, and promote physical and mental well-being [p953]. 154.text: The EU27 is ageing: life expectancy is 78.9 years for men and 84.2 for women, and the working-age population is shrinking, while older workers (55–64) increasingly supply labour [p818]. This indicates some convergence toward greater employment stability, though EU movers still had a higher share of fixed-term contracts than nationals [p485].

1.text: The pages attribute the rise mainly to the ongoing process of women’s emancipation and cohort-based improvements in labour force participation, especially among younger women [p1023][p1025]. In Germany, the participation rate of women aged 32 rose from 42% for those born in 1970 to 80% for those born in 1987, accompanied by reduced and postponed fertility; the pages note debate over whether this reflects higher participation/child penalty or wider societal changes in values around partnership, marriage and family [p1025].

2.text: The reported decrease, especially in Germany and Austria, is most likely due to the new obligation to notify posted workers in road freight transport and the EU Portal for road transport posting declarations becoming the obligatory prior declaration tool from 2 February 2022 [p1008]. This created a third administrative data source, and excluding road freight transport the 2021–2022 evolution was actually +14% in postings [p1008].

3.text: Low-educated EU movers are disproportionately concentrated in **Germany (37%), France (34%), Spain (33%) and Italy (33%)**, all above the EU average of 30% [p497]. Highly educated EU movers are disproportionately attracted to **Sweden (70%), Luxembourg (60%), Portugal (59%), Denmark (52%) and the Netherlands (51%)**, above the EU average of 32% [p497].

4.text: For wind and solar deployment under EU Green Deal targets, the estimate is about **130,000 to 145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU by 2030**, with associated skills investment of **EUR 1.1 to 1.4 billion** [p12][p138]. Separately, the NZIA needs assessment estimates **30,000 to 100,000 additional jobs by 2030** to produce wind and solar-related technologies, while REPowerEU targets would require **over 3.5 million jobs by 2030** [p138].

5.text: The share of employees working from home in the EU rose from 11.1% in 2019 to 19.8% in 2023 [p677]. Telework can foster an “always-on” culture with additional, unpredictable hours that may harm work-life balance, health and well-being; in a 2022 Eurofound survey in Belgium, France, Italy and Spain, over 80% of respondents were contacted for work outside contractual hours and nine out of ten responded [p677]. Policy responses include right-to-disconnect legislation in 13 Member States, with France, Spain, Belgium and Italy the first four, while the Commission ran a first-stage consultation from 30 April to 25 July 2024 and launched a July 2024 study [p678].

7.text: In Q4 2024, US labour productivity growth was 2.5%, which was 1.6 percentage points above the EU’s 0.9% growth [p863].

9.text: The variation is driven by countries’ current renewable installed capacity: Member States with higher shares of renewables today tend to have lower job creation and lower re-training costs per person in 2030, because additional job creation is not as high [p22][p138]. Countries with lower shares, such as Belgium, Italy and Ireland, are in a “catching-up” process, need about 1 job per thousand people in the labour force, and face re-training costs of €10 (Italy) to €13 (Belgium) per person [p22]. Conversely, Portugal and Sweden, with higher renewable shares (59% and 78%), should see job creation close to 0.4 jobs per thousand people [p22].

10.text: Voucher schemes show mixed results: ESPAN experts report generally quite low impact in Austria, Belgium and Greece, and a 2018 Belgian study estimated that less than 10% of domestic work paid via vouchers used to be undeclared work [p286]. Sweden’s RUT evaluations are more positive, suggesting a probable link to low undeclared work but remaining unsubstantiated [p287], while France’s CESU system is the strongest example, with informal employment falling from about 50% in 1996 to 20% in 2015—28% in 2005 and 25% in 2011—though 2024 research found 77% of employer families would use undeclared work or forgo services without its tax incentives [p187]. Tax incentives also vary: Germany saw little effect, whereas Spain’s 2011 introduction increased declared domestic workers over the following two years before plateauing [p287]. Both are criticized for regressive effects: in Germany relief rises with taxable household income, and in Sweden the top income decile received 40% of the total tax deduction in a 2020 report [p287].

12.text: High-digital-intensity occupations have a comparatively higher share of young workers—about one in four aged 15–29—and a lower share of older workers aged 55–64 [p881]. Residual green occupations have a lower share of workers aged 15–29, and the 56+ share is higher in the green future-oriented groups GDDI/GEDI/GNDI (17%/19%/20%) than in DH (15%) [p881].

13.text: In 2023, job vacancy rates were at or above 3% in professional, scientific and technical activities, information and communication, and construction [p691]. Labour shortages were also described as particularly persistent in the care sector, education, and STEM fields [p691].

14.text: Strong occupational gender segregation is a key reason: digital-intensive and green-task jobs are male-dominated, with women making up just 28% of green-task jobs and being underrepresented in ICT [p876]. This is reinforced by women’s STEM skills gap and disproportionate unpaid care responsibilities—7.7 million women in the EU remain outside the labour market due to caregiving versus only 450,000 men—limiting their participation in emerging green and digital industries [p931]. Women are also overrepresented in sectors more exposed to AI/automation and in care-related labour-shortage occupations, while men dominate construction-related occupations [p876].

15.text: The employment-rate disparities between EU movers and third-country nationals are particularly significant in Belgium (24 pps), the Netherlands (24 pps), and Germany (22 pps) [p478].

17.text: Gender disparities affect labour-market trends mainly through persistent sectoral segregation and unequal care responsibilities: gender gaps in employment and pay are narrowing and converging, but progress has slowed, and women remain more involved in housework and unpaid care [p116]. The EU labour market remains gender-segregated, with little progress over the last decade [p116]. In transforming sectors, male-dominated sectors may see relatively fewer flows out of employment because men make fewer employment transitions due to lower care participation, although the descriptive analysis finds no difference in the frequency of transitions men and women make between sectors [p25]. New green-transition job opportunities are expected in engineering, technician, maintenance and installation professions in clean energy technologies [p25].

18.text: EU movers face a higher AROP rate (22%, 7 pps above nationals) and a much higher housing cost overburden rate (19% vs 8% for nationals) [p504]. In-work poverty is also greater among temporary-contract workers (12.8%), part-timers (14.3%) and the self-employed (20.7%) than among permanent workers (5.3%), full-timers (7.1%) and employees overall (4%) [p531], so overrepresentation in non-standard work and high housing costs could explain the higher poverty risk.

19.text: **Answer:** The approach is holistic: research new vulnerabilities from digitalisation, focus on community well-being, and promote inclusive educational pathways, while investigating platformisation and algorithmic management without human oversight and stressing workers’ participation in technology implementation [p937]. It also involves **co-creating solutions** through listening to people (e.g., working-environment surveys, working groups, focus groups, interviews) and promoting employee wellbeing [p1097]. Digital tools should be tailored to labour-market demands and learners’ diverse needs, including physical and psychological well-being [p940].

20.text: The pages identify higher trade-union density and male dominance—less affected by inactivity due to caring responsibilities—as reasons workers in “energy-intensive industries” make fewer transitions to non-employment than other sectors [p12]. They also examine age, gender, and education/training participation: older workers make fewer sectoral transitions, no significant difference is observed between men and women, though women remain underrepresented at 26.7% in energy industries in 2023 and 14% in mining [p24]. Other parallel determinants include cyclicality and digitisation [p24].

21.text: In 2022, adult learning participation was highest among adults aged 25–64 with tertiary education at 65.7%, compared with 25.1% among those with lower secondary education or less [p76].

22.text: Between 2021 and 2022, EU movers’ net mobility rose from 296 000 to 358 000 (+21%), while third-country nationals’ net mobility rose much more sharply, from 556 000 to 2 456 000, a 1.9 million increase [p449]. EU/EFTA inflows of EU movers increased from 859 000 to 976 000 [p393], whereas third-country-national inflows increased from 1 426 000 to 3 324 000 [p396].

23.text: Digital-intensive future-oriented occupations show stronger employment conditions: over 90% of workers are full-time, most are permanent employees, part-time work is only 7% versus the EU average of 17.7% in 2021, and earnings predictability is highest in higher-digital-skills occupations [p884]. Green-focused future-oriented occupations are more mixed: some green new/emerging/enhanced jobs have very low part-time work (6%) and below-average job strain, but green in-demand jobs have above-average job strain and only about 50% of workers can accurately predict earnings in the next three months [p884][p906]. Digital-intensive occupations also have much lower job strain than the EU average, while earnings predictability is lowest in green jobs and residual labour-shortage occupations [p906].

24.text: PES support the green transition by smoothing job-to-job transitions and helping jobseekers and employers move into green industries with relevant skills, but defining “green jobs” is challenging due to no common agreement and insufficient internal capacity; over a third of PES have a green-jobs definition and a minority differentiate green skills, tasks and competencies [p1033]. For attracting third-country workers, an increasing number of PES are actively involved in recruitment outside the EU, often under bilateral mobility agreements, though their role depends on national mandates and most schemes are demand- or employer-driven with a job offer as a precondition [p1033]. In this area PES tend to perform administrative tasks such as admission decisions, work permits and labour-market tests, while facing challenges in identifying shortage occupations through labour-market intelligence and providing reliable information on work permits, qualification recognition and job opportunities, ideally via a single multilingual source with ministries and migration authorities [p1033][p1034].

26.text: The disparity is explained by inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493]. Around 36% of employed female EU movers work part-time versus 8% of male EU movers, a 28-pps gap, and the highest shares of female movers in part-time work are in Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%) [p493]. The report also notes this gender gap in part-time employment among EU movers is well above the 20-pps difference among nationals [p372].

27.text: The EU’s 2030 headline employment rate target is at least 78% of the working-age population [p658].

28.text: Nine EU Member States had ratified ILO Convention C189 by October 2024 [p310]: BE, DE, ES, FI, IE, IT, MT, PT, and SE [p255].

29.text: Involuntary part-time employment is most prevalent in Bulgaria and Romania (60% each), Italy (58%), Spain (51%), and Greece (48%) [p489]. The report attributes cross-country differences to varying labour-market conditions and economic structures, noting that part-time work is more often a choice where involuntary rates are low [p489]. More broadly, underemployment among part-time workers is linked to weak bargaining positions from limited education, skills, and experience, and to a lack of full-time alternatives, especially for low-educated people, migrants, young people, and those living without a partner [p850].

31.text: Nominal wage growth remained robust but moderated, reaching 5.0% in the EU in Q2 2024 (4.3% in the euro area), below 2023 rates [p715]. Thanks to lower inflation, real wage growth turned positive in Q3 2023 and reached 2.4% year-on-year in Q2 2024 (1.8% in the euro area) [p715]; real wages had fallen 3.9% in 2022 and 0.4% in 2023 before rebounding [p790]. For 2024, EU real wages are forecast to rise 2.3% after a 0.2% decrease in 2023, but remain 1.1% below their 2019 level [p791].

33.text: The projected increase in economically active people aged 55–68 in the EU is **8.8 million by 2030** [p833].

34.text: The provided pages do not quantify the impact of declining PISA scores on long-term EU economic growth. They warn that the decline poses a major risk to future labour productivity and competitiveness [p648] and could amplify long-term negative effects on human capital and eventually the economy [p132], with potential negative impacts on competitiveness and wage developments [p131].

37.text: High part-time employment can coincide with lower underemployment because national acceptability and prevalence of part-time work, part-time/full-time pay gaps, institutional settings, childcare/reduced-hours options, and household taxation shape whether part-timers want more hours [p848]. The report also notes that low underemployment can mask structural barriers and limited choices, especially for women, rather than simply reflecting preferred working hours [p853].

38.text: In 2023, the female employment rate among EU movers in the EU was **71%** [p491]. For comparison, the female employment rate was **72%** for nationals and **51%** for third-country nationals [p491].

40.text: Luxembourg’s nominal wage growth was below 3.2% in Q2 2024, whereas Eastern European Member States saw much higher growth—more than 11% in Bulgaria, Croatia, Latvia, Hungary, Poland and Romania, and 6–10% in Estonia, Lithuania and Slovakia [p788]. In real terms, Luxembourg’s wages decreased by 1.4 pps, while many central and eastern EU countries had relatively strong real wage growth in Q2 2024 [p791]. The review also notes Luxembourg experienced strong wage and ULC growth during the energy crisis, with signs of a weakening external position [p805].

41.text: By the 2024 Annual Report, the European Network of Public Employment Services had been operational for 10 years, having worked since 2014 [p1055], with the report noting “Celebrating 10 years” [p1038].

42.text: Southern European countries generally saw moderate wage growth and cost-competitiveness gains, with wage growth below benchmark predictions, while central and eastern European countries showed dynamic wage and ULC growth and growing competitiveness concerns [p801][p808]. The Baltic countries, Bulgaria, Croatia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Poland and Romania experienced strong wage and ULC growth during the energy crisis, and concerns about deteriorating cost competitiveness grew for Bulgaria, Czechia, Estonia, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia [p805]. The report stresses that higher productivity growth is needed to sustain further real wage growth [p805].

46.text: EU labour-market resilience was supported by strong labour-supply growth, which accelerated to nearly 1% in 2022 and 2023, with non-EU nationals contributing 1.24 million to the 2023 labour-force rise of almost 2 million and helping alleviate shortages [p704]. Firms retained more workers than needed, probably anticipating recovery [p704], while pandemic job-retention schemes and labour hoarding supported the labour share in 2020 [p799]. Improved matching and low long-term unemployment—partly reflecting the COVID-19 policy response that prevented scarring—also helped [p704], and in 2023 EU employment rose 1.2%, driven by trade, transport, accommodation and food services [p49].

47.text: Yes — the EU unemployment rate was 5.7% in February 2025, a record low and below 6% [p864][p861]. However, the provided pages do not give a direct February 2025 versus 2023 unemployment comparison, so they do not establish that the labour market was tighter than in 2023.

48.text: The 2024 EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages sets out 87 new actions across five domains: activating under-represented people, supporting skills/training/education, improving working conditions, enhancing fair intra-EU mobility, and attracting talent from outside the EU [p635]. It also includes the EU Talent Pool to match non-EU jobseekers with shortage vacancies, and skills initiatives such as individual learning accounts and micro-credentials [p771].

49.text: Denmark and Poland have abolished mandatory retirement ages as a valid reason to terminate labour contracts, while Belgium and Estonia have programmes in which training providers assess applicants’ competence by validating previous relevant experience [p839]. The Netherlands also screens job vacancy notices for discriminatory language under its “vacancies for all ages” initiative [p839].

50.text: In 2023, 14% of EU movers were on fixed-term contracts, down from 19% in 2018 [p372]. Third-country nationals were much more likely to hold fixed-term contracts, with the highest shares in Cyprus (55%), the Netherlands (45%), Poland (41%), and Portugal (40%) [p486].

52.text: In 2023, 96% of EU movers in healthcare professions had permanent contracts compared with 86% of nationals, a difference of 10 percentage points [p334][p394].

Earnings predictability is lowest in green jobs and residual labour-shortage occupations—about 50% in green in-demand and labour-shortage occupations can accurately predict earnings over the next 3 months—and highest in higher-digital-skills and AI-exposed occupations [p884][p906].

For occupations with higher digital skills intensity, the pages say a majority are employees on permanent contracts, but they do not give an exact percentage [p884][p906].

The largest increases since 2009 were around 30 pps in Hungary, Poland and Slovenia for ages 55–59, and in Denmark, Hungary and Slovakia for ages 60–64 [p821].

Among employed female EU movers, about 36% worked part-time versus 8% of male EU movers, a 28 pps gap [p493].
