65.text: The PES Network migrated its standalone `pesnetwork.eu` website to a central one-stop-shop for all Network outputs, including its podcast, and used collaborative platforms for Network work [p1043]. It also launched a PES Network LinkedIn group as an online space to engage the community and stakeholders [p1054]. In addition, the Digitalisation Working Group shared updates on IT projects and reforms and discussed sharing IT solutions and public-private partnerships [p1040].

67.text: Digitalisation and AI deepen platform-work vulnerability by enabling algorithmic management and surveillance that widen power imbalances between platforms and workers and let employers collect large data volumes to maximise productivity [p925]. AI also acts as a “new competitor” for human labour, reducing workers’ bargaining power and creating “invisible” AI workers who train large language models through repetitive tasks, sometimes exposed to damaging content [p925]. Stakeholders linked platformisation to “all-controlling technology in platform work,” taxing jobs, digital-skills gaps and AI-related job displacement [p924]. Some Member States are responding: Croatia’s Labour Act, effective 1 January 2024, makes digital labour platforms and aggregators jointly liable for salary payment and requires transparency, while Germany is drafting employee data protection law covering algorithmic management, video surveillance and AI systems [p686].

68.text: On average, yes: ELA estimates the undeclared-work share at 34% in the care sector versus nearly 70% in direct household employment [p164]. But this is not uniform across countries: in Austria and Germany the undeclared share is 90% or more in non-care domestic work and significantly lower in care-related services, while in Italy in 2022 undeclared work was evenly distributed across both sectors [p283]. In some countries, undeclared work is instead predominant in care, e.g. Bulgaria’s LTC sector and Ireland’s informal home care sector [p283].

70.text: The report adopts a forward-looking dynamic approach that combines labour-force participation rates with demographic projections for 2021–2070, adding nuance on women’s emancipation, educational profiles, and migration assumptions [p1023]. It also quantifies untapped labour potential—8 million people aged 20–29, 12 million aged 55–64, and 17 million women—and uses an “Education” scenario to simulate skill-composition effects on long-run GDP [p1023][p1015]. For care work, it calls for comprehensive, intersectional policies integrating migration, employment, social protection, and gender equality objectives [p195].

71.text: EU sector-to-sector transition rates in the overall economy mostly fell between 1.8% and 3.9%, remained relatively stable over 2010-2019, and showed a slight upward trend around 2016 in some Member States [p7][p24]. From 2018 to 2019, there was a net inflow of workers into all “transforming sectors” except mining and extraction [p24]. Older workers made fewer sector-to-sector transitions than younger workers, while no significant difference was observed between men and women [p24]. The LFS-based estimates cover 2010-2020, with 2019 as the main reference year because 2020 may be affected by COVID-19, and the retrospective question was discontinued afterwards [p3].

72.text: Future-oriented occupations accounted for 32% of workers in the EU in 2021 [p873].

73.text: France and Italy were the only countries where more than 10% of postings were temporary agency postings [p958]. Their shares were approximately 18% in France and 13% in Italy [p975]; the provided pages do not give an EU average for temporary agency postings.

74.text: By October 2024, only nine EU Member States had ratified ILO Convention C189: Belgium, Germany, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Malta, Portugal and Sweden [p310][p255]. The ratification years listed are Italy and Germany 2013; Ireland 2014; Belgium, Finland and Portugal 2015; Sweden 2019; Malta 2021; and Spain 2023 [p304].

75.text: Nine EU Member States have ratified ILO Convention C189 [p255][p304], while eight Member States apply the same labour-law and social-protection rules to domestic workers as to other workers without distinction [p231]. Thus, the number of ratifying countries is slightly higher—9 versus 8.

76.text: Labour-shortage occupations show the highest job strain among occupations of interest (48%), while AI-exposed occupations have below-average job strain and are among those with the lowest job strain [p887][p906]. Access to learning at the workplace is lowest for workers in labour-shortage jobs, whereas workers in AI-exposed occupations report a work environment that supports learning [p888].

77.text: Older workers move from unemployment to employment at higher rates when they complete more education/training [p828]. Denmark, with the greatest number of training hours (about 20% more than people aged 25–64 in the EU), has the highest transition rate from unemployment to employment among Member States (more than 30%), and older unemployed people also find jobs at relatively high rates in Germany, the Netherlands and Austria [p828]. In contrast, in Member States with low training levels (e.g. Bulgaria, Greece, Romania and Slovakia), older individuals transition from unemployment to employment at much lower rates (below 10% per quarter) [p828].

78.text: Converging to Sweden’s higher labour force participation rates by age, sex, and education would almost completely offset the projected negative impact of ageing on EU labour supply, leaving a decline of only 2.8 pp, or 5.9 million people, by 2070 [p1012].

79.text: In 2022, EU public expenditure on education was allocated roughly as follows: pre-primary and primary education 34%, secondary education 36.8%, and tertiary education 16.6% [p130]. Over 70% of public spending on education went to school education, which includes pre-primary, primary, and secondary levels [p130].

80.text: The pages identify Ukrainian nationality as predominant among posted third-country nationals in Belgium, Lithuania, the Netherlands, and Austria, where more than a quarter of posted TCNs are Ukrainian [p1008][p974]. They do not provide a cross-Member-State sectoral breakdown for TCNs; road freight transport is noted as a main posting sector generally [p1008].

81.text: In 2023, 35.5% of adults in Bulgaria had basic or above basic overall digital skills [p655].

82.text: Bulgaria and Poland had statutory minimum wages rise by more than 40% in nominal terms between January 2022 and July 2024 [p796], while real wage growth exceeded 4.0% in Q2-2024 [p639]. By contrast, real statutory minimum wages fell by 1.3% in France and by more than 3% in Czechia over the same period, despite nominal increases [p796].

83.text: High graduation numbers do not by themselves prevent shortages: shortages were documented in Ireland, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia and Romania, which had above-EU-average densities of medical doctor and nurse graduates but below-EU-average densities of available healthcare workers [p338]. Retention and mobility also matter—Italy faces insufficient medical school graduates plus an outflow of doctors, and returnee inflows are not apparent sufficient to offset outflows of EU movers [p358]. Data gaps may further obscure the picture, as EU movers in healthcare may be underrepresented in national statistics, including live-in care providers under legally ambiguous conditions [p334].

84.text: Based on EU-SILC data, minimum wage non-compliance is estimated to affect more than 8% of the workforce in Germany, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Lithuania, Hungary, Portugal and Sweden [p797]. The worker groups most affected are young people, unskilled workers, women, workers in smaller firms and part-time workers, with non-compliance also relatively higher in agriculture, construction and services [p797].

85.text: Labour-market transitions can support the green transition by moving workers out of shrinking or transforming sectors into expanding ones, helping avoid labour shortages in affected sectors such as construction and transportation; relatively high transitions in the most affected sectors can facilitate smoother adjustment [p46]. By 2050, the European Green Deal may bring large relative employment increases in water supply and waste management, construction, and wholesale/retail trade, while reducing employment in coke/refined petroleum, gas/steam/air conditioning, and mining [p2]. Skill demands also shift—e.g. by 2030 construction is expected to need more workers to install heat pumps or solar PVs while gas-fitter demand may fall, and automotive skills differ between internal-combustion and electric vehicles [p46][p2]. PES can smooth this transition by supporting jobseekers and employers to move into green industries with relevant skills, including through training, job creation programmes and active labour-market policies [p1033].

86.text: Among EU movers, about 36% of employed women worked part-time versus 8% of men, a 28-pps gap (vs 20 pps for nationals) [p493]. The report links high female-mover part-time rates to inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries; the highest shares were in Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%) [p493].

88.text: Yes. Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a higher-than-average incidence of permanent employment — 4 percentage points above the average of 69.7% — and fewer than average hold a temporary contract of less than a year (3 percentage points below the average of 8.3%) [p884].

89.text: Key factors include economic, ecological, digital, demographic and social transformations reshaping EU jobs, with ageing population, increased migration and skills gaps highlighted [p951][p938]. Proposed interventions include innovative and inclusive educational pathways, accessible upskilling/reskilling programmes, and better skills intelligence to anticipate future needs [p938]. The agenda also calls for research on labour mobility, remote work, platform work, and social protection coverage, while noting green investment is expected to yield a net increase of 2 million jobs in Europe by 2030 [p938][p954].

90.text: Women part-time workers are less likely to be underemployed (18%, and 16% for mothers of young children) than men, over a quarter of whom want longer hours; only about 8% of employed men work part-time, and 5% of fathers [p850]. Living with a partner is associated with lower underemployment (15%) than living without one (26%) [p850]. Regression results show women with small children and women with partners are 16 pp and 9 pp less likely to be underemployed than women without children/partners, while children or a partner have little effect for men; these gender, age and household differences are not explained by occupational or sectoral patterns [p851][p852]. The lower female underemployment reflects caring/time constraints and limited choice, whereas men’s part-time work is less socially accepted and more often involuntary; couples’ lower rate partly reflects two-earner household income, while singles rely on their own income and more often lack full-time alternatives [p850][p853].

91.text: Digitalisation and AI exposure create uneven labour-market risks: almost 40% of global employment is exposed to AI, and 27% of jobs in OECD countries rely on skills that could easily be automated by AI, with AI-exposed occupations concentrated among professionals (ISCO2), technicians and associate professionals (ISCO3), managers (ISCO1) and clerical support staff (ISCO4) [p917]. Digitalisation can also increase mental stress and skilled-worker shortages, requiring humane work design, worker participation in technology implementation and reassessment of the value of human work [p926]. The twin transitions are redefining vulnerability and deepening existing inequalities, especially for precarious workers, self-employed people and those facing discrimination, while data gaps and weak social protection remain challenges [p926].

92.text: In 2023, non-EU nationals accounted for **64.1%** of the total increase in the EU labour force [p755].

93.text: In 2022, EU movers had a lower AROPE rate (27%) than third-country nationals (46%), though higher than nationals (19%) [p504][p508]. Their severe material and social deprivation rate was also lower than TCNs’ (8% vs 16%) [p509], and their housing cost overburden rate (19%) was slightly below TCNs’ (26%) [p504]. The pages suggest differences may reflect movers’ characteristics such as education, skills, and employment sectors interacting with national labour-market contexts [p510], as well as arrangements like part-time work linked to parental-leave policies and labour-market demand [p493].

94.text: Benchlearning is described as a vehicle to support PES performance, including capacity building and data-driven/digitalisation strategies [p1056]. In 2024, the fourth Benchlearning cycle began with 15 assessments across LT, BG, LV, HR, AT, PT, HU, DE, EL, CZ, EE, NL, MT, IE and CY [p1056], and the Network lists “Improve PES performance through Benchlearning” among its 10-year achievements supporting PES to strengthen services and pioneer innovative digital processes [p1048].

95.text: In the EU in 2023, the tertiary-educated employment rate was 86.3%, while the gap between high- and low-educated workers aged 25–64 was 28.0 pps, implying a low-skilled employment rate of about 58.3% [p618].

96.text: Limited mobility in energy-intensive industries is likely explained by their demographic profile, as they are relatively male-dominated, which is associated with lower mobility into unemployment and inactivity [p13]. It also reflects high labour-market stability in these sectors, which can be positive for perceived job security, and the fact that they are relatively well-paid industries where wage premiums are reported [p13].

97.text: Career guidance shows a clear digital/green emphasis: 48% of PES report digital skills, 32% green skills, and 51% both, based on the 2024 PES Capacity Questionnaire [p1058]. This mirrors wider labour-market transformations, as the EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages aims to help the workforce adapt to demographic and technological changes and the twin transitions [p771]. The PES Network’s 2025 priorities continue skills intelligence, green transitions and digitalisation, with data and technology as ongoing priorities [p1047], while the 2025 Joint Employment Report calls for PES investment in digital infrastructure, career guidance, skills intelligence and staff training to support transitions [p615].

98.text: Factors include caregiving responsibilities—7.7 million women in the EU are outside the labour market because of caregiving versus 450,000 men [p931]—and a STEM skills gap that can hinder women’s participation in emerging green and digital industries [p931]. Gender segregation also persists in most future-oriented occupations, with many green and higher-digital-skills jobs being male-dominated [p905], and women are at higher risk of being left behind in the digital transition [p907]. This affects workforce composition: women were only 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023 and 20% of the “transforming sectors,” but 32% of renewable energy versus 22% of oil and gas, and 40% of solar PV versus 21% of wind [p6].

99.text: Older workers remained the main driver of EU labour-force growth from 2019 to 2023, adding about 1.2 million people yearly, while youth labour-force growth turned positive from 2021, reaching 19.3 million in 2023 versus 17.6 million in 2020 [p753]. The older-worker employment rate reached 63.9% in 2023, nearly 20 pps above 2009, with stronger gains for women [p563]. For youth, unemployment fell to 14.5% in 2023 from 15.1% in 2019 but stabilised, and the NEET rate declined to 11.2% [p656].

100.text: The projected investment in skills needed for additional wind and solar deployment to meet EU Green Deal targets is **EUR 1.1 to 1.4 billion by 2030** [p138][p25][p12].

101.text: The pages do not directly measure countries’ education investment, but they show that older unemployed people transition to employment at higher rates when they complete more education/training. Denmark, with the most training hours, has the highest transition rate (more than 30%), while low-training countries such as Bulgaria, Greece, Romania and Slovakia have rates below 10% per quarter [p828].

102.text: Based on the PHS Employment Monitor for 2024, more than 15% of workers surveyed reported undeclared care work in **Poland and Spain**, and **35% in Italy** [p165].

103.text: The green transition affects the entire EU economy, with significant transformations in energy industries, mining and quarrying, construction, manufacturing and waste management [p12]. Based on EU Labour Force Survey data, recent years saw a net inflow of workers into all “transforming sectors” except mining and extraction [p12]. Contrary to expectations, workers in energy-intensive industries overall make fewer transitions to non-employment than those in other sectors, possibly due to higher trade union density and male dominance [p12]. Delivering EU Green Deal wind and solar targets would require about 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU, with associated skills investment of EUR 1.1–1.4 billion by 2030 [p12].

104.text: The pages highlight vulnerable workers in precarious employment, self-employed individuals, and those facing discrimination, as well as people with disabilities, unpaid carers, and regional vulnerabilities/disparities [p926]. They also flag already marginalised social groups and workers in energy-intensive or fossil-fuel-dependent industries and the regions that depend on them [p933].

105.text: Portugal has a special “domestic service” regime outside the Labour Code, and even formalised carers mostly lack unemployment benefits because eligibility requires a full-time monthly contract and not opting for the lower-contribution “agreed regime,” which most do not have [p177]. Hungary’s government argues its 2011 legislative package is comprehensive for domestic workers [p257], but research reports carers are not monitored, lack access to workers’ representation and collective bargaining, and enjoy no social or legal protection or support [p177]. Social protection shortfalls therefore remain in Portugal’s unemployment/social protection for domestic service workers and in Hungary’s lack of monitoring, representation and legal/social protection [p177][p257].

106.text: The pages indicate the Draghi report projects the EU workforce to shrink by close to 2 million workers each year by 2040 [p1023]. However, the most optimistic scenario—simultaneously harnessing all existing labour-force activation potential by moving to Swedish participation rates—could “almost fully offset” the adverse effects of population ageing, not fully offset them [p1017].

109.text: Austria and France are among the countries where absolute regional income disparities declined (convergence), and since 2014 low-income regions tended to catch up, with France showing catching-up (-0.01) and Austria (-0.02) [p105][p106]. By contrast, Czechia and Sweden showed rising absolute income disparities (divergence), with Czechia’s standard deviation increasing by 20% between 2007 and 2022; Sweden is also an exception to relative convergence [p105][p106]. The difference is linked to metropolitan vs non-metropolitan income growth: in converging countries metropolitan regions grew more slowly than non-metropolitan ones, while in Sweden Stockholm was among the highest-growth regions and growth was lowest in Södermanland and Kronoberg [p106].

110.text: Yes. The report states that underemployment among part-time workers in the EU-27 declined steadily from 2013 to 2023, from around 30% of part-time workers in 2013 to less than 20% “today” [p847]. The number of underemployed part-time workers immediately available to work longer hours fell from over 8 million to about 5 million over 2013-2023 [p847].

111.text: Undeclared care workers lack legal protection and social protection in case of unemployment or illness, whereas declared workers are entitled to labour rights, overtime pay and paid leave [p177][p193]. The report also notes that care workers are more likely to have temporary contracts and to be undeclared, depriving them of legal guarantees and social protection [p177]. Even when formalised, carers may not enjoy the same protections: in Portugal, domestic service workers have a special regime outside the Labour Code, and most do not access unemployment benefits [p177].

112.text: The ISCO codes used to define domestic workers are 5152 (“butlers”), 5162 (“companions and valets”), 5322 (“home-based personal care workers”), and 9111 (“domestic cleaners and helpers”), added alongside NACE 97 workers [p240].

113.text: The pages do not provide an empirical assessment of the impact of Individual Learning Accounts (ILAs) on workforce development. They describe ILAs as combining financial and non-financial support to empower adults to develop skills throughout working life [p652], and as a European Skills Agenda flagship action to foster competence acquisition, increase adult participation in education and training, and improve skills-job matching [p771]; tailored training including via ILAs can also support older people’s employability [p737]. A study supporting the Commission’s impact assessment on ILAs found most respondents preferred training during working hours, or paid training leave if training occurred outside working hours [p923].

114.text: No. Although real wage growth turned positive and reached 2.4% year-on-year in Q2-2024 in the EU [p715][p639], real wages in 2024 are still forecast to be 1.1% below their 2019 level in the EU [p715][p791]. The pages also state that real wages in the EU and most Member States remain below pre-pandemic levels [p639].

115.text: Table 2.1 shows beta convergence (catching-up) for GDP per capita, GDHI, AROPE (total and children), housing cost overburden, and adult participation in learning in both 2007-2014 and 2014-2023; employment, unemployment, youth unemployment, NEET, and healthy life years for women show catching-up only in 2014-2023, while tertiary education attainment only in 2007-2014. Healthy life years for men show no robust evidence of convergence [p100].

116.text: Evidence on effectiveness is mixed: ESPAN experts report voucher impact on undeclared work is generally quite low in Austria, Belgium and Greece, with a 2018 Belgian study estimating that less than 10% of domestic work paid via vouchers used to be undeclared, while Sweden’s RUT evaluations suggest a probable link to low undeclared work but this remains unsubstantiated [p286][p287]. Tax-incentive impact also varies: Germany’s experts say tax incentives had little effect, whereas Spain’s 2011 introduction led to an increase in declared domestic workers over the following two years before plateauing [p287]. Coverage differs because vouchers create a traceable payment system but may be inefficient where they can only be used up to the marginal employment threshold, as in Austria, while tax deductions range from 5% in Portugal to 20% in most Member States using them, with Estonia and Spain using reduced social-security contributions instead [p285]. Equity concerns are especially strong for tax incentives, which are regressive—German relief rises with household taxable income, and Sweden’s highest income decile received 40% of the total tax deduction—while vouchers may ensure basic social-security coverage but can perpetuate low wages and mainly benefit higher-income households [p287][p194].

118.text: Yes. The inflow of EU movers to EU and EFTA countries rose from 859,000 in 2021 to 976,000 in 2022 (+14%), while outflow fell from 584,000 to 543,000 (-7%) [p443]. The inflow increase of about 117,000 outweighed the outflow decrease of about 41,000 [p443].

119.text: EU movers’ EU-wide median income was EUR 20 714 in 2022, higher than nationals’ EUR 19 506, even though movers’ income grew more slowly (1.9% vs 2.6% annually) [p524]. This apparent paradox reflects the migration pattern: movers tend to go to Member States with relatively high income levels, raising their EU-wide median despite lower relative earnings within each country [p524].

120.text: Using the 2023 figure of nearly 9.8 million ICT specialists and the 20 million target for 2030 [p656], the required annual growth rate is about **10.7% per year** over 2023–2030. Using the alternative “over 9.5 million” 2023 figure [p638] gives about **11.2% per year**.

121.text: The 2025 Joint Employment Report calls for strengthening active labour market policies and public employment services by investing in digital infrastructure and services, enhanced career guidance, counselling, skills intelligence and staff training, with the aim of supporting quality job creation and transitions [p615]. It also links this to integrating skills-intelligence tools and fostering individual training entitlements such as individual learning accounts and micro-credentials [p615].

123.text: Energy-intensive industries are significantly male-dominated and have higher trade union density, which may explain why their workers make fewer transitions to non-employment than workers in other sectors [p12][p25]. In 2023, only 10.9% of their workers received training, compared with 12.7% in the whole economy, even though these industries are more exposed to employment restructuring in the green transition [p25]. This low training participation risks prolonging skills shortages and hampers reskilling for the transition [p25].

126.text: The highest access to employer-funded training was in less digitally intensive green new and emerging occupations (56%) and green enhanced occupations (53%) [p903].

127.text: Research and innovation can address the twin transitions by integrating future work trends with green and digital transition policies, with innovation actions focused on accessible upskilling/reskilling and human-centric digital technologies [p950][p937]. It should target gaps such as the widening digital divide, equitable ICT access across regions, sectors, groups and SMEs, skills for the green and digital transitions, and new vulnerabilities from digitalisation [p936]. The ERA4FutureWork research streams cover the green transition and working life, the digital world of work, twin transitions and vulnerable groups, and future of work in EU public administrations [p950][p953]. Funding strategies should prioritise impactful future-of-work research and bridge the gap between research and policymaking [p946].

129.text: Principle 17 of the European Pillar of Social Rights specifically supports the inclusion of people with disabilities in the labour market [p929][p514].

130.text: Part-time workers living with a partner are less likely to be underemployed: about 15% versus 26% for those living without a partner in the EU [p850]. Regression results controlling for other factors and occupational/sectoral patterns find the probability is significantly lower for people living with partners than for singles, by 8 pp or more [p851]. The effect is much stronger for women, who are 9 pp less likely to be underemployed when living with a partner, while for men having a partner does not have a large effect [p852].

134.text: Yes. The ESDE 2023 report notes that, if supported by the right employment and education policies, net-zero policies could create between 884,000, one million, and 2.5 million jobs in some sectors by 2030 [p869]. Another page states green investment is expected to yield a net increase of 2 million jobs in Europe by 2030 [p954].

135.text: Belgium, Ireland and Italy are expected to face higher re-training costs per worker despite lower current renewable deployment, as they need about 1 additional job per thousand people in the labour force by 2030 and have comparatively low renewable shares of 27%–38% [p138]. Re-training expenses in 2030 are estimated at EUR 10 per person in the labour force for Italy and EUR 13 for Belgium [p22].

136.text: The year-on-year real wage growth in the EU was 2.4% in the second quarter of 2024 [p790][p715].

137.text: Shifting education levels raise individual wages: in the EU15, one additional year of education yields 4.1% (SE) to 9.7% (PT) for males and 3.8% (SE) to 13.7% (IE) for females [p1015]. For Europe and Central Asia, the average return is 7.3%, higher for females (9.8% vs 7.9% for males) and in low-income countries (9.3% vs 9.2% middle- and 8.3% high-income) [p1015]. At the macro level, human capital is a factor of production and also drives technological change through R&D, so it generates long-run growth; DG ECFIN-JRC estimates simulate increasing skill composition on long-run GDP as a lower-bound effect [p1015]. In 2023, EU employment growth was driven by 25-54 year-olds with tertiary education and older workers with secondary or tertiary education, consistent with reallocation to high-skilled occupations [p617].

138.text: In the EU, 44% of people aged 55–64 have at least basic digital skills, compared with 64% of those aged 25–54 [p828]. Older people complete fewer hours of education and training than younger people, although they work in jobs better matched to their skills and cognitive abilities [p840]. Among older individuals wanting to participate in training, health, age and course availability are main reasons for non-participation, while about 8% of adults in both age groups report lack of support [p828].

139.text: Yes. Unequal digitalisation across Europe can feed the digital divide, reduce productivity and workplace inequalities, and persistent trends threaten to exacerbate regional disparities and widen the gap between SMEs, mid-caps and larger businesses [p924]. Digitalisation is also linked to labour-market polarisation, with unskilled workers more exposed while the skilled workforce benefits [p925], and digital inaccessibility can hamper people with disabilities’ task performance, communication and career advancement [p929]. Research gaps include tackling the widening digital divide across regions, sectors, occupational and socioeconomic groups and ensuring equitable digital access among businesses, especially SMEs [p936].

140.text: The 2024-Q4 job-vacancy chart includes the EU, Netherlands, and Belgium, but the page does not print exact 2024-Q4 rates [p866]. For Q2-2024, Belgium had the highest vacancy rate at 4.4% and the Netherlands was next at 4.3% [p635].

142.text: The digital and green transitions can reinforce existing inequalities and create new vulnerable groups, with research still lacking on their interaction and on an intersectional approach to differentiated impacts [p928][p950]. For workers with disabilities in the EU, the employment rate is only 50.6% versus 74.8% for people without disabilities; teleworking may help some physical disabilities, but digitalisation can create new barriers for visual or auditory impairments, and expanded manual green roles may be less accessible for people with physical disabilities [p928]. More broadly, the transitions affect about 8 out of 10 workers, with 32% in future-oriented occupations and 28% of jobs in AI-exposed occupations in 2021 [p873].

143.text: Yes. Table 1 shows both Denmark and the Netherlands implemented a prior declaration tool and cover self-employed persons, with the Netherlands’ coverage limited to certain sectors [p963]. Page 974 confirms that Denmark and the Netherlands are among the four Member States requiring registration of incoming self-employed persons, and Table 6 reports both posted workers and self-employed persons for DK and NL [p974].

For example, in Switzerland 43% of nationals work part-time, compared with 27% of EU movers and 35% of TCNs [p487].

152.text: The European Commission’s ERA4FutureWork initiative was a joint DG Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion and DG Research and Innovation forum to foster dialogue among policymakers, social partners and stakeholders on research and innovation priorities for the future of work [p950][p952]. It organised four workshops between April 2023 and February 2024 on the green transition and working life, the digital world of work, the twin transitions and vulnerable groups, and the future of work in EU public administrations [p949][p952]. The resulting study examines gaps among Member States across these four streams and advocates a proactive, strategic integration of new work approaches, reindustrialisation and future work trends with green and digital transition policies [p950].

153.text: Job vacancies remained elevated in professional, scientific and technical activities; information and communication (ICT); administrative and support service activities; and accommodation and food service activities [p66][p691]. 154.text: The EU27 “transforming sectors” show older age profiles: water supply has a median age of 46 years and mining/construction 43 years [p5]. In mining, workers are mainly aged 30–50, with fewer workers aged 20–30, suggesting early retirement and lower attractiveness to young entrants [p5].

155.text: Men work part-time less often than women largely because of gendered attitudes and care roles: men are often seen as primary earners and women as primary caretakers, and nearly half of the EU population holds attitudes that at least partly support this distribution of paid and unpaid work [p850]. Only about 8% of employed men in the EU work part-time, and more than a quarter of male part-time workers say they would like to work longer hours [p850]. Part-time work is also rarely a preferred arrangement for men, while women more often face longer-term working-time constraints such as caring responsibilities [p853].

156.text: Foreign-born students underperform significantly relative to local-born peers whose parents have no migrant background in most EU countries, while native students with parents born abroad are partially catching up [p650]. Differences among all student groups are small only in Croatia, Malta, Ireland, and Cyprus [p650].

158.text: The share of underemployment in part-time work is particularly low among older workers, reaching just 12% [p850].

159.text: Real median disposable income at EU level rose from 97% of the 2010 level in 2015 to 118.5% in 2023, though it remained quite stable since 2020; flash estimates point to +6.0% nominal and +0.2% real for 2023 incomes [p82]. Financial distress for the lowest income quartile eased to 27.6% in July 2024 (-0.7 pp year-on-year), while tax-benefit systems raised the share of benefits excluding pensions in disposable income to 8.3% in 2023 from 7.1% in 2019 [p82][p62]. The AROP rate decreased slightly and income inequality remained stable [p86].

160.text: The report finds that the consumption footprint of the 20% of the EU population with the highest income is **1.8 times higher** than that of the poorest 20% [p139]. Chart A3.2 presents this consumption-footprint inequality as an S80/S20 ratio across Member States for **2021**, with the EU average excluding Italy because household income data are unavailable in the HBS [p50]. Higher-income households’ impacts are linked to mobility/transport (**22%**) and household goods/appliances (**11%**), while poorer households spend more of their income on food (**54%**) and housing-related expenses, especially energy (**25%**) [p139].

161.text: The officially documented EU-LFS-based number of domestic workers in 2023 is likely an underestimate: LFS data may undercount migrants and undeclared workers are less likely to respond, so the actual number is likely “(much) higher” than the estimates [p242]. Country examples support this: in Malta, about 15,000 undeclared domestic workers are estimated versus 4,400 recorded in the EU LFS, and in Cyprus 21,318 non-EU domestic workers in January 2023 exceeded the 20,000 LFS total for the same year [p281]. The pages do not provide a precise actual EU total.

They also need clear mutual expectations and a common vision in public-private procurement, and must align AI developments with PES strategies and integrate new AI solutions into existing systems and business processes [p1039].

175.text: Unpaid care work is linked to a much larger labour-market access penalty for women: 7.7 million women in the EU were outside the labour market due to caregiving in 2023, versus only 450,000 men [p931], and in 2022 34% of women vs one in four men were involved daily in unpaid care, while 63% of women vs around one in three men did housework daily [p109]. Women also provide more informal care (19.1% vs 14.8% of men) and are more likely to devote significant time to it, while male caregivers more often receive formal long-term care support (73% vs 61%) [p661]. For underemployment, having small children or a partner lowers women’s probability by 16 pp and 9 pp respectively, but has no large effect for men [p852]. On STEM, the pages only note that women lag in STEM skills, likely hindering participation in emerging industries [p931]; they do not directly estimate how unpaid care affects women’s STEM representation.

The report also notes EU movers’ participation stagnated at 3% between 2017 and 2022, compared with 7% for TCNs in 2022 [p516].

177.text: Targeted policies include upskilling and reskilling, lifelong learning and on-the-job training, linking education/training curricula to firms’ needs, and supporting labour reallocation and matching through effective public employment services, transferable social security and training rights, and housing policies; digital skills and coordinated identification of future skill needs are also key [p806]. Well-designed labour and social policies and strong social protection help absorb shocks and enable workers to “bounce forward” [p951]. Strengthening collective bargaining and social dialogue can also raise real wages and support fairer sharing of productivity gains [p115].

16.text: Gender segregation is high in future-oriented occupations, and occupations with higher digital-skills intensity are more male-dominated, with women underrepresented in ICT and older workers also underrepresented [p876]. EU-LFS 2021 data show AI-exposed occupations are broadly gender-balanced, with 52% of job holders being women, but women remain underrepresented in the occupations with the highest AI exposure, which may make them less prepared to benefit from AI [p878]. On training, workers in occupations with higher AI exposure have the lowest share who received no training in the preceding four weeks, followed by high-digital-skills occupations, and one in five report some education or training in that period, though the report says more can be done to improve uptake and opportunities in key occupations [p904].

17.text: Gender disparities shape EU labour-market trends in the green transition: women make up only 20% of the “transforming sectors” workforce, 14% of mining in 2022, and 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023 [p6][p24], and just 28% of green-task jobs [p876]. Because expected job losses are concentrated in male-dominated mining while gains are also in male-represented construction and waste management, the transition risks being gender-imbalanced unless women’s clean-energy employment increases [p6][p876]. However, sectoral transition rates show no significant difference between men and women, while gender composition and mobility vary across Member States [p24][p36].

18.text: The report suggests this reflects EU mobile workers’ challenges in accessing quality employment at the same level as the native population that can provide a decent income [p512]. It also notes that the in-work poverty rate measures employment quality and wage adequacy [p511]. The gap is especially pronounced in Member States with higher in-work poverty risk and a more challenging labour-market environment, such as Spain, where EU movers faced a 23% in-work poverty risk vs. the EU-27 average of 13% [p512].

19.text: The approach is human-centric: innovation should serve workers’ needs and values rather than dictate how they work, with workers involved early in designing and applying new technologies and with both physical and mental wellbeing promoted, including in relation to AI and virtual worlds [p953]. It also stresses humane work design, workers’ participation in technology implementation, and reassessing the value of human work as digitalisation increases mental stress and skilled-worker shortages [p926]. For platform work, it calls for regulatory protection, transparency, and worker participation in technology implementation, including against algorithmic management without human oversight [p937]. As an example, INESC TEC reports mental-health training for managers and collaborators (2023), psychosocial risk surveys (2019; repeated in 2024), flexible hours, a hybrid model, and a 4-day week pilot (2023) [p1098].

20.text: The pages identify age, gender, and participation in education/training as factors combined with sectoral mobility in the “transforming sectors” [p24]. Older workers make fewer sectoral transitions than younger workers, while no significant difference is observed between men and women; women remain underrepresented, at 26.7% in energy industries in 2023 and 14% in mining [p24]. Workers in energy-intensive industries make fewer transitions to non-employment than those in other sectors, possibly due to higher trade union density and male dominance reducing inactivity from caring responsibilities [p12]. Training and education in some key sectors is also lagging behind [p12].

Excluding guided on-the-job training, the high-qualified participation rate was 58.9% compared with 18.4% for the low-qualified, more than three times as high [p653].

22.text: Between 2021 and 2022, EU movers’ net mobility rose 21%, from 296,000 to 358,000, while third-country nationals’ net mobility jumped from 556,000 to 2,456,000—a 1.9 million increase [p449]. EU-27 EU-mover inflows rose from 762,000 to 860,000, compared with TCN inflows to EU/EFTA rising from 1,426,000 to 3,324,000 (EU-27: 1,381,000 to 3,252,000) [p366][p396]. Nationals’ net mobility stayed negative, with 255,000 more leaving than returning in 2022 [p449].

23.text: On employment conditions, [p883] reports that dependent employment on indefinite contracts is higher than average in most future-oriented occupations and is highest in occupations with a higher level of digital skills. It is lowest in the green new and emerging (GNE) group at 53% and in labour-shortage occupations at 69% [p883]. Thus, the page supports a contrast where digital-intensive future-oriented occupations have the strongest indefinite-contract incidence, while the green GNE group has the lowest among those cited [p883].

24.text: PES support the green transition by smoothing job-to-job moves and helping jobseekers and employers move into green industries with relevant skills, but defining “green jobs” is hard: over a third of PES have a definition, a minority differentiate green skills/tasks/competencies, and PES face insufficient internal capacity [p1033]. Related initiatives include a Toolkit to be published in early 2025 and a Taxonomy Working Group led by Sweden [p1033]. For third-country workers, PES roles are often administrative—admission decisions, work permits, labour-market tests, and sometimes working conditions—though more PES are involved in recruitment under bilateral mobility agreements; challenges include identifying shortage occupations via labour-market intelligence and providing reliable information on work permits, qualification recognition, and jobs [p1033][p1034].

25.text: The 2022 TCN inflow surge was largely attributed to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, with TCN arrivals doubling to 3,324,000 (+133%) [p444]. In Central Europe, Czechia’s TCN share reached 94%, and Ukrainian inflows rose from 32,000 in 2021 to 308,000 in 2022; by contrast, Slovenia’s and Croatia’s high TCN shares were described as longer-term trends not significantly driven by the Ukrainian conflict [p453]. Among other notable 2021–2022 TCN-share increases, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania rose by 31, 27 and 25 pps, while Western/EFTA examples Germany, Ireland, Portugal and Norway rose by 28, 24, 24 and 25 pps, though the page does not attribute those Western increases specifically to Ukraine [p453].

26.text: Female EU movers are much more likely than male EU movers to work part-time: in 2023, about 36% of employed female EU movers worked part-time versus 8% of male EU movers, a 28-pp gap [p493]. The highest female-mover part-time rates were in Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%), while male rates there were only 12%, 14% and 9% [p493]. The report links this to inequitable parental-leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493], as well as to economic structure, tourism/hospitality, high unemployment, employer cost/flexibility motives, and work-life-balance/flexible-work policies that particularly affect women [p488][p489].

29.text: Involuntary part-time employment is most prevalent in Bulgaria and Romania (60% each), Italy (58%), Spain (51%), and Greece (48%) in 2022 [p489]; in 2023, Romania, Italy, and Spain recorded shares above 50% [p675]. The pages attribute these differences to varying labour-market conditions and economic structures, noting that where involuntary part-time is low, part-time work may be more a choice than a necessity [p489].

30.text: The report links income inequality among mobile EU workers to destination-country income levels and migration patterns: movers tend to go to high-income Member States, raising their EU-wide median income even though they often earn less than nationals within each country [p524]. Country-specific distributions matter—12 of 22 Member States with data have higher inequality among EU movers than nationals, with the widest gaps in Bulgaria (by 8), Italy (3), Spain (2), Malta (2), and Denmark (2) [p526]. In Italy, movers’ S80/S20 ratio is 9 versus 5 for nationals and TCNs, reflecting low median incomes overall but a few high earners well above the rest [p525]; lower inequality appears in Ireland (3 vs 4) and Croatia/Hungary (2 vs 4), though small mover populations warrant caution [p526].

31.text: Strong nominal wage growth reached a record 6.1% in the EU in 2023, after 4.9% in 2022, and was still 5.0% in Q2-2024 [p785][p530]. As inflation eased, real wages rebounded from the second half of 2023 and reached 2.4% year-on-year in Q2-2024 (1.8% in the euro area), after falling 3.7% in 2022 and 0.2% in 2023 [p639][p715]. Despite this recovery, real wages in 2024 were still forecast to be 1.1% below their 2019 level in the EU [p715][p791].

32.text: In Sweden, inflows rose in all three age groups (20–34: 3k to 15k; 35–49: 2k to 7k; 50–64: 2k to 3k), while the 20–34 share fell 1 pp to 60% and the 35–49 and 50–64 shares each rose 1 pp to 30% and 11% [p377]. Slovenia’s inflows fell sharply (20–34: 12k to 1k; 35–49: 5k to 1k; 50–64: 2k to 0), with the 20–34 share rising 3 pp to 45% and the 35–49/50–64 shares falling to 35%/20%; Switzerland’s inflows increased (40k to 50k; 21k to 27k; 7k to 10k), with the 20–34 share down 2 pp to 57%, 35–49 up 1 pp to 32%, and 50–64 unchanged at 11% [p377]. Relative to the EU-27 2022 shares (20–34: 53%, 35–49: 31%, 50–64: 15%) [p375], Sweden and Switzerland remained more youth-weighted, which may sustain prime-age mobility into those destinations, whereas Slovenia’s contraction and lower 20–34 share could reduce its pull for mobile EU workers.

33.text: The projected increase in economically active people aged 55 to 68 in the EU is **8.8 million by 2030** [p833].

34.text: The pages do not quantify the impact of declining PISA scores on long-term economic growth. They state that worsening basic skills pose a major risk to the EU’s future labour productivity and competitiveness [p648][p649], and that PISA outcomes point to potential negative impacts on EU competitiveness and wage developments in the longer term [p131]. Separately, reducing inefficiencies in education spending could potentially increase annual GDP per capita growth by 0.8 pp in the long term [p133].

35.text: EU-LFS 2021 data suggest that occupations with higher exposure to AI are broadly gender-balanced, with a slightly higher proportion of current job holders being women (52%), although women remain underrepresented in occupations with the highest AI exposure [p878]. EWCTS data reveal similar findings [p878]. At a more granular level, both female and male workers experience approximately the same level of higher occupational exposure to AI, but gender segregation can be found in certain jobs with higher AI exposure [p905].

It suggests that where part-time work is common, arrangements may better match preferences, whereas underemployment often reflects constrained choice and workers’ weak labour-market position [p848][p849].

41.text: The 2024 Annual Report states that 2024 marked the 10-year anniversary of the PES Network [p1056].

42.text: Southern EU countries such as Greece, Spain, France, Italy, Cyprus and Malta had comparatively low wage and unit labour cost growth in 2022–2023, with high unit profits and moderate wage growth, suggesting room for sustainable wage increases if combined with higher productivity growth [p804]. By contrast, central and eastern EU Member States—including the Baltic countries, Bulgaria, Croatia, Hungary, Poland and Romania—saw strong wage and ULC growth during the energy crisis, and concerns about deteriorating cost competitiveness were noted for Bulgaria, Czechia, Estonia, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia [p805]. Cumulated over 2014–2022, wage growth was below benchmark in Greece, Croatia and Poland, but above benchmark in Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Romania [p800].

44.text: Age-based mobility shapes the challenge because older workers make fewer sector-to-sector transitions than younger workers in all Member States [p24], while younger workers participate more frequently in education and training and participation declines with age [p10]. Since the green transition requires significant reskilling/up-skilling in “transforming sectors” [p10], older workforces in those sectors face greater reallocation challenges. Table 2 shows median ages in transforming sectors in 2022 are often mid-40s (EU27: 43–46 across sectors B–H), with higher values such as DK mining at 51 and LV water at 54 [p35]. Country variation also matters: Estonia and Finland are generally more mobile across sectors, while some countries show significant younger–older mobility discrepancies, including Cyprus [p7].

45.text: Digital-intensive jobs have a younger age profile: occupations with higher digital skills intensity have about one in four workers aged 15–29 and a lower share aged 55–64, while residual green occupations have a lower share aged 15–29 [p881]. In Figure 6, higher-digital-skill occupations show 23% aged 25–34 and 15% aged 56+, whereas green enhanced and green new/emerging intermediate-to-low-digital occupations show only 4% aged 16–24 and 19–20% aged 56+ [p881]. For intermediate-to-low digital skills intensity, the shares of younger and older workers are roughly equal [p881].

46.text: EU labour-market resilience amid the slowdown reflects strong labour-supply growth—accelerating to nearly 1% in 2022 and 2023, with non-EU nationals adding 1.24 million to the 2023 labour-force rise of almost 2 million—which helped ease shortages [p704]. Firms also retained more workers than needed despite the slowdown, and job-seeker/vacancy matching improved, as shown by low long-term unemployment, partly due to the COVID-19 policy response [p704]. Despite GDP growth falling to 0.4% in 2023, unemployment stabilised around 6%, though cooling signs appeared such as a declining vacancy rate and fewer firms reporting labour shortages since early 2023 [p748][p772].

47.text: Yes. In February 2025, the EU unemployment rate reached a new record low of 5.7%, down 0.4 pp from February 2024 [p864]. In 2023, the EU unemployment rate was 6.1% [p66][p748], so the February 2025 rate was below 6% and lower than in 2023.

48.text: The 2024 EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages sets out 87 new actions across five domains: activating under-represented people, supporting skills/training/education, improving working conditions, enhancing fair intra-EU mobility, and attracting talent from outside the EU [p635]. It also includes measures such as the EU Talent Pool, the European Skills Agenda, individual learning accounts and micro-credentials, and increasing participation of older workers, women and young NEETs [p771].

49.text: Denmark and Poland have abolished mandatory retirement ages as a valid reason to terminate labour contracts [p839]. Belgium and Estonia have programmes in which training providers assess an applicant’s competence by validating previous relevant experience [p839]. Related measures include the Netherlands’ “vacancies for all ages” initiative, which screens job vacancy notices for discriminatory language, and France’s Public Employment Service selecting candidates for employer interviews based on aptitude tests without regard to age or previously held employment [p839].

50.text: In 2023, 14% of EU movers held fixed-term contracts, compared with 24% of third-country nationals; TCNs had the highest share among the three groups [p485]. Table 39 reports 843 EU movers (14%) and 2,192 TCNs (24%) on fixed-term contracts [p411].

51.text: Yes. France and Sweden are among five Member States that have raised statutory retirement ages since 2020 [p836], and the report projects an expected increase of 8.8 million active people aged 55–68 in the EU by 2030, mainly driven by already adopted retirement reforms [p833]. It also projects +6.0 million active people aged 55–64 and +2.8 million aged 65–68 by 2030, mostly due to ageing and anticipated pension reforms [p737].

52.text: The permanent contract rate was 96% for EU movers versus 86% for nationals in 2023, a difference of **10 percentage points** [p394].

53.text: Workers in labour-shortage occupations report the highest job strain (48%), while those in higher digital-skills-intensity occupations report the lowest (16%) [p891]. Green in-demand jobs are among those with high/above-average job strain [p887][p906]. For earnings predictability, only 50% of workers in residual labour-shortage occupations and green in-demand jobs could accurately predict their earnings over the next three months, whereas predictability is highest in higher digital-skills-intensity and AI-exposed occupations [p906].

54.text: Workers in occupations with higher digital skills intensity (DH) have a permanent-contract share of 79%, and AI-exposed occupations are 4 percentage points above the EU average of 69.7%, i.e. about 73.7% [p883][p884]. Both are therefore above the EU average.

55.text: In 2023, employment rates for older workers (55–64) were above 70% in Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Latvia, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden, while they were below 55% in Greece, Croatia, Luxembourg, Romania and Slovenia [p821]. Since 2009, the largest increases of around 30 pps were seen in Hungary, Poland and Slovenia for ages 55–59, and in Denmark, Hungary and Slovakia for ages 60–64 [p821].

Part-time work was slightly more common among TCNs than EU movers in 2023 (22% vs 21% at EU-27 level), while nationals were at 17% [p414]. Over 2018-2023, EU movers stayed around 21-22% part-time, whereas TCNs declined from 26% to 22% [p487].

60.text: No. The 2024 PES Capacity Questionnaire shows Member States split between having implemented ILAs, having plans for ILAs, having no plans, and not submitting feedback; only a few PES had begun introducing ILA schemes by summer 2024 [p1032].

61.text: Gender disparities stem from strong segregation in digital, green and labour-shortage occupations: women make up just 28% of green-task jobs and are underrepresented in ICT, while they perform more tasks prone to automation and are overrepresented in sectors exposed to AI [p876]. Care responsibilities and skills gaps also matter: 7.7 million women in the EU remain outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men, and women’s STEM skills gap can hinder participation in emerging green and digital industries [p931]. The green transition’s “transforming sectors” are male-dominated—women are only 20% of the workforce, 14% of mining workers in 2022, and 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023 [p6]. Policy should continue gender-equality actions at work and make lifelong learning accommodate care responsibilities [p875], treat care responsibilities as a top priority in twin-transition assessments [p931], and increase women’s employment in clean energy to support a gender-neutral transition [p6].

62.text: Yes. The gap in temporary employment between EU movers and nationals narrowed from 5 percentage points in 2018 to 3 percentage points in 2023 [p485].

63.text: The rise was largely driven by the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022: third-country nationals arriving in EU/EFTA countries increased from 1,425,000 in 2021 to 3,324,000 in 2022, a 133 % increase [p446]. This included a large influx of Ukrainian refugees, mostly women [p755].

64.text: Using the 15–64 employment rate, Greece rose from 56.5% in 2019 to 61.8% in 2023, a change of +5.3 pp [p722]. Portugal rose from 70.5% in 2019 to 72.5% in 2023, a change of +2.0 pp [p738].

65.text: The PES Network launched a dedicated LinkedIn group in July 2024 to increase its visibility, connect PES, encourage exchanges, and provide inspiration and best practices; by end-October 2024 it had nearly 500 members with active contributions [p1044]. It also used a social-media week of action and an anniversary PESPod podcast to share PES experiences and stories [p1048]. In addition, the Digitalisation Working Group supported PES IT experts in driving digital progress, and a mutual assistance project addressed digital matching tools for Luxembourg [p1054][p1050].

66.text: In the Netherlands, full-time employment among returning health workers rose from 0% in 2018 to 38% in 2023, while part-time fell from 100% to 62% [p430]. In Italy, the trend was opposite: full-time fell from 100% in 2018 to 69% in 2023, with part-time rising from 0% to 31% [p430]. Both sets of 2018 and 2023 values are shown in parentheses, indicating low reliability [p430].

67.text: Digitalisation and AI deepen platform-work vulnerability by widening power imbalances between platforms and workers and enabling algorithmic management and surveillance that maximise productivity at workers’ expense [p925]. Platform work itself combines low wages and missing social protection, with more than 28 million people estimated to work through digital labour platforms in 2020, 5.5 million incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earning less than the minimum wage [p552][p676]. AI also creates “invisible” AI workers doing repetitive and sometimes damaging content work, while reducing workers’ bargaining power [p925]. These risks intersect with false self-employment and atypical status, and require regulation of algorithmic management without human oversight and lack of transparency [p927][p937].

68.text: Not uniformly. In Austria and Germany, the estimated share of undeclared workers is 90% or more in the non-care sector and significantly lower in care-related services, and in Malta undeclared work is much more likely in non-care domestic work [p283]. However, Italy reported an even distribution across both sectors in 2022, while in Bulgaria most LTC domestic workers are argued to operate in the informal economy and Ireland has a significant informal home care sector [p283]. At EU level, the undeclared-work share is lowest (34%) in the care sector and highest (nearly 70%) in direct household employment [p164].

70.text: The report outlines a comprehensive set of measures under the March 2024 EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages to mobilise underutilised resources, including the EU Talent Pool, the European Skills Agenda with individual learning accounts and micro-credentials, and increasing participation among older workers, women, and young people not in education, employment or training [p771]. It stresses swift implementation of skills development and training, fair intra-EU mobility, and attracting and integrating talent from outside the EU to make the workforce adaptable to demographic and technological changes and mitigate ageing effects on labour supply [p771]. The Draghi report also identifies untapped potential of 8 million people aged 20-29, 12 million aged 55-64, and 17 million women [p1023].

71.text: The pages indicate that sectoral transitions were estimated yearly per Member State using EU LFS retrospective data for 2010–2020, with 2019 as the main reference year because 2020 may be affected by COVID-19 [p3]. For 2019, sector-to-sector mobility is shown by age and gender across Member States, but some estimates are unreliable and no sectoral transition data is available for Ireland [p33][p36]. The provided pages do not report a single EU-wide 2010–2020 movement pattern for transforming sectors.

74.text: By October 2024, only nine EU Member States had ratified ILO Convention C189 on Domestic Workers: Belgium, Germany, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Malta, Portugal, and Sweden [p310][p261]. The remaining 18 Member States had not ratified it [p231].

75.text: Nine EU Member States have ratified ILO Convention C189 [p231][p261], while eight Member States apply the same labour-law and social-protection rules to domestic workers as to other workers without distinction [p231][p261]. The ratification count is therefore one higher than the same-rules count.

76.text: AI-exposed occupations show below-average job strain [p906], and the text groups AI-exposed jobs with higher-digital-skills occupations as having the lowest job strain on average [p887]. By contrast, labour-shortage occupations report the highest proportion of job strain, at 48% in the EU27 EWCTS 2021 data [p887][p891]. For training, access to learning at the workplace is higher in higher-digital-skills occupations and AI-exposed workers report a learning-supportive environment, whereas it is lowest for workers in labour-shortage jobs [p888].

77.text: Evidence suggests training participation is associated with better unemployment-to-employment transitions for older workers: Denmark, which has the greatest number of training hours for older people (about 20% more than people aged 25–64 in the EU), also has the highest transition rate from unemployment to employment (more than 30%), while Germany, the Netherlands and Austria also combine relatively high training levels with high transition rates [p828]. By contrast, in low-training Member States such as Bulgaria, Greece, Romania and Slovakia, older individuals transition from unemployment to employment at rates below 10% per quarter [p828]. Training participation itself varies widely: in 2022 more than half of older people participated in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Sweden, but less than 15% did so in Bulgaria, Greece, Poland and Romania [p827].

78.text: Adopting Sweden’s higher labour force participation rates across Member States would almost fully offset the projected ageing-driven decline in the EU workforce: under the “MS→Sweden” scenario, the labour force would fall by only 2.8 pp, or 5.9 million people, by 2070 [p1012]. This contrasts with the standard “Static” scenario, in which the EU labour force declines by 20.2 pp, or about 42.8 million people, by 2070 [p1011]. The report therefore describes convergence towards Sweden’s participation levels as almost fully compensating for the workforce decline [p1012][p1013].

80.text: The pages do not provide an EU-wide ranking of predominant TCN nationalities; they show Ukrainians were particularly prominent in Belgium (9% of all posted workers) and Czechia (almost half of notifications were TCNs, mainly Ukrainians), while 41% of TCNs received by Bulgaria were Turkish [p959]. Across sectors, the main posting sectors overall were transport/storage (32.4%) and construction (30.7%); excluding transport, construction rises to 46.0% [p1002]. Country examples include Belgium (32% construction), Denmark (almost half in construction), France (31% construction, 26% manufacturing), Ireland (42% manufacturing, 35% construction), and Italy (37% manufacturing) [p959].

81.text: In Bulgaria, 35.5% of adults had at least basic digital skills in 2023, compared with 55.6% at EU level [p548].

82.text: Between January 2022 and January 2024, real statutory minimum wages increased by more than 10% in Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Germany, Latvia and Poland [p640]. By contrast, high inflation diminished these gains, with real statutory minimum wages falling by more than 3% in Czechia, Slovakia and Slovenia [p640].

83.text: High graduate output does not by itself eliminate shortages: Ireland, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia and Romania have above-EU-average densities of medical doctor and nurse graduates but below-EU-average densities of available healthcare workers [p338]. Shortages are also driven by an ageing population and rising vacancy rates in human health and social work, which increased in all but six EU/EFTA countries from 2017 to 2023 [p335].

84.text: Based on EU-SILC data, minimum wage non-compliance is estimated to affect more than 8% of the workforce in Germany, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Lithuania, Hungary, Portugal and Sweden [p797]. The workers most affected are young people, unskilled workers, women, workers in smaller firms and part-time workers, who are generally younger, less educated, more likely female, on fixed-term or part-time contracts, and employed by smaller firms [p797]. Non-compliance is also relatively higher in agriculture, construction and services than in manufacturing [p797].

85.text: Labour-market transitions can support the EU green transition by moving workers from carbon-intensive declining sectors into expanding “transforming sectors”; the paper finds a recent net inflow of workers into all transforming sectors except mining and extraction in the EU [p12], while CEDEFOP expects by 2050 large relative employment increases in water supply and waste management, construction, and wholesale/retail trade, and decreases in coke and refined petroleum, gas/steam/air conditioning, and mining [p2]. Since skills and occupations may need to change across or within sectors and geographically [p2], training is crucial, yet training and education in some key sectors is lagging behind [p12]. Delivering EU Green Deal renewable targets would require about 130,000 to 145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU for wind turbines and solar panels, with associated skills investment of 1.1 to 1.4 billion EUR by 2030 [p12].

86.text: The report attributes the high part-time rate among female EU movers—36% vs. 8% for male movers in 2023, a 28-pps gap—to factors including inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493][p372]. This gap is larger than the 20-pps difference among nationals [p372][p475]. The highest shares of female movers in part-time jobs are in Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%), where male EU movers’ part-time rates are much lower (12%, 14% and 9%, respectively) [p493].

88.text: Yes. Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a higher-than-average incidence of permanent employment, 4 percentage points above the average of 69.7% [p884].

89.text: Future EU labour-force trends are shaped by population ageing and decline, women’s emancipation, changing educational profiles, and migration assumptions [p1023][p1022]. The Draghi report identifies untapped participation potential of 8 million people aged 20–29, 12 million aged 55–64, and 17 million women [p1023]. Proposed interventions include investing in skills/human capital and activating labour-force participation; in the most optimistic scenario, moving to Swedish participation rates could almost fully offset the adverse effects of ageing, though investment alone cannot compensate for demographic decline [p1017][p1022].

90.text: Gender and household status both shape underemployment among EU part-time workers. In 2013–2023 predicted probabilities were higher for men (0.339) than women (0.242), for single men (0.355) than single women (0.295), and for fathers (0.344) than mothers (0.181) [p856]. Living with a partner lowers underemployment: about 15% of partnered part-timers were underemployed versus 26% of those without a partner, while women part-time workers had 18% underemployment and mothers of young children 16% [p850]. The drivers differ: men’s higher underemployment is linked to gendered earner/caretaker attitudes and men less often choosing part-time, whereas women’s lower rates reflect unpaid-care time constraints and lack of childcare/long-term care; couples can use two earners to make part-time viable, while singles rely on their own income and prefer full-time work [p850].

91.text: Digital transformation can widen labour-market inequalities because digitalisation is uneven across European businesses, which can hinder innovation, reduce productivity and feed workplace inequalities [p924]. Digitalisation can also self-reinforce social exclusion and strengthen already privileged positions, while changing workforce structures and creating new categories of vulnerable workers [p924]. In platform work and AI uptake, risks include all-controlling technology, physically and mentally taxing jobs, lack of relevant digital skills, job displacement, algorithmic management without human oversight and lack of transparency [p924][p937]; research should also anticipate future inequalities and avoid creating new vulnerable groups [p953].

92.text: Non-EU citizens accounted for **64.1%** of the total increase in the EU labour force in 2023 [p755].

93.text: EU movers generally fare better than third-country nationals (TCNs) but worse than nationals: in 2022, 27% of EU movers were at risk of poverty and social exclusion (AROPE) versus 46% of TCNs [p504][p508], and their severe material and social deprivation rate was 8% versus 16% for TCNs [p509]. The housing cost overburden rate was 19% for EU movers and 26% for TCNs [p504]. These differences may reflect different national contexts and labour markets, as well as movers’ characteristics such as education, skills, and employment sectors interacting with national circumstances [p510].

94.text: Benchlearning supports PES modernisation by systematically comparing PES organisational set-ups and outcomes against an “ideal PES” and enabling institutional learning among peers [p1045]. Its 4th cycle launched in January 2024, with 15 assessments covering PES including Lithuania, Bulgaria, Latvia, Croatia, Austria, Portugal, Hungary, Germany, Greece, Czechia, Estonia, the Netherlands, Malta, Ireland and Cyprus [p1045][p1056]. The updated methodology reflected new labour-market trends and PES challenges, emphasising greater flexibility, user-friendliness and effectiveness [p1045], and it produced practical peer advice for Estonia on topics such as Austria’s quality assessment and performance-management systems and Germany’s evaluation of labour-market measures [p1045].

96.text: The pages attribute the lower mobility of energy-intensive-industry workers partly to their relatively male-dominated demographic profile, which is linked to lower mobility into unemployment and inactivity, and to the sectors’ high labour-market stability [p13]. That stability is positive for perceived job security and may also reflect relatively well-paid industries with reported wage premiums [p13].

97.text: The PES Network links guidance, skills intelligence, training and upskilling to the speeding-up “triple (demographic, green and digital) transition” and to employers’ difficulties finding the right skills [p1057]. This mirrors digital labour-market change: EU ICT specialists rose by 59.3% since 2013 to over 9.5 million in 2023, but only 19% were women, and 4 in 10 adults and one-third of workers lack basic digital skills [p638]. It also mirrors green restructuring: 1.8–3.9% of EU workers switch sector annually, and the green-economy workforce share rose from 2.2% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2021, while workers in higher-AI-exposure jobs are least likely to report no recent training [p638][p904].

98.text: Factors include strong gender segregation in green, digital and labour-shortage occupations and male dominance of “transforming sectors”: women were only 20% of the “transforming sectors” workforce and 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023, while renewable energy had 32% women vs 22% in oil and gas, and solar PV 40% vs wind 21% [p6][p876]. Only 14% of shortage occupations are gender-balanced, and women make up just 28% of green-task jobs; future-oriented green new/enhanced/in-demand occupations with intermediate to low digital skills are almost exclusively male [p876]. This produces segregated workplaces: about 80% of workers in future-oriented green shortage occupations with intermediate to low digital skills report fewer than half of colleagues are women, and 36% report no or nearly no women colleagues [p877].

99.text: In 2023, the EU employment rate rose by 1.7 pp for older workers (55–64) to 63.9%, compared with a 0.4 pp rise for young workers (15–24) to 35.2% [p72]. Over 2019–2023, the older-worker employment rate increased by 5.3 pp, versus 1.7 pp for younger workers [p72]. 103.text: The green transition is expected to transform specific “transforming sectors”—mining and quarrying, manufacturing, electricity/gas/steam and air conditioning, water supply/waste, construction, and transportation/storage—affecting labour demand, skills, occupations and wages and prompting sectoral transitions [p24][p2]. In the EU, year-on-year sector-to-sector transition rates fall between 1.8–3.9 and are relatively stable, with a slight increase around 2016 in some Member States; from 2018–2019 there was a net inflow of workers into all transforming sectors except mining and extraction [p24]. Older workers make fewer sectoral transitions than younger workers, no significant difference is observed between men and women, but women remain underrepresented—26.7% in energy industries in 2023 and 14% in mining [p24]. CEDEFOP projects that by 2050 the European Green Deal may lead to large relative employment increases in water supply/waste management, construction, and wholesale/retail trade and decreases in coke/refined petroleum, gas/steam/air conditioning, and mining [p2].

109.text: Austria and France show regional income convergence: their absolute income disparities decreased [p105], and low-income regions were catching up with high-income regions (beta coefficients -0.02 for Austria, 2014-2021, and -0.01 for France, 2014-2021) [p106]. By contrast, Czechia and Sweden showed a rise in absolute income disparities, i.e. divergence [p105], and neither had robust evidence of catching-up [p106]; Czechia’s standard deviation increased by 20% between 2007 and 2022 [p105]. These differences are closely related to metropolitan versus non-metropolitan income growth: in converging countries metropolitan regions generally had slower median income growth than non-metropolitan regions, while in Sweden Stockholm was among the regions with the highest median income growth and growth was lowest in non-metropolitan Södermanland and Kronoberg [p106].

116.text: Voucher systems’ impact on undeclared domestic work is generally low (AT, BE, EL), and in Austria vouchers are scarcely used [p286], although Austrian household service vouchers formalised 1.55 million working hours in 2006–2013 [p188]. In Belgium, a 2018 study estimated that less than 10% of domestic work paid via vouchers used to be undeclared [p286], while 2021 research found service vouchers halved undeclared work in covered activities, mainly due to competitive formal-market pricing [p188]. Tax incentives’ impact varies: Germany reports little effect, whereas Spain’s 2011 introduction increased declared domestic workers over the following two years before plateauing [p287]. Tax incentives are regressive—German relief rises with taxable household income and non/low taxpayers benefit little or not at all, and in Sweden the highest income decile received 40% of the total tax deduction [p287]; coverage also differs because vouchers can be combined with tax incentives (BE, FR, HR, LU, SE) and may be limited by marginal-employment thresholds (AT), while tax deductions range from 5% in Portugal to 20% in most Member States using them [p285].

121.text: Digital transformation in European PES is being pursued through further digitalised, data-driven and personalised services building on AI and partnerships [p1057], including digital matching tools, AI job matching practices, and PES digital services to integrate vulnerable jobseekers [p1050]. 123.text: Workers in energy-intensive industries (EII) are relatively male-dominated and show high labour-market stability: from 2014–2023 they had higher year-to-year employment retention and fewer transitions into inactivity/unemployment than the total economy [p13]. Women remain underrepresented in “transforming sectors,” with only 26.7% female workers in energy industries in 2023 and 14% in mining [p24]. Training participation in EII reached 10.9% in 2023, still below the EU whole-economy average of 12.7%, indicating a skills-investment gap for the transition [p15].

17.text: Gender disparities shape EU labour-market trends because the “transforming sectors” are male-dominated: women made up only 20% of their workforce, just 14% of mining in 2022, and 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023, though the gap is smallest in Lithuania and Bulgaria at 31% [p6]. Expected job losses in mining and gains in construction/waste management therefore fall disproportionately on men, while women’s underrepresentation limits their access to emerging clean-energy jobs; increasing women’s employment in clean energy is described as key to a gender-neutral transition [p6]. Men in male-dominated sectors also make fewer transitions to non-employment due to lower caring responsibilities, although no significant gender difference is found in sector-to-sector transition frequency [p25][p12].

Access to social protection also varies across Member States and worker categories, with coverage gaps for non-standard workers [p531].
