By contrast, green in-demand jobs and green/digital occupations experiencing labour shortages have above-average job strain, and only 50% of workers in residual labour-shortage and green in-demand jobs could accurately predict earnings over the next three months [p906]. Access to learning is higher in higher digital-skills-intensity occupations, around average in residual green jobs, and lowest for workers in labour-shortage jobs [p888].

24.text: PES support the green transition by smoothing job-to-job transitions and helping jobseekers and employers move into green industries with relevant skills, but they face challenges defining “green jobs” due to no common agreement and insufficient internal capacity; over a third of PES have a green-jobs definition, while a minority differentiate green skills, tasks and competencies [p1033]. For third-country recruitment, an increasing number of PES are actively involved, often under bilateral mobility agreements, though their role depends on national mandates and most schemes are demand- or employer-driven with a job offer as a precondition [p1033]. PES there mainly perform administrative tasks such as admission decisions, work permits and labour-market tests, and face challenges in identifying shortage occupations, providing reliable work-permit and qualification-recognition information, and cooperating with migration authorities [p1033][p1034].

25.text: The 2022 TCN inflow into the EU/EFTA reached 3,324,000, a 133% increase, largely attributed to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine [p446][p444]. In Central Europe, Czechia’s TCN share rose to 94%, with Ukrainian inflows increasing from 32,000 in 2021 to 308,000 in 2022, while Slovenia’s and Croatia’s high TCN shares reflected longer-term trends rather than being significantly driven by the Ukrainian conflict [p453]. In Western Europe, several countries also saw notable TCN-share increases between 2021 and 2022, such as Germany (+28 pps), Ireland (+24 pps), and Portugal (+24 pps), though Germany did not report specific data for Ukrainian nationals [p453][p444].

26.text: Female EU movers are much more likely than male EU movers to work part-time—about 36% versus 8%, a 28-percentage-point gap—with the highest female mover rates in Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%) [p493]. The report says this may be explained by inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493].

27.text: The EU’s 2030 headline employment rate target is 78% [p658].

The pages attribute these differences to varying labour-market conditions and economic structures, noting that in low-incidence countries part-time work may be more a choice than a necessity [p489].

31.text: Strong nominal wage growth reached a record 6.1% in 2023, after 4.9% in 2022, but real wages still fell by 3.9% in 2022 and by 0.4% in 2023 as a whole [p785][p790]. As inflation fell, real wage growth turned positive in the second half of 2023 and reached 2.4% year-on-year in Q2 2024, while nominal wage growth moderated to 5.0% [p785][p790]. Despite this rebound, real wages in 2024 were still forecast to be 1.1% below their 2019 level in the EU [p791][p715].

32.text: In Sweden, the 20–34 share fell 1 pp to 60% in 2022, while 35–49 and 50–64 each rose 1 pp to 30% and 11%; counts rose from 3k to 15k, 2k to 7k, and 2k to 3k [p377]. In Switzerland, the 20–34 share fell 2 pp to 57%, 35–49 rose 1 pp to 32%, and 50–64 stayed at 11%, with counts rising to 50k, 27k, and 10k respectively [p377]. These are modest, mixed shifts, so they do not overturn the broader pattern of rising EU/EFTA inflows—859,000 in 2021 to 976,000 in 2022—or the continued dominance of 20–34-year-olds in many countries [p443][p458].

33.text: The projected increase is **8.8 million** economically active people aged **55–68** in the EU by 2030, comprising **6.0 million** aged 55–64 and **2.8 million** aged 65–68 [p833][p737].

The report concludes that both female and male workers experience approximately the same level of higher occupational AI exposure, but at a more granular level gender segregation persists in certain high-AI-exposure jobs, including in health, finance, and statistics [p905].

37.text: Countries with high part-time employment can have lower underemployment because part-time work is more often voluntary: involuntary part-time rates are low in the Netherlands (3%), Denmark and Germany (6%), Switzerland (7%) and Austria (8%), where part-time may be “more as a choice than a necessity” [p489]. This suggests labour-market preferences and institutional/cultural norms—such as work-life balance and flexible-work policies—shape whether part-time work is desired, while national underemployment also depends on acceptability, pay gaps, reconciliation options and taxation [p489][p848][p853].

Real wage growth was expected to exceed 5% in Bulgaria, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland and Romania in 2024 [p791].

By contrast, the Baltic countries, Bulgaria, Croatia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Poland and Romania experienced strong wage and ULC growth with the energy crisis, and Luxembourg, Hungary, Romania and Slovakia showed weakening external positions and/or export-market-share losses [p805]. High wage growth has raised cost-competitiveness concerns in Bulgaria, Estonia, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary and Romania, reducing scope for further wage increases unless productivity growth accelerates [p726].

The page gives gender percentages at the occupational-group level, not for each individual occupation within them [p877].

44.text: Older workers make fewer sectoral transitions than younger workers in all Member States [p24], and older workers receive the least training across the “transforming sectors” [p25]. This age pattern can make reallocation and reskilling into new green industries harder, especially given already low training participation in key sectors—only 10.9% of energy-intensive-industry workers received training in 2023 versus 12.7% economy-wide [p25].

45.text: Digital-intensive jobs have a higher share of young workers—about one in four aged 15–29—and a lower share aged 55–64, while for intermediate-to-low digital skills the younger and older shares are roughly equal [p881]. In contrast, residual green occupations have a lower share of workers aged 15–29, and less digitally intensive new/emerging/enhanced green jobs have higher shares aged 56+ [p881][p880]. Figure 6 shows, for example, higher-digital occupations (DH) at 23% aged 25–34 and 15% aged 56+, versus GEDI green jobs at 20% aged 25–34, 32% aged 45–54 and 19% aged 56+ [p881].

46.text: EU labour-market resilience amid the slowdown was supported by strong labour supply: labour force growth accelerated from 0.3% per year in 2015-2019 to nearly 1% in 2022 and 2023, with non-EU nationals contributing 1.24 million to the 2023 rise of almost 2 million [p704][p752]. Improved job matching, reflected in low long-term unemployment, also helped, while firms retained more workers than needed, i.e. labour hoarding [p704][p71]. Labour demand eased from 4% growth in Q1 2022 to 0.7% in Q4 2023, but supply kept increasing and stable low unemployment likely reflected improved matching [p752].

47.text: Yes. The EU unemployment rate reached a record low of 5.7% in February 2025 [p864], below the 6.1% rate in 2023 [p66], indicating a tighter labour market than in 2023.

48.text: The 2024 Action Plan on labour and skills shortages sets out 87 new actions across five domains: activating under-represented people, supporting skills/training/education, improving working conditions, enhancing fair intra-EU mobility, and attracting talent from outside the EU [p635]. Specific measures include the EU Talent Pool to match non-EU jobseekers with shortage occupations, the European Skills Agenda’s individual learning accounts and micro-credentials, and efforts to raise participation among older workers, women, and young people not in education, employment or training [p771].

49.text: Denmark and Poland have abolished mandatory retirement ages as a valid reason to terminate labour contracts, while the Netherlands screens job vacancy notices for discriminatory language under its “vacancies for all ages” initiative [p839]. Belgium and Estonia have programmes in which training providers assess applicants’ competence by validating previous relevant experience, and France’s Public Employment Service selects candidates for employer interviews based on aptitude tests without regard to age or previously held employment [p839].

51.text: Yes. The report projects an EU increase of 6 million active people aged 55–64 and 2.8 million aged 65–68 by 2030, mostly due to ageing and already adopted pension reforms [p737]. It also notes that France and Sweden are among Member States that raised statutory retirement ages since 2020, and Sweden allows phased retirement and deferral to a higher age [p836].

52.text: The difference is 10 percentage points: 96% of EU movers in healthcare had permanent contracts in 2023, compared with 86% of nationals [p394].

53.text: Workers in green jobs facing labour shortages have above-average job strain, whereas digital-intensive roles have the lowest job strain at 16% [p887][p891][p906]. For earnings predictability, only 50% of workers in green in-demand jobs and residual labour-shortage occupations can accurately predict their earnings over the next three months, while predictability is highest in occupations with higher digital skills intensity [p906].

54.text: Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a permanent-contract share 4 percentage points above the EU average of 69.7%, i.e. about 73.7% [p884]. Occupations with higher digital skills intensity have the highest share, shown as 79%, compared with the same EU average of 69.7% [p883][p884].

55.text: In 2023, employment rates for older workers aged 55–64 were above 70% in Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Latvia, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden, but below 55% in Greece, Croatia, Luxembourg, Romania and Slovenia [p821]. The largest increases since 2009, around 30 pps, were observed in Hungary, Poland and Slovenia for ages 55–59 and in Denmark, Hungary and Slovakia for ages 60–64 [p821].

56.text: EU movers show robust labour-market outcomes across age groups; the oldest cohort’s activity rate is 77% for EU movers versus 66% for third-country nationals [p494]. On part-time work, EU movers consistently had around 21–22% part-time employment from 2018 to 2023, while third-country nationals declined from 26% in 2018 to 22% in 2023 [p487]. Among EU movers in 2023, 36% of employed women worked part-time versus 8% of men, a 28-percentage-point gap, compared with a 20-point gap for nationals [p493].

57.text: Under the static scenario, the EU labour force is projected to decline by about **42.8 million people by 2070** [p1011].

58.text: A population equivalent to 10% of Estonia’s nurse population is residing and working in other EU Member States or EFTA countries [p343].

60.text: No. Figure 6 shows that Member States were divided by summer 2024: with only a few PES having begun introducing ILA schemes, while others had no ILA but plans, no plans, or did not submit feedback [p1032].

61.text: Strong gender segregation persists in digitalisation, decarbonisation and labour-shortage occupations: women make up just 28% of green-task jobs and are underrepresented in ICT [p876]. Causes include disproportionate care responsibilities—7.7 million women in the EU are outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men—and a STEM skills gap [p931]. Women also perform more tasks prone to automation and are overrepresented in sectors exposed to AI, while green-transition job shifts affect male-dominated mining, engineering, construction and energy [p876][p931]. Policy actions should identify green/digital skills and provide effective future-fit training and retraining, tackle the digital divide and ensure fair ICT access across groups and SMEs, and treat care responsibilities as a top priority, noting that higher women’s labour-market participation is associated with a 10% reduction in unemployment [p936][p931].

62.text: Yes. The fixed-term contract gap between EU movers and nationals narrowed from 5 pps in 2018 to 3 pps in 2023, as EU movers fell from 19% to 14% and nationals from 14% to 11% [p485].

63.text: The rise was largely driven by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine: the inflow of third-country nationals doubled between 2021 and 2022 to 3,324,000, a 133% increase [p444]. The sharp 2022 increase is attributed to the significant influx of people fleeing the war [p459].

64.text: From 2019 to 2023, the employment rate (15–64) rose from 56.5% to 61.8% in Greece (+5.3 pps) [p722] and from 70.5% to 72.5% in Portugal (+2.0 pps) [p738].

65.text: The PES Network shares knowledge through digital channels such as the PES Knowledge Centre, where 3 new PESPod episodes were released in 2024 [p1051], and through the PES Practice Repository, which published practices including EVADES and AI Job Matching from Spain and cost-effective indicators from Poland by December 2024 [p1050]. It also runs a Digitalisation Working Group chaired by NL [p1050], and a Working Group on evidence-based service design explored how digital tools and AI can support jobseekers’ online job search behaviour [p1038].

66.text: Among returning health workers, Italy’s full-time share fell from 100% in 2018 to 69% in 2023, while part-time rose from 0% to 31% [p430]. The Netherlands moved in the opposite direction: full-time rose from 0% in 2018 to 38% in 2023, with part-time falling from 100% to 62% [p430]. Thus Italy remained majority full-time in 2023, whereas the Netherlands remained majority part-time; all these values are marked as low reliability [p430].

67.text: Digitalisation and AI deepen platform-work vulnerability by enabling algorithmic management and surveillance that widen power imbalances between platforms and workers, while platform work is marked by low wages, lack of social protection, and impacts on vulnerable groups [p925]. In the EU, platform-economy revenues grew almost fivefold between 2016 and 2020, more than 28 million people were estimated to work through digital labour platforms in 2020, 5.5 million were estimated to be incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earned less than the minimum wage [p552]. Algorithmic systems used by platform companies create regulatory needs around ethical, fair and transparent management and human oversight [p944]. Vulnerable workers also include those in non-standard employment and “false” self-employment, who often face challenges in pay, working conditions, job security and social benefits [p927].

68.text: No. Evidence is mixed: in Austria and Germany the estimated share of undeclared workers is 90% or more in the non-care sector and significantly lower in care-related services, and in Malta undeclared work is much more likely in non-care domestic work [p283]. However, Italy reported an even distribution across both sectors in 2022, while Bulgaria’s LTC sector and Ireland’s informal home care sector show undeclared work as predominant in care-related work [p283].

70.text: The report’s approach combines productivity growth with activation of untapped labour potential: it cites possible contributions of 8 million people aged 20–29, 12 million aged 55–64, and 17 million women [p1023]. It adds a dynamic perspective by combining labour force participation rates with demographic projections for 2021–2070, accounting for women’s emancipation, educational profile changes, and migration assumptions [p1023][p1022]. It concludes that skills investment cannot compensate for demographic decline but can mitigate worker reductions, and that harnessing all activation potential—moving to Swedish participation rates—could almost fully offset ageing effects [p1017]; related policies include fair wages, skills, integration of women, young people, persons with disabilities and migrants, childcare, long-term care, and flexible retirement pathways [p787].

71.text: EU sector-to-sector transition rates mostly fell between 1.8% and 3.9%, remained relatively stable over 2010–2019, and showed a slight upward trend around 2016 in some Member States [p7]. From 2018–2019, all “transforming sectors” except mining/extraction experienced net inflows of workers, while mining was the only transforming sector with a net outflow [p9][p24]. Older workers make fewer sectoral transitions than younger workers, with no significant difference between men and women [p24]. The analysis treats 2019 as the main reference year because 2020 results may be sensitive to COVID-19, and the retrospective transition question was discontinued from the LFS after that [p3].

74.text: ILO Convention C189 had been ratified by nine EU Member States: Belgium, Germany, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Malta, Portugal and Sweden [p255]. The ratification years listed are Italy and Germany 2013; Ireland 2014; Belgium, Finland and Portugal 2015; Sweden 2019; Malta 2021; and Spain 2023 [p304].

75.text: Nine EU Member States have ratified ILO Convention C189 [p231][p304], while eight Member States apply the same labour law and social protection rules to domestic workers as to other workers without distinction [p231]. The summary table lists the eight as BG, CZ, DK, EE, HR, LT, LV and SK [p261].

76.text: AI-exposed occupations have below-average job strain and are among the lowest-strain groups, while labour-shortage occupations report the highest job strain among occupations of interest, at 48% [p887][p891][p906]. For training, AI-exposed occupations have the lowest share of workers who received no education or training in the preceding four weeks, whereas access to learning at the workplace is lowest for workers in labour-shortage jobs [p904][p888].

77.text: Leading EU countries combine high training participation with stronger older-worker transitions: in 2022 over half of older people trained in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Sweden [p827], and Denmark—where older people completed about 20% more training hours than the EU 25–64 average—had the highest unemployment-to-employment transition rate at more than 30% [p828]. Lagging countries show the opposite: less than 15% of older people trained in Bulgaria, Greece, Poland and Romania in 2022 [p827], and older individuals in Bulgaria, Greece, Romania and Slovakia transitioned from unemployment to employment at below 10% per quarter [p828]. Adult-learning data also place Sweden (66.5%), Hungary (62.2%), the Netherlands (56.1%) and Germany (53.7%) highest in 2022, versus Bulgaria (9.5%), Greece (15.1%), Poland (20.3%) and Czechia (21.2%) lowest [p653].

78.text: Converging to Sweden’s labour force participation rates by age, sex, and education would almost completely offset the projected negative impact of ageing on EU labour supply, reducing the expected labour force decline to only 2.8 pp, or 5.9 million people, by 2070 [p1012]. Combining all forms of activation through the Swedish scenario would therefore almost fully compensate for the workforce decline [p1013].

79.text: In 2022, EU public expenditure on education was distributed as follows: pre-primary and primary education 34%, secondary education 36.8%, and tertiary education 16.6% [p130]. School education overall received over 70% of public spending on education [p130].

81.text: In Bulgaria, 35.5% of individuals aged 16–74 had basic or above basic overall digital skills in 2023, compared with 55.6% in the EU [p548][p581].

82.text: Belgium and Poland are examples where statutory minimum wage increases translated into real growth: real statutory minimum wages rose by more than 10% between January 2022 and January 2024 [p640]. By contrast, Czechia and Slovakia saw real statutory minimum wages fall by more than 3% over the same period despite nominal increases [p640], and the decline is also noted through July 2024 [p796].

83.text: The report cautions that the “surplus” is only true when considering retirement replacement, assuming current doctor/nurse ratios are sufficient and retirement is the main reason for leaving the profession—neither always holds [p340]. It also notes low or fluctuating densities and retention/attraction problems, with EU-mover and returnee inflows not clearly sufficient to offset outflows [p340][p358]. Statistical underrepresentation of EU movers in healthcare, including legally ambiguous live-in care, can further obscure workforce needs [p334].

84.text: Based on EU-SILC data, minimum wage non-compliance is estimated to affect more than 8% of the workforce in Germany, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Lithuania, Hungary, Portugal and Sweden [p797]. The workers most affected are young people, unskilled workers, women, workers in smaller firms and part-time workers; they are generally younger, less educated, more likely to be female, on fixed-term or part-time contracts, and employed by smaller firms [p797].

85.text: Labour market transitions can support the green transition by moving workers out of shrinking or transforming sectors and into expanding sectors, helping avoid worsening labour shortages in affected areas such as construction and transportation [p46]. The “transforming sectors” include mining and quarrying, manufacturing, electricity/gas/steam/air conditioning, water/waste, construction, and transportation/storage, which face positive, neutral, or negative employment changes and changing skill/task demands [p2]. However, training and education are lagging in some key sectors, while additional wind and solar deployment would require about 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU, with skills investment of EUR 1.1–1.4 billion by 2030 [p12].

86.text: The pages attribute the high part-time rate among female EU movers—36% vs 8% for male EU movers in 2023, a 28-pp gap [p493]—to factors including inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493]. They also note that women are more likely than men to be employed on part-time and fixed-term contracts [p493]. Sectoral structure such as tourism/hospitality and high unemployment are cited for higher part-time rates among EU movers in Greece, Spain, France and Italy, but not specifically for the gender gap [p488].

87.text: No. The pages identify skills shortages as a bottleneck and note public-sector skills needs, particularly in public procurement [p921][p25], but they do not state that projected green-transition job growth is contingent on resolving public-sector skills shortages in clean energy.

88.text: Yes. Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a higher-than-average incidence of permanent employment, 4 percentage points above the average of 69.7% [p884].

89.text: Key factors are demographic ageing and a shrinking working-age population, alongside women’s emancipation, rising educational attainment, and differing migration assumptions [p1023][p818]. The Draghi report projects the EU workforce shrinking by close to 2 million workers each year by 2040 [p1023], while the EU labour force is expected to decline by 0.3% annually over the projection period [p818]. Proposed responses include activating untapped labour potential—8 million young people aged 20–29, 12 million people aged 55–64, and 17 million women [p1023]—plus pension reforms and policies supporting older workers, women, and low-skilled people toward the 78% EU employment target by 2030 [p818]. Investing in skills is also emphasized, though it can mitigate rather than compensate for demographic decline; moving to Swedish participation rates could almost fully offset ageing effects [p1022][p1017].

90.text: Women part-time workers are less likely to be underemployed (18%, and 16% among mothers of young children) than men, of whom only about 8% work part-time but more than a quarter of male part-timers want longer hours [p850]. Part-time workers living with a partner have lower underemployment (about 15%) than those living without a partner (26%) [p850]. Regression results show women and people living with partners have significantly lower underemployment probabilities than men and singles, by 8 pp or more, and these differences are not explained by occupational or sectoral patterns [p851]. The drivers differ: women’s lower underemployment reflects caring/time constraints and lack of care services, men’s higher underemployment reflects gendered earner attitudes and part-time being rarely preferred, while singles rely more on their own income and are more likely to prefer full-time work [p850].

91.text: Uneven digitalisation of businesses across Europe can widen the existing digital divide, hinder innovation and productivity, and feed workplace inequalities, with SME digital-technology uptake and digital intensity still insufficient and uneven [p924]. Digitalisation can self-reinforce social exclusion, while platformisation creates unequal, exploitative labour dynamics with low wages and no social protection for vulnerable groups; AI-enabled algorithmic management widens power imbalances between platforms and workers and creates “invisible” AI workers [p924][p925]. Labour-market polarisation means unskilled workers are more exposed to digitalisation while the skilled workforce benefits, although generative AI may significantly impact high-skilled workers and replace routine jobs [p925][p552]. In 2020, more than 28 million people were estimated to work through digital labour platforms, 5.5 million were estimated to be incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earned less than the minimum wage [p552].

92.text: Non-EU nationals accounted for 64.1% of the total increase in the EU labour force in 2023 [p755].

93.text: In 2022, 27% of EU movers were at risk of poverty and social exclusion (AROPE), compared with 46% of third-country nationals (TCNs) and 19% of nationals [p508]. EU movers also had a lower housing-cost overburden rate (19%) than TCNs (26%) [p504]. The provided pages do not identify factors explaining the EU-mover versus TCN gap; they only note that SILC-based TCN data include all non-EU citizens, including EFTA countries [p508].

94.text: Benchlearning supported PES modernisation through its 4th cycle, launched in January 2024, with 15 assessments covering the PES of Lithuania, Bulgaria, Latvia, Croatia, Austria, Portugal, Hungary, Germany, Greece, Czechia, Estonia, The Netherlands, Malta, Ireland, and Cyprus [p1045]. It uses an updated methodology emphasising greater flexibility, user-friendliness, and effectiveness, and systematically compares PES organisational setups and outcomes against an “ideal PES” via quantitative performance data plus self-, peer-, and expert review [p1045]. For example, the Estonian PES received practical tips from other PES on quality assessment and performance management (Austria), cooperation with employers (Lithuania), evaluation and decision support tools (Germany), labour demand barometer measures (Finland), and decision support tools (Belgium VDAB) [p1045].

96.text: Energy-intensive industries (EII) are less dynamic than the total economy: from 2014 to 2023, a higher share of EII workers remained employed year-to-year and EII saw fewer outflows into inactivity and unemployment [p13]. The pages attribute this lower mobility partly to the relatively male-dominated demographic profile of the EII workforce, and also to high labour-market stability in these sectors, which are described as relatively well-paid industries where wage premiums are reported [p13].

97.text: PES career guidance increasingly emphasizes digital skills (48% of countries), green skills (32%), and both (51%) [p1058]. This mirrors the digital transformation: EU ICT specialists rose 59.3% since 2013 to over 9.5 million in 2023, while 4 in 10 adults lack basic digital skills [p638]. It also mirrors the green transition, with the green economy’s workforce share rising from 2.2% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2021 and 1.8–3.9% of EU workers switching sectors annually [p638], while green investment is expected to yield a net increase of 2 million jobs by 2030 [p954].

98.text: Factors include persistent caregiving responsibilities (7.7 million EU women outside the labour market vs 450,000 men) and a STEM skills gap that hinders women’s entry into emerging green industries [p931], as well as strong gender segregation in green occupations, where women make up just 28% of green-task jobs [p876]. In the energy workforce, women were only 26.7% in 2023, with 32% in renewables vs 22% in oil and gas, and 40% in solar PV vs 21% in wind [p6]. Women also made up only 14% of mining workers in 2022 and 20% of the “transforming sectors” workforce, with the smallest gap in Lithuania and Bulgaria at 31% [p6].

99.text: In 2023, older workers (55–64) were a major contributor to EU employment growth: 41 million participated and 39 million were employed, with activity and employment rates of 67% and 63.9%, about 20 pps above 2009 [p819]. From 2019 to 2023, older workers remained the main driver of labour-force growth, adding about 1.2 million people yearly, while young workers’ labour force began growing again from 2021 and reached 19.3 million in 2023 versus 17.6 million in 2020 [p753]. The 2023 employment growth was also noted as driven by older workers aged 55–64 with secondary or tertiary education, alongside prime-age 25–54 workers with tertiary education [p617].

100.text: For wind and solar deployment, the associated investment in skills is projected at **EUR 1.1 to 1.4 billion by 2030** [p25][p21]. Separately, retraining, reskilling and upskilling in manufacturing of strategic net-zero technologies is estimated at **EUR 3.1 to 4.1 billion by 2030** [p138].

102.text: The countries reported with more than 15% of domestic care work undocumented are **Poland, Spain, and Italy** [p165]. The PHS Employment Monitor reports more than 15% in Poland and Spain and 35% in Italy [p165]; Spain also has estimates of 30–32% or 36%, and Italy’s 2023 estimate is about 47% [p165].

103.text: The green transition transforms key sectors—mining and quarrying, manufacturing, energy, water/waste, construction and transportation—affecting labour demand, skills, occupations and wages, and causing sectoral transitions [p24]. EU LFS data show average year-on-year sector-to-sector transition rates of 1.8–3.9 in the EU, and from 2018–2019 there was a net inflow of workers into all “transforming sectors” except mining and extraction [p24]. Older workers make fewer sectoral transitions than younger workers, no significant difference is observed between men and women, and women remain underrepresented—26.7% in energy industries in 2023 and 14% in mining—while energy-intensive workers make fewer transitions to non-employment than other sectors [p24]. Impacts vary within sectors: mining may lose workers, while by 2030 construction is expected to need more workers to install heat pumps or solar PVs and fewer gas fitters [p46].

104.text: The pages highlight workers with disabilities—especially women and young people with disabilities—as particularly vulnerable, with an EU employment rate of only 50.6% versus 74.8% for people without disabilities [p928]. They also identify vulnerable workers in precarious employment, self-employed individuals, those facing discrimination, unpaid care workers, and people in regional vulnerabilities [p926]. Workers in energy-intensive/fossil-fuel-dependent industries and their regions [p933], as well as skilled workers in transition industries [p946], are also highlighted.

105.text: Portugal has a specific legal regime for domestic service workers outside the Labour Code, but many still lack unemployment benefits because access requires a full-time monthly contract and not opting for the lower-contribution “agreed regime”; most work for several employers and opt for that regime [p177]. Portugal also amended its labour code in 2023 to better protect domestic workers and introduced 2023–2024 legislation on informal caregivers [p544]. In Hungary, carers’ situation is “not monitored at all,” and they lack access to workers’ representation and collective bargaining, social/legal protection and support, with exploitation common and no quality control [p177].

These figures are not cumulative because the three groups overlap [p818], so they cannot fully offset an annual loss of that scale.

109.text: Austria and France show absolute convergence and catching-up (beta coefficients -0.02 for Austria 2014-2021 and -0.01 for France 2014-2021), while Czechia and Sweden show rising absolute income disparities/divergence and no robust catching-up evidence (Czechia 2014-2022; Sweden 2014-2021) [p105][p106]. Relative median incomes converged in seven of nine countries, but Sweden was an exception; Czechia’s absolute dispersion rose yet relative dispersion declined because the increase was less than the cross-regional average median income [p106]. The difference is linked to metropolitan vs non-metropolitan income growth: in converging countries metropolitan median income growth was slower than in non-metropolitan regions, e.g. Austria’s slow growth in Graz, Innsbruck, Linz-Wels, Salzburg und Umgebung, and Vienna, whereas in Sweden Stockholm had among the highest median income growth and Södermanland and Kronoberg the lowest [p106].

111.text: Undeclared care workers lack legal protection and social protection, including in case of unemployment or illness, and are at high risk of exploitation [p177][p194]. They are also paid less than declared workers in similar jobs, while declared workers are entitled to labour rights plus additional compensation such as overtime pay and paid leave [p193]. Evidence also indicates care workers are more likely to have temporary contracts and to be undeclared, depriving them of legal guarantees and social protection [p177].

113.text: Evidence on the actual workforce impact of Individual Learning Accounts (ILAs) is limited. The Commission states that ILA initiatives, as flagship actions of the European Skills Agenda, “will foster the acquisition of competences and increase the participation of adults in education and training, thus improving the matching of skills and jobs” [p771]. As of summer 2024, however, only a few PES had begun introducing ILA schemes, and a thematic report was due in 2025 [p1032]. 116.text: Voucher systems are direct, traceable instruments but are implemented differently and can be inefficient against under-declared work when capped at the marginal-employment threshold (AT); their impact is generally low in AT, BE and EL, though a 2018 Belgian study estimated that less than 10% of domestic work paid via vouchers used to be undeclared [p285][p286]. Tax incentives are also direct financing tools, often linked to vouchers (BE, FR, HR, IT, LT, RO, SE) or administrative simplification (DE, LU), with deductions of 5% in Portugal versus 20% in most Member States using them; effects vary, with little effect in Germany but an increase in declared domestic workers in Spain after their 2011 introduction, since plateaued [p285][p287]. France’s CESU shows the strongest documented reduction, with informal employment falling from about 50% in 1996 to 20% in 2015 (28% in 2005 and 25% in 2011), while 77% of employer families said in 2024 they would resort to undeclared work or forgo services without the system’s tax incentives [p187]. Equity impacts differ: tax incentives are regressive—German relief rises with taxable household income, Sweden’s top income decile received 40% of total tax deduction in 2020, and France’s tax advantages mainly benefited the top 10%—and low deduction thresholds may fail to incentivise regularisation (AT, DE), whereas vouchers could be extended to more professions in Belgium [p287][p187][p311].

123.text: Workers in energy-intensive industries (EII) are relatively male-dominated and show high labour-market stability: from 2014–2023 in the EU27 they had consistently higher employment-to-employment transitions and fewer outflows into inactivity/unemployment than the total economy, partly linked to relatively well-paid industries with wage premiums [p13]. Women remain heavily underrepresented in the “transforming sectors,” with only 26.7% female workers in energy industries in 2023 and 14% in mining [p24]. For the green transition, this stability is positive for job security, but high-carbon jobs face higher displacement risks—20% higher odds of unemployment—and workers changing employment often move to another emission-intensive occupation, so re-skilling, up-skilling and employment support are needed [p14].

152.text: The ERA4FutureWork initiative was launched by the European Commission to foster stakeholder dialogue and identify R&I priorities, with four workshops covering the green transition and working life, the digital world of work, the twin transitions and vulnerable groups, and the future of work in EU public administrations [p949]. 154.text: The EU27 labour market shows an ageing workforce through rising participation and employment of people aged 55–64: in 2023, 41 million participated and 39 million were employed, with activity and employment rates of 67% and 63.9%, almost 20 pps higher than in 2009 [p819]. Yet older workers remain underrepresented, with activity and employment rates still 20 and 18 pps below prime-age workers [p726], while the EU labour force is projected to decline by 0.3% per year until 2070 despite older-worker employment rising from 62.3% in 2022 to 72.3% in 2070 [p818].

155.text: Men in the EU work part-time less often than women partly because gendered attitudes identify men as primary earners and women as primary caretakers; nearly half of the EU population holds attitudes that at least partly support this distribution of paid and unpaid work [p850]. These attitudes help explain why men take up part-time work less often than women and, when they do, are less likely to see it as a desired choice [p850].

157.text: Care allowances are typically financial benefits or payments made to either carers or care recipients; they can be “unbound,” allowing beneficiaries to spend the resources freely, or “bound,” requiring documentation of how funds are spent [p185]. They are increasingly used as an instrument to fight undeclared care work by formalising care relationships and providing financial incentives to declare care work [p185].

The share of households in financial distress fell from a peak of 17.5% in August 2023 to 15.7% by March 2025, 1.3 pp lower than March 2024 [p844]. Longer term, real GDHI per capita rose 11.8% from EUR 15,450 in 2014 to EUR 17,283 in 2022 [p89], and the EU GDHI per capita index stood at 111.1 in 2023, 0.6 points higher than in 2022 [p689].

177.text: A comprehensive policy mix is needed: active support for quality employment and education (including underrepresented groups), hiring incentives in greener parts of the economy, fair tax-benefit and social protection systems, and better working conditions [p26]; this should be paired with reskilling/upskilling, job-to-job transitions, quality employment and integration of underrepresented groups [p44].
