16.text: Gender segregation persists in future-oriented work: ICT and higher-digital-intensity occupations are male-dominated, with women underrepresented, while critical labour-shortage and care occupations have higher shares of women [p876][p905]. The report notes that greater gender parity in these occupations could boost labour-market participation in jobs relevant to the digital and green transitions [p905]. Unequal training access compounds this: EU adult learning rose only from 37.4% in 2016 to 39.5% in 2022, and only 55.6% had at least basic digital skills in 2023 [p585]. Women also lag in STEM skills, and 7.7 million women remain outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men, limiting long-term adaptability [p931].

17.text: Gender disparities are significant in the EU’s “transforming sectors,” where women are only 20% of the workforce, 14% of mining workers in 2022, and 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023 [p6]. Because expected job losses are mainly in male-dominated sectors such as mining, but employment gains are also expected in male-represented construction and waste management, women may not automatically benefit; increasing women’s employment in clean energy is therefore key [p6]. Care responsibilities also keep 7.7 million women outside the labour market versus 450,000 men, and women’s STEM skills gap may hinder participation in emerging green and digital industries [p931].

18.text: EU mobile workers may face challenges accessing quality employment at the same level as natives that can provide a decent income [p512]. In-work poverty reflects the quality of employment and adequacy of wages [p511], and differences may also be shaped by movers’ characteristics such as education, skills, or employment sectors interacting with national labour-market circumstances [p510].

19.text: The approach is human-centric: it aims to ensure innovation serves workers’ needs and values and does not dictate how they work, involves workers early in the design and application of new technologies, and promotes physical and mental well-being by examining the effects of AI and virtual worlds [p953]. It also stresses workers’ participation in technology implementation and regulatory protections against algorithmic management without human oversight and lack of transparency [p937]. The executive summary similarly frames this stream as involving workers in new technology design and application while promoting well-being and mental health in the workplace [p950].

20.text: In EU “transforming sectors,” 2018–2019 saw a net inflow of workers into all except mining and extraction [p24]. Workers in “energy-intensive industries” make fewer transitions to non-employment than other sectors, attributed to higher trade union density and male dominance reducing inactivity from caring responsibilities [p12]. Older workers make fewer sectoral transitions, with no significant male-female difference in transitions, though women remain underrepresented—26.7% in energy industries in 2023 and 14% in mining [p24]. Training participation is high in energy but low in mining and construction, high-carbon jobs face 20% higher odds of unemployment, and retraining costs vary with country labour costs, around EUR 1 per labour-force person in Bulgaria and Hungary in 2030 [p14][p24].

21.text: In 2022, 58.9% of high-qualified adults participated in learning, compared with only 18.4% of low-qualified adults, meaning the high-qualified were more than three times as likely to participate [p653]. This gap widened slightly from 2016, when the rates were 58.1% and 17.9% respectively [p653].

22.text: Between 2021 and 2022, EU movers’ net mobility rose 21%, from 296,000 to 358,000, while third-country nationals’ net mobility jumped from 556,000 to 2,456,000 [p449]. EU/EFTA inflows of EU movers increased from 859,000 to 976,000 [p393], whereas inflows of third-country nationals rose much more sharply, from 1,426,000 to 3,324,000 [p396].

23.text: Digital-intensive future-oriented occupations show more stable employment: permanent employment is highest in occupations with higher digital skills [p883], over 90% work full-time and part-time is far below the EU average of 17.7% in 2021 [p884], and earnings predictability is highest in higher-digital-skills and AI-exposed occupations [p884]. Green-focused occupations are more mixed: self-employment is uncommon except in less digitally intensive enhanced green jobs (9% with employees, 10% solo) and residual green jobs (11% and 22%) [p882], permanent employment is lowest in GNE at 53% [p883], and only about 50% in green in-demand jobs can accurately predict earnings in the next three months [p882]. Part-time work is nevertheless lowest in green new/emerging/enhanced jobs with labour shortages (6%) and green in-demand jobs with labour shortages (7.5%) [p884].

24.text: For the green transition, PES are expected to smooth the transition and support jobseekers and employers moving to green industries with relevant skills, but defining green jobs is challenging: over a third of PES have a definition, and a minority differentiate green skills, tasks and competencies [p1033]. Current examples include Portugal’s PES protocol with the Renewable Energies Association in June 2023 for a Training Centre for Energy Transition, training around 25 000 persons in green skills, and Greece’s PES programme launched in September 2024 for green skills for 50 000 employees with RRF support [p671]. For third-country workers, attracting talent is increasingly important, but most schemes are demand- or employer-driven and PES often perform administrative tasks such as admission decisions, work permits, labour market tests and working conditions, although more PES now actively recruit outside the EU, often under bilateral mobility agreements and depending on their mandate [p1033]. The third-country role also requires labour-market intelligence to identify shortage occupations and reliable multilingual information on work permits, qualification recognition and jobs, coordinated with ministries and migration authorities [p1033][p1034].

25.text: The pages show the Ukraine conflict drove a large overall TCN inflow, which doubled between 2021 and 2022 to 3,324,000 (+133%) [p444][p446]. In Central Europe, Czechia’s TCN share reached 94% and Ukrainian inflow rose from 32,000 in 2021 to 308,000 in 2022, while Poland hosted 957,505 Ukrainian refugees and had a substantial TCN net inflow due to the war [p453][p446][p455]. For Western Europe, the pages do not give a full comparison; they note Germany’s TCN share rose 28 pps, but Germany and Poland did not report specific Ukrainian-national data [p453][p444].

26.text: The report attributes the higher part-time prevalence among female EU movers to inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493]. It also points to flexible-work policies and cultural/social norms around work-life balance, particularly for women balancing work and family responsibilities [p489]. For example, female EU movers’ part-time rates are 47% in Switzerland, 45% in Austria and 44% in Germany, while male EU movers’ rates are 12%, 14% and 9%, respectively [p493].

27.text: The EU’s 2030 employment rate target is at least 78% of the working-age population [p704][p621].

28.text: Nine EU Member States have ratified ILO Convention C189: BE, DE, ES, FI, IE, IT, MT, PT, and SE [p255][p261].

29.text: Involuntary part-time employment is most prevalent in Bulgaria (60%), Romania (60%), Italy (58%), Spain (51%) and Greece (48%) in 2022 [p489]; in 2023, Romania, Italy and Spain recorded the highest shares, above 50% [p675]. The pages attribute these differences to varying labour-market conditions and economic structures, noting that in low-incidence countries part-time work may be more a choice than a necessity [p489].

31.text: Strong nominal wage growth reached a record 6.1% in 2023 and was still 5.0% in Q2-2024 [p785][p715]. As inflation eased, real wage growth turned positive in Q3-2023 and reached 2.4% year-on-year in Q2-2024 (1.8% in the euro area), after earlier real-wage losses [p715][p790]. Despite this rebound, real wages in 2024 were forecast to remain 1.1% below their 2019 EU level and below pre-pandemic levels in eight Member States [p715][p530].

33.text: The projected increase is **8.8 million** economically active older people aged **55 to 68** in the EU by **2030** [p840][p833].

34.text: Declining PISA scores are described as posing a major risk to the EU’s future labour productivity and competitiveness [p648], with potential negative impacts on EU competitiveness and wage developments in the longer term [p131]. The deterioration in basic skills can also adversely affect labour productivity and EU competitiveness, hindering wage developments over time [p64]. The pages do not quantify a direct effect on long-term economic growth.

35.text: EU-LFS 2021 data show that occupations with higher AI exposure are broadly gender-balanced, with a slightly higher share of job holders being women (52%), and EWCTS data reveal similar findings [p878]. However, women remain underrepresented in occupations with the highest AI exposure, and gender segregation persists in certain high-AI-exposure jobs, even though female and male workers experience approximately the same level of higher occupational AI exposure overall [p878][p905].

37.text: The pages note there is no clear link between national part-time employment levels and underemployment among part-timers; underemployment is somewhat more common where part-time work is a lower share of employment [p847]. National underemployment depends on a complex mix including acceptability of part-time work, institutional settings, part-time/full-time pay gaps, work-family reconciliation options, and household taxation [p848]. This suggests that in countries where part-time work is common and accepted, it may more often reflect preferred working-time arrangements rather than constrained lack of full-time work [p848][p853].

38.text: In 2023, the EU employment rate for women rose to **70.2%**, while the rate for men was 80.4%, leaving a gender employment gap of 10.2 pp [p72].

40.text: Luxembourg’s real wages decreased by 1.4 pps in Q2 2024, after a strong rebound in 2023 [p791][p639]. By contrast, central and eastern Member States generally had relatively strong real wage growth—except Slovenia and, to a lesser extent, Czechia—and 2024 growth was expected to exceed 5% in Bulgaria, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland and Romania [p791]. The compensation-per-employee PPS graph includes Luxembourg alongside these countries, but the provided text gives no numerical PPS comparison [p815].

41.text: The Network has worked to enhance co-operation between PES since 2014 [p1055], so by the 2024 Annual Report (published January 2025 [p1029]) it had been operational for about 10 years.

42.text: Southern European countries experienced moderate wage growth below the benchmarks predicted by macroeconomic drivers, alongside cost-competitiveness gains, suggesting some remaining room for wage increases [p808][p801]. By contrast, central and eastern European countries showed dynamic wage and ULC growth and competitiveness losses, with concerns for Bulgaria, Czechia, Estonia, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia [p805][p801]. Higher productivity growth is needed to sustain stronger wage growth [p808].

43.text: At the grouping level, Figure 3 shows the green increased-demand group (GDDI) is male-dominated at about **73% men**, and the green new/emerging group (GNDI) is male-dominated at about **66% men** [p877]. The pages do not list individual occupations within these green groupings, only these aggregate categories [p877].

44.text: Age-based mobility matters: in all Member States, older workers make fewer sector-to-sector transitions than younger workers [p24], and older workers receive the least training across “transforming sectors” [p25]. Since the green transition is expected to require sectoral labour transitions and reskilling in these sectors [p24][p25], lower mobility and training among older workers can make it harder to move labour into new green industries. The median age in transforming sectors is around 43–46 across the EU27, varying by sector and Member State [p35].

45.text: Jobs with greater digital skills intensity have a comparatively higher share of young workers—about one in four aged 15–29—and a lower share aged 55–64, while occupations with intermediate to low digital skills have roughly equal younger and older shares [p881]. In contrast, residual green occupations of interest have a lower share of workers aged 15–29, indicating scope to make these jobs more attractive to younger workers [p881].

46.text: EU labour-market resilience amid the slowdown reflected an expanding labour force: since 2019 employment rose by about 5.5 million while the labour force grew by roughly 4 million and unemployment fell by 1.4 million, with non-EU nationals adding 1.24 million to the 2023 labour-force rise of almost 2 million [p704]. Improved matching and the COVID-19 policy response helped keep long-term unemployment low, while firms retained more workers than needed in anticipation of recovery [p704]. Labour demand remained resilient to the economic slowdown and job creation was stronger in sectors with high labour shortages; the vacancy rate fell from 2.9% in Q1-2023 to 2.4% in Q2-2024 but stayed above the 2013-2019 average of 1.7% [p632]. Increased immigration of working-age third-country nationals and improved skills matching also eased labour and skills shortages [p619].

48.text: The March 2024 EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages sets out 87 new actions across five domains: activating under-represented people, supporting skills/training/education, improving working conditions, enhancing fair intra-EU mobility, and attracting talent from outside the EU [p635]. It includes measures such as the EU Talent Pool, the European Skills Agenda, individual learning accounts and micro-credentials, and increasing participation of older workers, women and young people not in education, employment or training [p771].

49.text: Denmark and Poland have abolished mandatory retirement ages as a valid reason to terminate labour contracts, while Belgium and Estonia have programmes in which training providers assess applicants’ competence by validating their previous relevant experience [p839]. The Netherlands also screens job vacancy notices for discriminatory language under its “vacancies for all ages” initiative [p839].

50.text: In the EU in 2023, 14% of EU movers held fixed-term contracts (843 thousand) compared with 24% of third-country nationals (2,192 thousand) [p411]. TCNs were much more likely to have fixed-term contracts, including 45% in the Netherlands, 41% in Poland, 40% in Portugal, and 55% in Cyprus [p486].

51.text: Yes. Since 2020, France and Sweden are among five Member States that raised statutory retirement ages, and Sweden also has phased retirement and deferred-retirement options [p836]. Projections indicate that, mostly due to ageing and already adopted pension reforms, the EU’s active population aged 55–64 will rise by 6 million and those aged 65–68 by 2.8 million by 2030 [p737].

52.text: The permanent contract rate was 96% for EU movers versus 86% for nationals in 2023, a difference of **10 percentage points** [p394][p351].

53.text: Workers in green in-demand jobs and labour-shortage occupations have above-average job strain, while occupations with higher digital-skills intensity have much lower job strain, including below the EU average [p906]. Only about 50% of workers in green in-demand jobs and labour-shortage occupations can accurately predict their earnings over the next 3 months, whereas earnings predictability is highest in higher digital-skills-intensity and AI-exposed occupations [p884][p906].

54.text: Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a permanent-contract rate 4 percentage points above the EU average of 69.7%, i.e. 73.7% [p884]. For occupations with higher digital skills intensity, Figure 7 shows 80% on permanent contracts [p883], compared with the EU average of 69.7% [p884].

55.text: In 2023, the EU employment rate for older workers aged 55–64 was 63.9%, 18 pps below the 82.2% rate for prime-age adults (25–54) [p659]. Employment rates of older workers were above 70% in Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Latvia, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden, while they were below 55% in Greece, Croatia, Luxembourg, Romania and Slovenia [p821]. The largest increases since 2009 (around 30 pps) were in Hungary, Poland and Slovenia for ages 55–59, and in Denmark, Hungary and Slovakia for ages 60–64 [p821].

56.text: In 2023, EU movers had higher labour-market integration than third-country nationals: activity 83% vs 72%, employment 78% vs 63%, and unemployment 7% vs 12% [p474]. Both EU movers and TCNs work part-time more often than nationals, but the pages do not give a TCN part-time rate; for EU movers, 36% of employed women worked part-time vs 8% of men, a 28-pps gap [p474][p493].

57.text: Under the static scenario, the EU labour force is projected to decline by about 42.8 million people by 2070 [p1011].

58.text: A population equivalent to 10% of Estonia’s nurse population is residing and working in other EU Member States or EFTA countries [p343].

60.text: No. The report shows variation: 13 of 31 PES were designing pilots or had plans to introduce ILAs, while 2 of 31 had a supporting role [p1031]; Figure 6 also distinguishes Member States with implemented ILAs, plans, no plans, and no questionnaire feedback [p1032].

61.text: Gender disparities are driven by unpaid care: 7.7 million women in the EU remain outside the labour market due to caregiving, versus only 450,000 men, and care inequalities persist among employed women [p931]. Occupational segregation and skills gaps also matter: women lag in STEM, are underrepresented in ICT, and make up just 28% of green-task jobs, while only 14% of labour-shortage occupations are gender-balanced [p876][p931]. Women also perform more tasks prone to automation and are overrepresented in sectors more exposed to AI [p876]. Policy should prioritise care responsibilities in assessing the twin transitions [p931] and use the 2024 Action Plan to tackle labour and skills shortages, which focuses on supporting underrepresented people into the labour market, skills/training/education, and improving working conditions [p914].

62.text: Yes. The share of fixed-term contracts fell from 19% to 14% for EU movers and from 14% to 11% for nationals between 2018 and 2023, so the gap narrowed from 5 percentage points to 3 percentage points [p485].

63.text: The rise was largely driven by the Russian aggression against Ukraine, which caused a significant influx of third-country nationals into the EU [p444][p446]. Inflows of TCNs doubled between 2021 and 2022 to 3,324,000, a 133% increase [p444].

64.text: From 2019 to 2023, Greece’s employment rate rose from 56.5% to 61.8%, a change of +5.3 pp [p722]. Portugal’s employment rate rose from 70.5% to 72.5%, a change of +2.0 pp [p738].

65.text: The PES Network uses a dedicated LinkedIn group, launched in July 2024, as an online space to connect PES, encourage exchanges, promote the Network to partners/stakeholders, and share inspiration and best practices; by end-October 2024 it had nearly 500 members [p1044]. It also supports PES IT experts through the Digitalisation Working Group, which helps drive digital progress within their organisations [p1054]. Its outputs include webinars and reports, and PES practices are published in the PES Practice Repository [p1050].

66.text: In the Netherlands, full-time employment among returning health workers rose from (0%) in 2018 to (38%) in 2023, while part-time fell from (100%) to (62%) [p430]. In Italy, full-time employment fell from (100%) in 2018 to (69%) in 2023, with part-time rising from (0%) to (31%) [p430]. Thus the Netherlands moved toward more full-time work, while Italy moved in the opposite direction; both sets of values are marked as low reliability [p430].

67.text: Digitalisation and AI deepen platform-work vulnerabilities by enabling algorithmic management and surveillance that widen power imbalances between platforms and workers, while platform work itself is marked by low wages, lack of social protection, and risks for vulnerable groups [p925]. In the EU, platform-economy revenues grew almost fivefold between 2016 and 2020, more than 28 million people were estimated to work through digital labour platforms in 2020, 5.5 million were estimated to be incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earned less than the minimum wage [p552]. Stakeholders also identified “all-controlling technology in platform work” among four main digitalisation concerns [p924]. Some Member States are responding through platform-work and algorithmic-management rules, such as Croatia’s joint liability and transparency requirements and Germany’s work on employee data protection covering video surveillance and AI systems [p686].

68.text: Not uniformly. EU estimates indicate undeclared work is lowest in the care sector (34%) and highest in direct household employment (nearly 70%) [p164], and ESPAN experts report much higher undeclared shares in non-care domestic work in Austria and Germany and more undeclared non-care work in Malta, while Italy reported an even distribution in 2022 [p283]. However, some countries report the opposite pattern: in Bulgaria most LTC domestic workers are informal, and Ireland has a significant informal home-care sector [p283].

69.text: Estonia moved PhD students from student to employee status with a €1400 per month net salary and 80% of time reserved for research, alongside industry PhD programmes and doctoral schools [p1073]. Slovenia introduced 2013 legislation allowing staff to combine a full-time position with an additional 20% part-time appointment to ease transitions across positions, though this creates extra work pressure [p1066]. Germany is only mentioned as using the Habilitation as a method of training supervisors, with no recruitment or advancement initiative described [p1073].

70.text: The report outlines an integrated approach through the March 2024 EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages, which aims to mobilise underutilised resources, boost workforce adaptation, and use the EU Talent Pool to match non-EU jobseekers with shortage occupations [p771]. It combines the European Skills Agenda’s upskilling and reskilling actions—including individual learning accounts and micro-credentials—with efforts to raise participation among older workers, women, and young people not in education, employment or training, plus fair intra-EU mobility and attraction of non-EU talent [p771]. For older workers, it also calls for pension reforms such as raising statutory retirement ages, restricting early retirement, and allowing flexible work-retirement combinations; projections show +6 million active people aged 55–64 and +2.8 million aged 65–68 in the EU by 2030 [p737].

71.text: EU sector-to-sector transition rates in the overall economy mostly fell between 1.8% and 3.9%, remaining relatively stable over 2010–2019 with a slight upward trend around 2016 in some Member States [p7][p24]. From 2018 to 2019, mining was the only “transforming sector” with a net outflow of workers, while all others had net inflows, although the energy sector’s net inflow may conceal within-sector variation [p9][p24]. Older workers tend to make fewer sector-to-sector transitions than younger workers, with no significant difference between men and women, and “transforming sectors” generally retain relatively more workers except water supply/waste management, where slightly more leave [p7][p9][p24]. The retrospective transition question was discontinued from the LFS from 2020, so 2019 is the main reference year and 2020 results may be sensitive to COVID-19 [p3].

72.text: Future-oriented occupations accounted for 32% of workers in the EU in 2021 [p873].

73.text: Only France and Italy reported more than 10% of postings as temporary agency postings [p958]. Their shares were approximately 18% in France and 13% in Italy [p975]. The provided pages do not give an EU average for temporary agency postings, so a comparison to the EU average cannot be made.

74.text: By October 2024, only nine EU Member States had ratified ILO Convention C189: Belgium, Germany, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Malta, Portugal, and Sweden [p310][p304]. Ratification years were Italy and Germany 2013; Ireland 2014; Belgium, Finland, and Portugal 2015; Sweden 2019; Malta 2021; and Spain 2023 [p304].

75.text: Nine EU Member States have ratified ILO Convention C189 [p231][p255], while eight Member States apply the same labour-law and social-protection rules to declared domestic workers as to other workers [p231][p261].

76.text: AI-exposed occupations have below-average job strain, while labour-shortage occupations report the highest job strain at 48% [p887]. For training, AI-exposed occupations have the lowest share of workers who received no education or training in the preceding four weeks, whereas the lowest level of employer-provided training was for the residual critical labour-shortage occupations [p904][p903].

77.text: Higher training participation/intensity among older workers coincides with higher unemployment-to-employment transition rates: Denmark, where older people complete about 20% more training hours than EU 25–64, has the highest transition rate (more than 30%), and Germany, the Netherlands and Austria also combine high training with relatively high job finding [p828]. By contrast, low-training Member States such as Bulgaria, Greece, Romania and Slovakia have older-worker transition rates below 10% per quarter [p828]. Participation varies widely: more than half of older people trained in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Sweden in 2022, versus less than 15% in Bulgaria, Greece, Poland and Romania [p827]; AES adult-learning rates were highest in Sweden (66.5%), Hungary (62.2%), the Netherlands (56.1%) and Germany (53.7%), and lowest in Bulgaria (9.5%), Greece (15.1%), Poland (20.3%) and Czechia (21.2%) [p653].

78.text: Under the standard “Static” scenario, the EU labour force is projected to decline by 20.2 pp, or about 42.8 million people, by 2070 [p1011]. If all Member States gradually converged to Sweden’s labour force participation rates by age, sex, and education, the projected decline would be only 2.8 pp, or 5.9 million people, by 2070—almost completely offsetting the negative impact of ageing [p1012]. Combining all forms of activation through adoption of Swedish participation rates would therefore almost fully compensate for the decline in the workforce [p1013].

79.text: In 2022, EU public expenditure on education was allocated roughly as follows: pre-primary and primary 34%, secondary 36.8%, and tertiary 16.6% [p130].

80.text: Predominantly, posted third-country nationals (TCNs) are Ukrainian in several Member States (Belgium, Lithuania, the Netherlands, and Austria), while Lithuania also reports many Belarusians and Bulgaria reports 41% Turkish TCNs [p1008][p960][p959]. TCN postings are most frequently sent by companies established in Poland (30%) and Lithuania (18%) [p973]. Common sectors vary by country: construction and manufacturing in Lithuania, the Netherlands, France, and Sweden, construction in Belgium, manufacturing in Italy, and transport in Austria [p960][p959].

81.text: In 2023, 35.5% of adults in Bulgaria had at least basic digital skills, compared with 55.6% at EU level [p548].

82.text: Between January 2022 and July 2024, statutory minimum wages rose nominally by more than 10% in all Member States with such wages; in real terms they rose by more than 10% in eight countries and by 4–10% in six, with Bulgaria and Romania among those with nominal increases above 40% [p796]. By contrast, real statutory minimum wages fell by 1.3% in France and by more than 3% in Czechia and Slovakia over the same period, as inflation eroded the gains [p796].

83.text: High graduation numbers do not by themselves eliminate shortages: Ireland, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia and Romania have above EU-average densities of medical doctor and nurse graduates but below EU-average densities of available healthcare workers [p338]. Retention and mobility also undermine graduate supply—Italy faces doctor outflows, Latvia has the equivalent of 15% of its doctors practising in other Member States, and returnee inflows are not clearly sufficient to offset outflows [p358].

84.text: Based on EU-SILC data, minimum wage non-compliance is estimated to affect more than 8% of the workforce in Germany, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Lithuania, Hungary, Portugal and Sweden [p797]. The workers most affected are young people, unskilled workers, women, workers in smaller firms and part-time workers; they are generally younger, less educated, more likely female, and more likely on fixed-term or part-time contracts in smaller firms [p797].

85.text: Labour-market transitions can support the green transition by moving workers into expanding sectors and facilitating smoother adjustment to expected sectoral changes, helping avoid worsening labour shortages in affected sectors such as construction and transportation [p46]. In the EU, recent years saw a net inflow of workers into all “transforming sectors” except mining and extraction [p12]. However, training and education in some key sectors is lagging, while delivering EU Green Deal wind and solar targets would require about 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU, with associated skills investment of EUR 1.1–1.4 billion by 2030 [p12].

86.text: The report attributes high female mover part-time rates to inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493]. In 2023, 36% of employed female EU movers worked part-time versus 8% of male movers, a 28-pp gap that exceeds the 20-pp gap for nationals [p493][p475]. Broader evidence also links parenthood and care responsibilities to the gap: among employed women with children, 31.8% worked part-time versus 5.0% of men, and informal long-term care responsibilities contribute further [p660].

88.text: Yes. Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a higher-than-average incidence of permanent employment, 4 percentage points above the EU average of 69.7% [p884].

89.text: Future EU labour-force trends are shaped by demographic decline and ageing, women’s empowerment/emancipation, rising educational attainment, and migration assumptions [p1022][p1023]. The Draghi report identifies potential contributions of 8 million young people aged 20–29, 12 million people aged 55–64, and 17 million women [p1023]. Proposed responses include investing in skills and using untapped labour-force participation and employment; in the most optimistic scenario, harnessing all activation potential and moving to Swedish labour-force participation rates could almost fully offset ageing effects [p1017][p1022]. In the EU in 2022, 46.6% of people aged 25–64 engaged in education or training in the prior 12 months, up 2.9 pp from 2016, with barriers including training schedule, family reasons, and costs [p67].

90.text: Among EU part-time workers in 2023, 18% of women were underemployed versus more than a quarter of men, and mothers had a lower rate (16%) than fathers; 15% of part-time workers living with a partner were underemployed versus 26% of those without a partner [p849][p850]. Regression results for 2013–2023 confirm that women and partnered workers have significantly lower underemployment probabilities—by 8 pp or more—and this is not explained by occupational or sectoral patterns [p851]; predicted probabilities are 0.339 for men vs 0.242 for women, 0.308 for partnered vs 0.237 for single workers, and 0.181 for mothers vs 0.344 for fathers [p856]. The underlying factors differ: women’s unpaid care/time constraints and lack of care services limit their ability to consider longer hours, while men’s part-time work is less often desired and shaped by gendered earner attitudes; partnered workers can rely on two-earner household income, whereas singles rely on their own income and more often prefer full-time work [p850].

91.text: Digital transformation creates labour-market risks through unequal digitalisation of businesses, which can hinder innovation, reduce productivity and feed workplace inequalities, while digitalisation can self-reinforce social exclusion and create new categories of vulnerable workers [p924]. Platformisation is linked to unequal, exploitative labour dynamics, low wages and lack of social protection for vulnerable groups; in 2020 more than 28 million people were estimated to work through digital labour platforms, 5.5 million were estimated to be incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earned less than the minimum wage [p552][p925]. AI and automation can replace routine jobs and generative AI may significantly affect high-skilled workers, while algorithmic management widens platform–worker power imbalances and AI as a “new competitor” reduces workers’ bargaining power [p552][p925]. Digitalisation also increases labour-market polarisation: unskilled workers are more exposed to digitalisation risks while the skilled workforce benefits, creating a need for upskilling and reskilling [p925].

92.text: Non-EU nationals accounted for **64.1%** of the total increase in the EU labour force in 2023 [p755].

93.text: EU mobile workers face lower poverty/social exclusion risks than third-country nationals but higher risks than nationals: in 2022, 27% of EU movers were at risk of poverty and social exclusion (AROPE) vs 46% of TCNs [p508]; their severe material and social deprivation rate was 8% vs 16% for TCNs [p509], and their housing cost overburden rate was 19% vs 26% for TCNs [p504]. The pages note considerable country-level variation and suggest that different national contexts and labour markets, as well as movers’ education, skills, or employment sectors, may shape these outcomes [p510].

94.text: Benchlearning is used as a vehicle to support PES performance, within a work programme strand on enhancing capacity building, data-driven PES and digitalisation strategies, including AI [p1056]. In 2024 the fourth Benchlearning cycle began, with 15 assessments taking place in LT, BG, LV, HR, AT, PT, HU, DE, EL, CZ, EE, NL, MT, IE and CY [p1056]; the PES Network also links this modernisation work to mutual assistance programmes and its Digitalisation Working Group [p1054].

95.text: In 2023, people with tertiary education had an EU employment rate of 86.3%, while the gap between high- and low-educated persons aged 25–64 was 28.0 pps, implying about 58.3% for the low-skilled [p618]. For the narrower 25–54 age group, the rate was 89.7% for tertiary education versus 64.1% for lower education [p72].

96.text: The report attributes lower mobility out of energy-intensive industries into inactivity and unemployment partly to their relatively male-dominated demographic profile, and says their lower employment mobility corroborates high labour-market stability, possibly explained by these being relatively well-paid industries with wage premiums [p13].

97.text: PES career guidance is shifting toward digital and green competencies: 51% of PES report changes in guidance focus on both digital and green skills, 48% on digital skills and 32% on green skills [p1058]. This mirrors labour-market change: EU ICT specialists rose 59.3% since 2013 to over 9.5 million in 2023, while 4 in 10 adults lack basic digital skills, and green-economy employment grew from 2.2% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2021 [p638]. The report also identifies acute labour and skills shortages in sectors key for the green and digital transitions [p787]. SMEs face matching problems—52% report difficulty finding workers with the right skills and 63% are held back by skills shortages—while RRF funds support training in digital skills and green competences [p652].

98.text: Factors include strong gender segregation in green/digital occupations, with women making up just 28% of green-task jobs [p876], plus care responsibilities and STEM skills gaps that hinder women’s participation in emerging green and digital industries [p931]. In energy, women were only 26.7% of the total energy workforce in 2023, with renewable energy at 32% versus oil and gas at 22%, and solar PV at 40% versus wind at 21% [p6]. Mining was 14% women in 2022, and women made up only 20% of the workforce in “transforming sectors” (31% in Lithuania and Bulgaria) [p6]. This composition means green-transition job losses are expected mainly in male-dominated sectors such as mining, while gains in construction or waste management are also male-represented, so raising women’s employment in clean energy is key to a gender-neutral transition [p6].

99.text: In 2023, EU employment growth was driven by labour-force expansion led by highly educated and older workers [p618]. Older people (55–64) reached a 67.0% participation rate and 63.9% employment rate, with their share of total employment close to 20% [p618]; their employment rate was nearly 20 pps higher than in 2009 [p563]. By contrast, youth (15–24) participation was 41.2% and employment 35.2%, returning only to pre-2008 crisis levels, while the NEET rate fell to a record low 11.2% [p618]. Youth unemployment remained more than twice the overall rate [p563], whereas older unemployment was 4.6%, 0.9 pps below prime-age workers [p822].

100.text: The projected investment in skills needed to support the EU’s green transition is **EUR 1.1 to 1.4 billion by 2030** [p25][p21]. This is associated with the additional skilled workers required for wind and solar deployment under EU Green Deal targets [p25][p12].

101.text: The pages suggest a positive association: older unemployed people transition to employment at higher rates when they complete more education, and Denmark—where older people complete about 20% more training hours than the EU average for ages 25–64—also has the highest transition rate, over 30% [p828]. In contrast, low-training Member States such as Bulgaria, Greece, Romania and Slovakia have transition rates below 10% per quarter [p828]. Graph 3.18 also presents training amounts alongside unemployment-to-employment transition rates for older people [p710].

102.text: Countries reported above 15% include **Poland and Spain (more than 15%) and Italy (35%)** in the PHS Employment Monitor 2024; **Portugal** is also reported at **48% of domestic workers not registered in social security in 2023** [p165]. Spain has estimates of **30–32%**, with higher estimates of **36%**, and Italy’s 2023 estimate is about **47%** undeclared workers in the sector [p165].

103.text: The green transition affects the whole EU economy but drives significant transformations in “transforming sectors” such as energy industries, mining and quarrying, construction, manufacturing and waste management [p12]. Using EU LFS data, the report finds that from 2018–2019 there was a net inflow of workers into all transforming sectors except mining and extraction in the EU, while the overall year-on-year sector-to-sector transition rate was 1.8–3.9 and relatively stable, with a slight increase around 2016 in some Member States [p24]. Contrary to expectations, workers in energy-intensive industries make fewer transitions to non-employment than workers in other sectors [p12][p24]. The report also notes that older workers make fewer sectoral transitions than younger workers, no significant difference is observed between men and women, and women remain underrepresented—only 26.7% of energy-industry workers in 2023 and 14% in mining [p24].

104.text: The pages highlight workers with disabilities—including women and young people with disabilities and those with visible or invisible disabilities—as particularly vulnerable to the digital and green transitions [p928]. They also identify people in precarious employment, the self-employed, people facing discrimination, unpaid carers, and regional vulnerable groups [p926], as well as emerging vulnerable groups such as skilled workers in transition industries [p946].

105.text: Portugal has a special “domestic service” regime outside the Labour Code, and unemployment benefits are granted only to domestic workers hired full-time on a monthly basis with a written contract registered with social security; most work for several employers and opt for the lower-contribution “agreed regime” [p177][p269]. In Hungary, most domestic workers—including employees in simplified employment and the self-employed—have formal access to labour protection and all insurance-based benefits, but those under Act XC of 2010 do not and may only get basic healthcare if they pay their own health insurance [p269][p275]. Shortfalls remain in Portugal’s unemployment/social-protection conditions and in Hungary’s Act XC category; Hungarian carers are also reported as unmonitored, with no access to workers’ representation or collective bargaining and no social or legal protection [p177].

108.text: Yes—the report states underemployment is more common among young part-time workers [p849], and people aged 55–64 account for about a quarter of part-timers but less than 15% of the underemployed [p846]. Chart 10 shows age 20–29 rather than 20–34, so the exact 20–34 band is not reported [p849].

109.text: Austria and France were among five countries with falling absolute regional income disparities (convergence) [p105], and show catching-up beta coefficients of -0.02 for Austria (2014–2021) and -0.01 for France (2014–2021) [p106]. By contrast, Czechia and Sweden were among four countries with rising absolute disparities (divergence) [p105]; Czechia’s standard deviation rose by 20% between 2007 and 2022 [p105], and neither Czechia nor Sweden shows robust evidence of catching-up [p106]. The difference is linked to metropolitan vs non-metropolitan income growth: in converging countries metropolitan regions had slower median income growth than non-metropolitan ones, e.g. slow growth in Austrian major metropolitan regions [p106], whereas in Sweden Stockholm had among the highest median income growth and non-metropolitan Södermanland and Kronoberg the lowest [p106]. For Czechia, absolute dispersion increased but less than the cross-regional average of median incomes, implying a decline in relative income dispersion [p106].

110.text: Yes. As labour demand increased, underemployment among part-time workers declined steadily: around 30% of part-time workers were underemployed in 2013, compared with less than 20% in 2023, and the number of underemployed workers available to work longer hours fell from over 8 million to about 5 million over 2013–2023 [p847].

111.text: Declared care workers are entitled to labour rights and social protection, including additional compensation, overtime pay and paid leave, whereas undeclared care workers lack legal protection and access to social protection in case of unemployment or illness [p193][p177]. Undeclared care workers also face poorer job security and lower wages than those who declare their work [p173][p193]. Even when legalised, some carers—such as domestic service workers in Portugal—may not enjoy the same legal and social protections as other workers [p177].

112.text: The ISCO codes used are 5152 (“butlers”), 5162 (“companions and valets”), 5322 (“home-based personal care workers”), and 9111 (“domestic cleaners and helpers”) [p240][p230]. These are added alongside NACE 97 workers, excluding unpaid family workers [p240][p230]. The pages also note that ISCO 9121 (“launderers and pressers”) and ISCO 5311 (“childcare workers”) were not considered domestic workers [p241].

113.text: Evidence from the Netherlands and Austria suggests that Individual Learning Accounts can boost training participation and learning intentions among older adults [p838]. ILAs enable both employed and not employed individuals to accumulate funds for labour-market-relevant training [p838]. As of summer 2024, however, only a few Public Employment Services had begun introducing ILA schemes [p1032].

114.text: No. Real wage growth reached 2.4% year-on-year in Q2-2024, but real wages in the EU remained below pre-pandemic levels on average and in eight Member States [p530]. Real wages in 2024 were still forecast to be 1.1% below their 2019 level in the EU [p715].

115.text: According to Table 2.1, the social indicators showing beta convergence (catching-up) in both 2007-2014 and 2014-2023 were the AROPE rate, AROPE rate of children, housing cost overburden, and adult participation in learning [p100]. Healthy life years for women showed catching-up only in 2014-2023, while tertiary education attainment showed it only in 2007-2014 [p100].

116.text: Table 5.1 lists voucher systems in AT, BE, EL, FR, HR, IT, LT, LU, RO and SE, while tax incentives are listed in BE, DE, DK, EE, ES, FI, FR, HR, HU, IT, LT, LU, PT, RO and SE [p284]. Voucher impact is generally “quite low” in AT, BE and EL; a 2018 Belgian study estimated less than 10% of voucher-paid domestic work used to be undeclared, while Sweden’s RUT evaluation suggests a probable but unsubstantiated link to low undeclared work [p286][p287]. Tax-incentive impact varies across six reports (BE, DE, ES, FR, IT, SE): Germany reports little effect, whereas Spain’s 2011 introduction increased declared domestic workers over the following two years before plateauing [p287]. Tax incentives also show a regressive distributional profile: in Germany wealthier households get greater relief, and in Sweden the highest income decile received 40% of total tax deductions under a 2020 report [p287].

117.text: In 2024, the PES Network carried out two Mutual Assistance projects and a Working Group on PES Digitalisation met twice [p1040]. The Luxembourg project, completed in April 2024, focused on using AI to develop a matching tool, with support from Belgium-VDAB and Sweden; the Romanian project began in October 2024 and focused on HR strategies, onboarding, guidance and training for new staff, and national-to-local guidance [p1040][p1042]. The digitalisation working group focused on IT projects and reforms, the AI Act, digitalisation and AI across customer journeys, and sharing IT solutions and public-private partnerships [p1040].

118.text: Yes—for EU movers, inflows rose by 117,000 (859,000 to 976,000) while outflows fell by 41,000 (584,000 to 543,000) in 2022, so the inflow increase was larger [p443].

119.text: EU movers’ EU-wide median income was higher than nationals’ in 2022 (EUR 20 714 vs EUR 19 506), even though nationals’ median income grew faster (2.6% annually vs 1.9% for movers) [p524]. This apparent paradox reflects the migration pattern: EU movers tend to go to Member States with rather high income levels, raising their EU-wide median despite typically earning less than nationals within each Member State [p524].

120.text: Using nearly 9.8 million ICT specialists in 2023 [p656] and the 20 million target for 2030 [p638], the required annual increase is about **10.7% per year** over seven years.

121.text: European PES have advanced digital transformation by using AI across the customer journey—including profiling, matching and career guidance—to enhance service delivery and personalised support for jobseekers, employers and employees [p1039]. AI adoption is expanding rapidly, with positive outcomes reported based on soft indicators; profiling applications are most frequent, followed by career guidance [p1040]. AI tools are positioned as a supplement to human judgement and decision-making, not a replacement for staff [p1040].

122.text: Spain has a published PES Practice on “AI Job Matching” [p1050]. Luxembourg had a Mutual Assistance project on using AI to develop a matching tool, supported by Belgium-VDAB and Sweden [p1040].

123.text: Workers in energy-intensive industries (EII) are relatively male-dominated and have high labour-market stability; in 2014–2023 EU27 they remained in employment more and had fewer outflows to inactivity/unemployment than the total economy [p13]. This lower mobility is likely linked to their male-dominated profile and relatively well-paid, stable jobs [p13]. However, women remain underrepresented in transforming sectors, at only 26.7% in energy industries and 14% in mining in 2023 [p24], and high-carbon workers face higher displacement risks, with 20% higher odds of unemployment, so reskilling/upskilling and employment support are needed for the green transition [p14].

125.text: Social investment, especially in early childhood education and care (ECEC), can improve parents’—particularly mothers’—labour market participation and help narrow gender employment and pay gaps [p121]. Recent estimates in eight Member States show that raising under-3 ECEC participation to 50% could improve mothers’ labour participation rates by 5% to 30%, with a 9 pp to 21 pp increase for mothers from low-income families, potentially helping to halve the gender gap [p126].

126.text: The future-oriented occupations with the highest access to employer-funded training are less digitally intensive green new and emerging occupations (56%) and green enhanced occupations (53%), such as life science professionals, physicists, astronomers and financial analysts [p903].

127.text: R&I can identify the skills required for the green and digital transitions and support future-fit training and retraining, while tackling the digital divide by promoting fair and equal access to ICTs across regions, sectors, occupational and socioeconomic groups and equitable digital access for SMEs [p936]. The ERA4FutureWork initiative uses stakeholder dialogue across the green transition, digital world of work, vulnerable groups, and EU public administrations to set R&I priorities [p949]. Its agenda proposes innovative educational programmes, analysis of labour mobility patterns and skills shortages, and assessment of work platformisation as an analytical foundation for sustainable and equitable societies founded on decent work [p951]. Skills intelligence and development are also described as key to a fair, green transition, despite gaps between training provision and workforce needs [p921].

128.text: Only Finland saw regional differences in tertiary education attainment fall between 2007 and 2022 [p104].

129.text: Principle 17 of the European Pillar of Social Rights specifically supports the inclusion of people with disabilities in the labour market and society [p929]. It is also cited as emphasising inclusion of persons with disabilities into the labour market [p514].

130.text: Part-time workers living with a partner are much less likely to be underemployed than those without a partner: about 15% versus 26% in the EU [p850]. Regression analysis finds that people living with partners have a lower probability of underemployment by 8 pp or more [p851], with women with partners 9 pp less likely than women without partners, while partnership has no large effect for men [p852].

131.text: Between 2017 and 2023, women made up approximately **90–94%** of EU healthcare movers, compared with **79–80%** of national healthcare workers [p347].

132.text: Italy, Spain, Romania and Greece had vocational education and training graduate employment rates below 70% in 2023 [p651].

133.text: EU-LFS 2021 data show AI-exposed occupations are broadly gender-balanced, with women holding 52% of jobs, but women remain underrepresented in the highest-AI-exposure occupations and the “AI workforce” is small and male-dominated, which may make women more vulnerable to the digital transition and less able to benefit from AI [p878]. Gender segregation also persists within high-AI sectors: healthcare shortage occupations have high AI exposure and are majority women, while mathematicians have a high AIOE of 1.516 and are predominantly male [p878]. Although both women and men experience approximately the same level of higher occupational AI exposure, granular gender segregation in certain high-AI-exposure jobs means inclusive digital transformation must address these disparities [p905].

134.text: No. The pages state that green investment is expected to yield a net increase of 2 million jobs in Europe by 2030 [p954], not 2.5 million.

135.text: Belgium, Ireland and Italy are expected to face higher re-training costs per worker while having relatively low renewable shares and undergoing a “catching-up” process in wind and solar deployment [p138]. Re-training costs in 2030 are estimated at EUR 10 per person in the labour force for Italy and EUR 13 for Belgium [p22].

136.text: Real wages in the EU grew by 2.4% year-on-year in Q2-2024 [p530].

137.text: Projected shifts toward higher education in the EU workforce imply long-term GDP gains: under the assumption that a 1 pp rise in the high-skilled share raises GDP per capita by 0.3 pp after 50 years (0.15 pp after 25 years), the 14.15 pp increase in the high-skilled share projected for 2020-2045 would amount to 2.12 pp in 2070 and 4.24 pp in 2095 [p1016]. Simulated one-pp shifts to medium skills imply long-run GDP effects of 0.27-0.9 pp, while shifts to high skills imply 0.32-0.82 pp [p1016]. However, skills investment cannot compensate for the EU’s demographic decline, though it can mitigate the reduction in the number of workers, and the human-capital growth already embedded in the EU population could be a competitive advantage [p1017].

138.text: Among those aged 55–64, 44% have at least basic digital skills, compared with 64% of those aged 25–54 [p828]. Older people complete fewer education and training hours than younger people, but they work in jobs better matched to their skills and in less dynamic workplaces, and report less need for skills development [p840]. Older individuals wanting training cite health, age and course availability more often, and cost less often, than younger people; about 8% in both age groups cite lack of support [p828].

139.text: Yes. The report notes that unequal digitalisation of businesses across Europe can feed the existing digital divide, hinder innovation and productivity, and “feed into workplace inequalities”; persistent unequal digitalisation threatens to exacerbate regional disparities and widen the gap between SMEs, mid-caps and larger businesses, while digitalisation can create new categories of vulnerable workers [p924]. It also finds persistent risks to upward convergence on skills, with substantial disparities between Member States and no signs of convergence [p627], and highlights platform-work challenges and employers’ difficulties finding workers with necessary skills [p676].

140.text: The provided pages do not give exact 2024-Q4 job-vacancy rates for the Netherlands and Belgium; Chart 4 presents them with the EU and other Member States for 2024-Q4 [p866]. The latest explicit figures are for Q2-2024: Belgium 4.4% and the Netherlands 4.3%, the highest in the EU, versus an EU vacancy rate of 2.4% [p635][p632].

141.text: Yes. Finland’s gender employment gap is reported as nearly non-existent at 0.2 pps [p659], while Sweden’s gap among EU movers is 2 pps, with Swedish nationals at 3 pps [p492].

142.text: The reports frame the twin green and digital transitions as jointly reshaping vulnerability itself, creating new risks and deepening existing inequalities for precarious, self-employed and discriminated workers [p926]. Specific intersection challenges include skills mismatch and digital exclusion, gig-economy job security, and displacement of traditional industries toward greener sectors [p928]. For workers with disabilities, EU employment is 50.6% versus 74.8% for people without disabilities; telework may help some physical disabilities, but digitalisation can create barriers for visual or auditory impairments, and expanded manual green roles may be less accessible for physical disabilities [p928]. Green investment is expected to yield a net increase of 2 million jobs in Europe by 2030 [p954], while the European Commission has convened stakeholders specifically on the twin transitions and vulnerable groups [p949].

143.text: Yes. The table note states that for DK and NL the data include both posted workers and self-employed persons [p1002]. Table 1 also indicates that Denmark and the Netherlands cover self-employed persons under their declaration tools, with sectoral limits [p963].

144.text: Yes. In Q2-2024, the Netherlands had a job vacancy rate of 4.3%, while Poland was among the countries with the lowest rates, below 1% [p635].

145.text: The share of EU movers with low education rose from 28% in 2018 to 30% in 2023, an increase of 2 percentage points [p420][p497].

146.text: Within future-oriented occupations, recent training participation is lowest among the residual group of critical labour-shortage occupations, where only a minority received training in the preceding four weeks [p903][p907]. Among “transforming” sectors, mining and construction receive below-average training, with construction having the lowest adult learning scores [p25]. The provided pages do not explain the reasons for this pattern.

147.text: For EU movers, Table 36 implies total self-employment of about 9% in 2017 and 8% in 2023, with 10% in 2018, 11% in 2019, 5% in 2020 (low reliability), 8% in 2021 and 9% in 2022 [p408]. The report describes the series as starting around 10% in 2018, dipping to approximately 4% in 2020, rebounding to around 9% by 2022 and stabilising slightly below that in 2023 [p482]. Third-country nationals were about 11% in 2017 and 8% in 2023, with a low of 6% in 2020, 9% in 2021 and around 8% thereafter, so both groups ended near 8% but EU movers showed a sharper COVID dip and rebound while TCNs fell from a higher 2017 level [p408][p482].

148.text: In EFTA countries, part-time work is generally more prevalent among nationals than among EU movers [p487]. For example, in Switzerland 43% of nationals work part-time, compared with 27% of EU movers and 35% of third-country nationals [p487]. Figure 33 also compares part-time contracts across EU and EFTA countries in 2023 [p488].

150.text: The EU employment rate for people aged 20–64 was **75.3% in 2023**, up **0.7 pp** from 2022 [p72]. It was also described as a new record high, growing further to **75.8% in Q2-2024** [p680].

151.text: Slovakia’s self-employment rate for domestic workers is **28%** in 2023 [p321]; the report also describes it as around **30%** [p244].

152.text: The ERA4FutureWork initiative, proposed by DG Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion and DG Research and Innovation, created a forum for Member States to discuss R&I priorities and facilitated dialogue among policymakers, social partners, academia and VET providers [p950]. It examined gaps in Member State R&I across four streams: the green transition and working life; the digital world of work; the twin transitions and vulnerable groups; and the future of work in EU public administrations [p950]. Four workshops were held between April 2023 and February 2024 to propose a path for future collaboration [p952], and the study advocates a proactive, strategic integration of new work approaches, reindustrialisation and future work trends with green and digital transition policies [p950].

153.text: In 2023, job vacancy rates remained highest in **administrative and support service activities (4.3%)**, **accommodation and food service activities (3.8%)**, **professional, scientific and technical activities (3.7%)**, and **information and communication (3.4%)** [p75].

154.text: The EU27 labour market shows a substantial and rising presence of older workers: in 2023, 41 million people aged 55–64 participated and 39 million were employed, with activity and employment rates of 67% and 63.9%, almost 20 pps higher than in 2009 and more than four times the increase for prime-age workers [p819]. This increased participation has compensated for the negative labour-supply impact of population ageing [p819]. In “transforming sectors,” EU27 median ages are 43–46, with water supply the oldest at 46 and mining and construction at 43 [p35][p5].

155.text: Men work fewer part-time jobs partly because gendered attitudes identify men as primary earners and women as primary caretakers, so part-time work is less often a desired choice for men; when men do work part-time, more than a quarter report wanting longer hours [p850]. In 2023, 27.9% of women aged 20–64 in the EU worked part-time, compared with 7.7% of men [p660].

157.text: Care allowances are typically financial benefits or payments made to either carers or care recipients; they can be “unbound,” allowing beneficiaries to spend resources freely, or “bound,” requiring documentation of how funds are spent [p185].

158.text: 12% of older part-time workers in the EU are underemployed [p850].

159.text: Overall household financial conditions improved as real gross disposable household income rose 2.5% in Q3 2024 compared with Q3 2023, faster than real GDP growth of 1.3%, driven mainly by employee compensation rising 2.7% year-on-year [p844]. The share of households reporting financial distress fell from its 17.5% peak in August 2023 to 15.7% by March 2025, a 1.3 pp drop compared with March 2024 [p844]. Reliance on savings also declined from 12.9% in May 2023 to 11.5% in March 2025, while the share incurring debt was 4.2% in March 2025, down 0.3 pp year-on-year [p845].

161.text: The officially documented EU-27 figure for 2023 is about **4.08 million domestic workers** (4,080.8 thousand), or **2.1% of all people at work**, based on EU LFS data and a deliberately “conservative” definition [p318][p241]. This is likely an underestimate: LFS data may miss undeclared and some migrant workers, and the report notes the actual number is likely “(much) higher” [p242]. For context, using a 2019 estimate that 50% of domestic workers were undeclared, the actual EU total was estimated at **12.8 million to 18 million**, but the pages do not provide an equivalent 2023 actual figure [p241].

162.text: PES face resource challenges (staff capacities, access to software), process challenges (integrating evidence capture into development cycles), cultural challenges (incentivising staff to use new methods), and issues around data quality/analysis, data protection, and balancing user concerns with stakeholder involvement [p1039]. For AI specifically, PES must carefully balance privacy, efficiency, accuracy, fairness, lawfulness and innovation [p1039]. They also face difficulties transitioning from experimental AI to production-ready systems and must balance business priorities, legal/ethical requirements, experimentation and explainability [p1040].

164.text: The average age of a miner worker in Poland is 39 years [p5].

165.text: Yes. Evidence from Greece indicates wage subsidies are particularly effective at boosting employment for long-term unemployed people, compared with participants unemployed for less than one year [p142]. Three years after entering the programme, wage subsidy participants are almost twice as likely to be employed as similar comparison-group individuals [p142].

166.text: Approximately **88.8%** of young people aged 15–29 in the EU were employed, in education, or in training in 2023, since the NEET rate was **11.2%** [p74].

168.text: The Joint Employment Report 2025 links weak productivity growth to **a decline in technological innovation and adoption, insufficient reallocation of capital and labour across firms, and the ageing workforce** [p634].

169.text: For incoming posted workers in 2023, EL reported a total of 3,999 persons versus a breakdown sum of 3,997, a difference of 2 [p999]. IT reported 34,988 versus a breakdown sum of 36,313, so its total was lower by 1,325 [p999]. LT reported 5,806 versus a breakdown sum of 4,929, so its total was higher by 877 [p999].

170.text: Bulgaria, Croatia, Poland, Romania and Slovakia show a rather homogeneous working-age population, mostly composed of nationals [p465].

171.text: Workers aged 15–29 had a lower share in (residual) green occupations of interest [p881].

172.text: In Italy, EU mover health workers aged 35–39 fell from 8,000 in 2018 to 6,000 in 2023, a decline of 2,000, while those aged 55–59 fell from 19,000 to 16,000, a larger decline of 3,000 [p423].

173.text: Yes. In Denmark, the female share of EU mover inflows rose from 38% in 2021 to 40% in 2022, a 2 percentage-point increase [p373].

174.text: About 25% of posted workers to France were third-country nationals (TCNs) in 2022 [p959].

175.text: Unpaid care work disproportionately constrains women’s labour-market access: in the EU, 7.7 million women remain outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men [p931]. In 2022, 34% of women were involved daily in unpaid care versus one in four men, and 63% of women did daily housework versus around one in three men [p109]; another source reports 92% of women as regular carers and 81% as daily carers versus 68% and 48% of men [p929]. For STEM, the pages show women significantly lag in STEM skills, likely hindering their participation in emerging industries [p931], and strong gender segregation persists in digital/green occupations, with women making up just 28% of green-task jobs [p876]. The provided pages do not directly quantify how unpaid care specifically affects STEM representation, but they separately document heavier care burdens for women and women’s underrepresentation/skills gaps in STEM-related sectors [p931][p876].

176.text: Yes. TCNs’ participation in formal education and training rose from 5% in 2018 to 8% in 2020 and was 7% in 2022, while EU movers remained around 3% [p518]. TCNs also increased from 4% in 2017 to 7% in 2022, compared with EU movers at about 3% [p505].

177.text: Targeted policies include upskilling/reskilling, lifelong learning and on-the-job training, stronger links between education/training curricula and firms’ needs, and support for labour reallocation and matching through effective public employment services, transferable social security and training rights, and housing policies [p806]. The EU also promotes individual learning accounts, micro-credentials, active labour market policies and public employment service capacity, plus support schemes for fair restructuring and job transitions [p615][p771]. For the green transition, measures include targeted training from emission-intensive into green sectors, greener curricula, skills anticipation strategies, hiring incentives, fair tax-benefit and social protection systems, and better working conditions [p26]. Complementary measures should ensure well-functioning social protection, equal opportunities and support for job polarisation and displaced workers [p806].

178.text: The pages list OECD Employment Outlook editions for **2018** [p813], **2023** [p814], and **2024** [p814] as published by OECD Publishing, Paris.

179.text: Among occupations of interest, those with higher digital skills intensity report the lowest proportion of job strain, at 16% [p887][p891].
