1.text: The rise is partly a demographic cohort process: in Germany, women’s participation at age 32 increased from 42% for those born in 1970 to 80% for those born in 1987 [p1025]. This improvement is accompanied by reduced and postponed fertility, with debate over whether it reflects a “child penalty” from higher participation or wider societal changes in values around partnership, marriage, and family [p1025]. Education also matters: higher education raises labour force participation for all age and sex groups and narrows gender gaps [p1026].

2.text: Germany’s 2022 decline is attributed mainly to the “EU Portal for road transport posting declarations,” obligatory from 2 February 2022, which moved posted drivers’ declarations out of the national prior declaration tools [p1008][p959]. Germany’s reported postings fell by 34% compared with 2021, but excluding road freight transport they increased by 17% [p959]. The report also says declines in Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Slovakia, and Slovenia were most likely the result of the EU Portal [p977].

3.text: Low-educated EU movers are disproportionately concentrated in Germany (37%), France (34%), Spain (33%) and Italy (33%), above the EU average of 30% [p497]. Highly educated EU movers are disproportionately concentrated in Sweden (70%), Luxembourg (60%), Portugal (59%), Denmark (52%) and the Netherlands (51%), above the EU average of 32% [p497].

4.text: The reports estimate that additional wind turbine and solar panel installations needed to deliver the EU Green Deal targets would require about **130,000 to 145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU by 2030** [p12][p19][p25].

5.text: Telework prevalence in the EU rose from 11.1% in 2019 to 19.8% in 2023 [p677]. It can foster an “always-on” culture: a 2022 Eurofound survey in Belgium, France, Italy and Spain found over 80% were contacted outside contractual hours and nine out of ten responded, with over-connection often perceived as harming work-life balance, health and well-being [p677]. Policy responses include the European Parliament’s 2021 resolution, followed by a Commission study and a two-stage consultation whose first stage ran 30 April–25 July 2024 [p678]; right-to-disconnect legislation exists in 13 Member States, with France, Spain, Belgium and Italy the first four [p678].

6.text: The pages do not directly link S80/S50 trends to high-income households’ pandemic-recovery shifts; they show S80/S50 slightly declined below its 2010 level by 2023 [p698], while top-quintile net wealth grew most in absolute terms between 2017 and 2021 and the top 10% wealth share fell during COVID-19 [p91].

7.text: The US labour productivity growth was 2.5% in Q4 2024, 1.6 percentage points above the EU’s 0.9% [p863].

8.text: The average duration per posting in 2022 was about **115 days** in the Member States that reported such data [p958]. The unweighted average posting period per **posted worker** was **223 days** [p980].

9.text: Variation in per-person re-training costs reflects countries’ current renewable installed capacity and the resulting additional job creation: Member States with higher existing capacity tend to have lower re-training expenses per person, while “catching-up” countries face higher costs as wind and solar deployment stimulates new skillsets and tasks [p22]. Costs are also scaled by Member State service-worker wage levels using Eurostat labour cost data, so lower relative wages reduce estimated training costs [p18].

10.text: Evidence is mixed and often anecdotal: ESPAN experts report that voucher impact on undeclared work is generally quite low in Austria, Belgium and Greece, with a 2018 Belgian study estimating that less than 10% of domestic work paid via vouchers used to be undeclared [p286]. Some voucher systems show larger formalisation effects: France’s CESU is estimated to have cut informal employment from about 50% in 1996 to 20% in 2015 [p187], Belgium’s service vouchers halved undeclared work in covered activities according to 2021 research [p188], and Austria’s DLS formalised 1.55 million working hours between 2006 and 2013 [p188]. Tax incentives vary too: Germany’s had little effect, Spain’s 2011 introduction increased declared domestic workers over the following two years before plateauing, and Sweden’s RUT shows a probable but unsubstantiated link to low undeclared work [p287].

12.text: In Figure 6, the high-digital-intensity (DH) group has 23% aged 25–34, 27% aged 35–44, 28% aged 45–55, and 15% aged 56+, with the 16–24 share not shown [p881]. The green future-oriented groups GDDI/GEDI/GNDI have 25–34 shares of 20%/20%/21% and 56+ shares of 17%/19%/20%, so the high-digital group has a somewhat younger core-age profile and a lower older-worker share [p881]. The text also notes that jobs with greater digital skills intensity have about one in four workers aged 15–29 and a lower share aged 55–64 [p881].

13.text: In 2023, job vacancy rates were at or above 3% in professional, scientific, and technical activities; information and communication (ICT); and construction [p691]. These were the sectors identified as experiencing notable labour shortages [p691].

14.text: Gender disparities stem from strong occupational segregation: digital-intensive and green-task jobs are male-dominated (women are just 28% of green-task jobs), while critical labour-shortage and care jobs are female-dominated (nearly two in three workers) [p876]. Care responsibilities keep 7.7 million EU women outside the labour market versus 450,000 men, and women in temporary/informal work spend twice as much time on unpaid care daily as women in permanent jobs [p931]; 92% of women are regular carers versus 68% of men [p929]. Women also lag in STEM skills, limiting entry to emerging green/digital industries, while green-transition job shifts are concentrated in male-dominated sectors such as mining, engineering, construction and energy [p931]. In ICT, only 19% of specialists were women in 2023, and shortages were worsened by poor hiring foresight, ineffective skills-demand alignment and women’s underrepresentation [p638][p876].

15.text: The employment-rate disparities between EU movers and third-country nationals are particularly significant in Belgium (24 pps), the Netherlands (24 pps), and Germany (22 pps) [p478].

16.text: The report finds strong gender segregation in digital/technical occupations: women are underrepresented in ICT and green-task jobs, while high digital-skills occupations are more male-dominated and women are more concentrated in intermediate/low digital-intensity and critical labour-shortage care roles [p876][p905]. It concludes that greater gender parity in these occupations could boost labour-market participation in digital and green transition jobs and support more balanced, inclusive labour markets [p905]. On training, workers in higher digital-skills and higher-AI-exposure occupations have less “no recent training,” but the report says more can be done and does not explicitly link unequal training access by gender [p904].

17.text: Gender disparities shape the EU green-transition labour market: women are heavily underrepresented in “transforming sectors,” at only 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023 and 14% of mining in 2022, while job losses are expected mainly in male-dominated mining and gains in construction/waste management where men are also overrepresented [p6]. Care responsibilities keep 7.7 million EU women outside the labour market versus 450,000 men, and women’s STEM skills gap may hinder participation in emerging green/digital industries [p931]. Although men and women show no significant difference in sectoral transition frequency, the wind/solar rollout is estimated to need 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers and EUR 1.1–1.4 billion in skills investment by 2030, making women’s inclusion in clean-energy training key [p24][p25].

18.text: The report suggests EU mobile workers face “challenges in accessing quality employment at the same level as the native population that can provide a decent income” [p512]. At EU level, EU movers had a higher in-work poverty risk (13%) than nationals (8%) in 2022, and the gap was especially pronounced in Member States with a more challenging labour-market environment, such as Spain (15 pps), Malta (14 pps), Cyprus (14 pps), and Italy (7 pps) [p512].

19.text: The reports frame a human-centric digital work environment as one where innovation serves workers’ needs and values rather than dictating how they work, with workers involved early in the design and application of new technologies [p953]. They also stress promoting physical and mental well-being, including exploring the effects of AI and virtual worlds on workers [p953], and call for humane work design plus workers’ participation in technology implementation to address mental stress and skills shortages [p926]. For platform work, they emphasise regulatory protection of workers’ rights and workers’ participation in technology implementation, including concerns about algorithmic management without human oversight and lack of transparency [p937].

20.text: Determinants include age—older workers make fewer sectoral transitions than younger workers—and participation in education and training, while no significant difference in sectoral transitions is observed between men and women, though women remain underrepresented in transforming sectors [p24]. In energy-intensive industries, lower transitions to non-employment may be due to higher trade union density and significant male dominance, which reduces transitions into inactivity from caring responsibilities [p12]. Sector-specific changes in demand and required skills/tasks also shape workforce dynamics [p46].

21.text: In the EU, adults with high qualifications participated in learning at 58.9% in 2022, compared with 18.4% for low-qualified adults, making the high-qualified more than three times as likely to participate [p653]. The gap widened slightly since 2016, when the rates were 58.1% and 17.9%, respectively [p653].

22.text: Between 2021 and 2022, inflows of EU movers to EU/EFTA countries rose from 859 000 to 976 000 (+14%), while their net mobility increased by 21%, from 296 000 to 358 000 [p443][p449]. Third-country nationals showed a much larger surge: their EU/EFTA inflows rose from 1 426 000 to 3 324 000, and net mobility jumped from 556 000 to 2 456 000, a 1.9 million increase [p396][p449].

23.text: Digital-intensive future-oriented occupations show the most stable conditions: permanent/indefinite contracts are highest in occupations with higher digital skills intensity, and these occupations also have much lower job strain and the highest earnings predictability [p883][p906]. Green-focused occupations are more mixed: permanent contracts are lowest in green new/emerging occupations at 53% and in labour-shortage occupations at 69% [p883], while only 50% of workers in green in-demand jobs and residual labour-shortage occupations could accurately predict earnings over the next three months [p906]. Job strain is below average in less digital-intensive new, emerging and enhanced green occupations, but above average in green in-demand jobs and green/digital occupations experiencing labour shortages [p906].

24.text: For the green transition, PES are developing strategies and implementing training, job-creation and active labour-market measures, while piloting green-job taxonomies and task-based approaches; challenges include no common definition of “green” and insufficient internal capacity, with over a third of PES having a green-jobs definition [p1033]. For third-country workers, an increasing number of PES are actively involved in recruitment outside the EU, often under bilateral mobility agreements, but their role depends on mandates and Member State conditions and tends to be administrative—admission, work permits and labour-market tests [p1033]. Both roles rely on partnerships and labour-market intelligence, but third-country recruitment additionally requires reliable multilingual information on work permits, qualification recognition and job opportunities [p1033][p1034].

25.text: The report links the 2022 third-country-national inflow surge to Russian aggression, with TCN arrivals reaching 3,324,000 (+133%) [p446]. In Central Europe, Czechia’s TCN share was heightened by Ukrainian inflows, which rose from 32,000 in 2021 to 308,000 in 2022, while Slovenia and Croatia’s high TCN shares were described as longer-term rather than significantly Ukraine-driven [p453]. Poland hosted 957,505 Ukrainian refugees as of 11 June 2024, though Germany and Poland did not report specific Ukrainian entry data [p446][p444]. Western countries also saw TCN share increases—Germany +28 pps, Ireland +24 pps, Portugal +24 pps—but the pages do not directly attribute those increases to Ukraine [p453].

26.text: The disparity is explained by inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493]. Among EU movers, about 36% of women work part-time versus 8% of men, a 28 pp gap [p493]. In the countries with the highest female mover part-time rates—Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%)—male EU movers’ rates are much lower at 12%, 14% and 9%, respectively [p493].

27.text: The EU’s 2030 employment rate target is 78%, as set by the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan [p704].

28.text: Nine EU Member States had ratified ILO Convention C189 by October 2024: Belgium, Germany, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Malta, Portugal, and Sweden [p310][p255].

29.text: In 2022, the highest involuntary part-time shares among part-time workers were in Bulgaria and Romania (60% each), Italy (58%), Spain (51%), and Greece (48%) [p489]. In 2023, Romania, Italy, and Spain still recorded shares above 50% [p675]. The pages attribute cross-country differences broadly to varying labour-market conditions and economic structures, noting that in low-incidence countries part-time work may be more a choice than a necessity [p489].

31.text: Strong nominal wage growth—6.1% in 2023 after 4.9% in 2022—combined with falling inflation turned real wage growth positive in the second half of 2023, reaching 2.4% year-on-year in Q2 2024 (1.8% in the euro area) [p785][p790][p715]. Nominal wage growth had moderated to 5.0% in Q2 2024 (4.3% in the euro area), while real wages had fallen by 3.9% in 2022 and 0.2% in 2023 overall [p785][p790]. Despite the rebound, EU real wages in 2024 were still forecast to be 1.1% below their 2019 level [p715][p791].

32.text: From 2021 to 2022, Sweden’s 20–34 share fell 1 pp (61% to 60%), its 35–49 share rose 1 pp (29% to 30%), and its 50–64 share rose 1 pp (10% to 11%); Slovenia’s 20–34 share rose 3 pp (42% to 45%), while 35–49 fell 2 pp (37% to 35%) and 50–64 fell 1 pp (21% to 20%); Switzerland’s 20–34 share fell 2 pp (59% to 57%), 35–49 rose 1 pp (31% to 32%), and 50–64 stayed at 11% [p377]. These mixed country shifts contrast with the EU-wide stock trend, where the 20–34 cohort shrank 3 pps and the 50–64 cohort expanded 3 pps between 2018 and 2023 [p460]. They may change the age profile of mobile workers available to destination labour markets, but the provided pages do not quantify the resulting labour-mobility effects [p377][p460].

33.text: The projected increase is **8.8 million** economically active people aged 55–68 in the EU by 2030, calculated as **6.0 million** aged 55–64 plus **2.8 million** aged 65–68 [p737][p833][p840].

34.text: The provided pages do not quantify a direct effect of declining PISA scores on long-term economic growth. They warn that worsening basic skills pose a major risk to the EU’s future labour productivity and competitiveness, with potential negative impacts on competitiveness and wage developments in the longer term [p131][p648][p574].

35.text: AI-exposed occupations are broadly gender-balanced: EU-LFS 2021 data show a slightly higher proportion of job holders are women (52%), but women remain underrepresented in the occupations with the highest AI exposure [p878]. At a more granular level, gender segregation persists in certain jobs with higher AI exposure, and both women and men experience approximately the same level of higher occupational exposure to AI [p878][p905].

37.text: Countries with higher part-time employment may have lower underemployment because national differences in the **acceptability and prevalence of part-time work**, institutional settings, part-time/full-time pay gaps, work-family reconciliation options, and taxation shape whether part-timers want more hours [p848]. The report also says acceptability and remuneration of part-time work play a role in underemployment [p853]. This suggests lower underemployment can reflect part-time work being a genuine preference where it is normalized and supported—but it can also “mask underlying labour market issues” and limited choices, especially for women facing structural barriers [p853].

38.text: In 2023, the EU employment rate for women aged 20–64 was **70.2%** [p72]. For **EU movers** specifically, the female employment rate was **71%** in 2023 [p491].

40.text: Luxembourg ranks at the top of the compensation-per-employee-in-PPS graph [p815], but its wage growth was below 3.2% in Q2 2024 and real wages fell by 1.4 pps after a strong 2023 rebound [p788][p791]. This contrasts with Eastern European Member States, where nominal wage growth exceeded 11% in Bulgaria, Croatia, Latvia, Hungary, Poland and Romania, and real wage growth was relatively strong in many central and eastern EU countries [p788][p791].

41.text: The PES Network had been operational for 10 years: it has worked since 2014, and 2024 marked its 10-year anniversary [p1055][p1056]. The 2024 Annual Report was published in January 2025 [p1029].

42.text: Southern European countries such as Greece, Spain, France, Italy, Cyprus and Malta had comparatively low wage and unit labour cost growth in 2022–2023, with high unit profits and moderate wage growth, suggesting some room for wage increases [p804]. By contrast, the Baltic countries, Bulgaria, Croatia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Poland and Romania experienced strong wage and ULC growth with the energy crisis, and concerns grew about deteriorating cost competitiveness in Bulgaria, Czechia, Estonia, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia [p805]. The report concludes that several Southern European countries gained cost competitiveness and had wage growth below benchmarks, while many central and eastern European countries experienced competitiveness losses [p808].

44.text: Age-based mobility trends matter because older workers make fewer sector-to-sector transitions than younger workers in the EU [p24], and older workers receive the least training across “transforming” sectors [p25], which can constrain reallocation into green industries. Mobility also varies across Member States: Estonia and Finland appear generally more mobile across sectors, while some countries show significant discrepancies between younger and older workers’ mobility [p7].

45.text: Digital-intensive jobs have a higher share of young workers—about one in four aged 15–29—and a lower share aged 55–64, while occupations with intermediate-to-low digital skills have roughly equal younger and older shares [p881]. Green occupations of interest have a lower share of workers aged 15–29, especially residual green occupations, indicating scope to make them more attractive to younger workers [p881].

46.text: EU labour-market resilience was supported by an expanding labour supply: labour force growth accelerated to nearly 1% in 2022 and 2023, with non-EU nationals contributing 1.24 million to the 2023 total labour force rise of almost 2 million [p704]. Improved matching, evidenced by a low long-term unemployment rate and the COVID-19 policy response that prevented unemployment scarring, also helped [p704]. Firms retained more workers than needed in anticipation of recovery [p704], while labour demand remained resilient and job creation was stronger in sectors facing labour shortages [p632].

47.text: Yes. The EU unemployment rate reached a new record low of 5.7% in February 2025 [p861][p864], below the 6.1% unemployment level reported for 2023 [p66].

48.text: The March 2024 EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages sets out 87 new actions across five domains: activating under-represented people, supporting skills/training/education, improving working conditions, enhancing fair intra-EU mobility, and attracting talent from outside the EU [p635]. Related measures include the EU Talent Pool, the European Skills Agenda, individual learning accounts and micro-credentials, and boosting participation of older workers, women and young people not in education, employment or training [p771].

49.text: Denmark and Poland have abolished mandatory retirement ages as a valid reason to terminate labour contracts, while Belgium and Estonia have programmes in which training providers assess applicants’ competence by validating previous relevant experience [p839]. The Netherlands screens job vacancy notices for discriminatory language under the “vacancies for all ages” initiative, and France’s Public Employment Service selects candidates for employer interviews based on aptitude tests without regard to age or previously held employment [p839].

50.text: In 2023, 14% of EU movers held fixed-term contracts, compared with 24% of third-country nationals [p485][p411]. Table 39 shows 843 EU movers and 2,192 third-country nationals on fixed-term contracts in 2023 [p411]. Thus TCNs had a 10 percentage-point higher fixed-term contract share than EU movers [p485][p411].

51.text: Yes. France and Sweden are among five Member States that have raised statutory retirement ages since 2020 [p836]. Currently adopted retirement reforms are the main factor behind the projected increase in active people aged 55–68, expected to bring 6.3 million new active individuals into the labour market by 2030 [p833]; overall projections show +6 million active people aged 55–64 and +2.8 million aged 65–68 in the EU by 2030, mostly due to ageing and already adopted pension reforms [p737].

52.text: The difference is 10 percentage points: 96% of EU movers in healthcare had permanent contracts in 2023, compared with 86% of nationals [p394].

53.text: Workers in green in-demand jobs facing labour shortages have above-average job strain, whereas occupations with higher digital skills intensity have the lowest job strain at 16% [p887]. Earnings predictability is about 50% in green in-demand jobs and labour-shortage occupations, while it is highest in higher-digital-skills and AI-exposed occupations [p884][p906].

54.text: Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a permanent-contract rate of 73.7%, which is 4 percentage points above the EU average of 69.7% [p884]. Occupations with higher digital skills intensity have the highest permanent-contract share, shown as 79% in Figure 7, compared with the same 69.7% EU average [p883][p884].

55.text: In 2023, the EU employment rate for older workers aged 55–64 reached 63.9%, still 18 pps below the prime-age rate (82.2%) [p659]. It was above 70% in Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Latvia, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden, but below 55% in Greece, Croatia, Luxembourg, Romania and Slovenia [p821][p659]. The largest increases since 2009 were around 30 pps in Hungary, Poland and Slovenia for ages 55–59, and in Denmark, Hungary and Slovakia for ages 60–64 [p821].

56.text: In 2023, EU movers had higher labour-market integration than third-country nationals: activity 83% vs 72%, employment 78% vs 63%, and unemployment 7% vs 12% [p474]. For part-time work, EU movers stayed around 21–22% from 2018 to 2023, while TCNs declined from 26% in 2018 to 22% in 2023, making their rates similar by 2023 [p487]. Both groups work part-time more often than nationals, whose rate was 17% [p487].

57.text: Under the static scenario, the EU labour force is projected to decline by about 42.8 million people by 2070 [p1011].

58.text: A population equivalent to 10% of Estonia’s practicing nurse population is residing and working in other EU Member States or EFTA countries [p343].

60.text: No. Figure 6 shows Member States split between having implemented ILAs, having no ILA but plans, having no plans, and not submitting feedback; only a few PES had begun introducing ILA schemes in summer 2024 [p1032]. The report also notes that 13 out of 31 PES were designing pilots or had plans to introduce ILAs, while 2 out of 31 were taking a supporting role [p1031].

61.text: Underlying causes include strong gender segregation: most future-oriented occupations are male-dominated, women make up just 28% of green-task jobs, and ICT occupations underrepresent women and older workers [p876]. Care responsibilities also constrain participation: 7.7 million women in the EU remain outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450 000 men, and women lag in STEM skills, hindering entry into emerging green and digital industries [p931]. Policy actions should include accessible upskilling and reskilling programmes and inclusive educational pathways [p941], lifelong learning organised to accommodate care responsibilities [p875], and prioritising care responsibilities while closing the STEM skills gap [p931]. Women’s participation in future-oriented green and digital jobs is also framed as necessary for an inclusive transition [p876].

62.text: Yes. The gap in temporary/fixed-term employment between EU movers and nationals narrowed from 5 percentage points in 2018 to 3 percentage points in 2023, as EU movers’ share fell from 19% to 14% and nationals’ from 14% to 11% [p485].

63.text: The rise was largely driven by the Russian aggression against Ukraine, which caused a significant influx of Ukrainian refugees; third-country national inflows doubled between 2021 and 2022 to 3,324,000 (+133%) [p444][p446]. It also partly reflects the post-pandemic resurgence of migration flows, particularly the large influx of Ukrainian refugees, who were mostly women [p755].

64.text: Greece’s employment rate (15–64) rose from 56.5% in 2019 to 61.8% in 2023, a change of +5.3 pp [p722]. Portugal’s rose from 70.5% to 72.5%, a change of +2.0 pp [p738].

65.text: The PES Network launched a LinkedIn group as an online space to engage its community and stakeholders, and its Digitalisation Working Group supports PES IT experts in driving digital progress [p1054]. It also produces PESPod episodes on the PES Knowledge Centre and disseminates news and newsletters [p1051], while publishing PES Practices in the PES Practice Repository [p1050].

66.text: In the Netherlands, full-time employment among returning health workers rose from 0% in 2018 to 38% in 2023, while part-time employment fell from 100% to 62% [p430]. In Italy, full-time employment fell from 100% in 2018 to 69% in 2023, with part-time rising from 0% to 31% [p430]. Thus, the Netherlands moved toward more full-time work, while Italy moved in the opposite direction; all these values are marked as low reliability in parentheses [p430].

67.text: Digitalisation has mainstreamed platform work into unequal, exploitative labour dynamics marked by low wages and absent social protection, especially for vulnerable groups lacking alternative income [p925]. AI-enabled algorithmic management widens power imbalances between platforms and workers and enables invasive data collection and surveillance to maximise productivity [p925], while AI also acts as a “new competitor” reducing workers’ bargaining power and creating “invisible” AI workers exposed to repetitive and potentially damaging content [p925]. In the EU platform economy, revenues grew almost fivefold between 2016 and 2020, more than 28 million people were estimated to work through digital labour platforms in 2020, 5.5 million were estimated to be incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earned less than the minimum wage [p552]. The 2024 platform work Directive aims to address bogus self-employment through a legal presumption of employment and to ensure transparency, fairness and accountability on algorithmic management [p552].

68.text: No, not uniformly across European countries. In Austria and Germany the estimated share of undeclared workers is 90% or more in the non-care sector and significantly lower in care-related services, and in Malta undeclared work is much more likely in non-care domestic work [p283]. However, Italy reported an even distribution across both sectors in 2022, while in Bulgaria most LTC domestic workers are argued to operate in the informal economy and Ireland has a significant informal home care sector [p283].

69.text: Estonia’s approach includes a doctoral studies reform—junior researcher positions with wages/social guarantees, an industrial PhD scheme, and MSCA Seal of Excellence funding for incoming postdocs [p1089]—and it has introduced a new track tenure model [p1068]. Germany is cited for a tenure track example in Annex 9.1, framed as bridging R2 short-term contracts to a permanent R3 position [p1075]. Slovenia is only listed as a participating country [p1106]; the pages do not describe a Slovenian initiative, so no comparison can be made for Slovenia.

70.text: The report outlines an integrated approach through the EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages, mobilising underutilised resources via the EU Talent Pool, the European Skills Agenda, individual learning accounts and micro-credentials, while increasing participation among older workers, women and young people not in education, employment or training, and promoting intra-EU mobility and attraction/integration of non-EU talent [p771]. It also stresses fair working conditions and adequate wages, minimum wage protection and collective bargaining, integration of women, young people, persons with disabilities and those with a migrant background, plus targeted activation and skills policies, affordable childcare and long-term care, pension reforms and flexible working arrangements to support older workers [p787].

71.text: Across 2010–2019, EU sector-to-sector transition rates mostly fell between 1.8% and 3.9%, remained relatively stable, and showed a slight upward trend around 2016 in some Member States [p7][p24]. From 2018 to 2019, all “transforming sectors” except mining had net inflows of workers, while mining was the only transforming sector with a net outflow [p9][p24]. Older workers make fewer sectoral transitions than younger workers, with no significant difference between men and women [p24].

72.text: Future-oriented occupations accounted for 32% of workers in the EU in 2021 [p873].

74.text: By October 2024, only nine EU Member States had ratified ILO Convention C189: Belgium, Germany, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Malta, Portugal and Sweden [p310][p255]. The listed ratification years are Italy and Germany 2013; Ireland 2014; Belgium, Finland and Portugal 2015; Sweden 2019; Malta 2021; and Spain 2023 [p304].

75.text: Nine EU Member States have ratified ILO Convention C189 [p231][p255], while eight Member States apply the same labour-law and social-protection rules to domestic workers as to other workers without distinction [p231][p261]. The ratified count is therefore one higher.

76.text: Labour-shortage occupations report the highest job strain (48%), while AI-exposed occupations have below-average job strain and are among those with the lowest job strain [p887][p906]. For training, AI-exposed occupations have the lowest share of workers who received no education or training in the preceding four weeks, whereas access to learning is lowest for workers in labour-shortage jobs [p904][p888].

77.text: Recent evidence links more training completed by people aged 55–64 to higher unemployment-to-employment transitions: Denmark had about 20% more training hours than EU 25–64 year-olds and the highest transition rate (more than 30%), while low-training Bulgaria, Greece, Romania and Slovakia had rates below 10% per quarter [p828]. In 2022, more than half of older people participated in training in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Sweden, versus less than 15% in Bulgaria, Greece, Poland and Romania [p827]. Overall adult-learning participation in 2022 was highest in Sweden (66.5%), Hungary (62.2%), the Netherlands (56.1%) and Germany (53.7%), and lowest in Bulgaria (9.5%), Greece (15.1%), Poland (20.3%) and Czechia (21.2%) [p653]. The report says this pattern is consistent with research showing education and training policies are among the most effective tools for promoting older workers’ employment, especially when combined with search assistance and counselling [p828].

78.text: Converging to Sweden’s higher labour-force participation rates by age, sex, and education would almost completely offset the projected negative impact of ageing on EU labour supply: the labour force would decline by only 2.8 pp, or 5.9 million people, by 2070 [p1012]. This is far smaller than the standard “Static” scenario’s projected decline of 20.2 pp, or about 42.8 million people, by 2070 [p1011]. Combining all forms of activation, as in the Swedish-rate scenario, would almost fully compensate for the workforce decline [p1013].

79.text: In 2022, EU public expenditure on education was allocated roughly as follows: pre-primary and primary **34%**, secondary **36.8%**, and tertiary **16.6%** [p130]. Over **70%** went to school education overall [p130].

80.text: The predominant posted third-country nationals are Ukrainians, especially in Belgium, Lithuania, the Netherlands, and Austria [p1008][p974]; Lithuania’s posted workers are mainly Ukrainian and Belarusian TCNs [p960], while 41% of TCNs received by Bulgaria were Turkish [p959]. TCN-specific sector evidence is limited, but Lithuanian posting undertakings mainly employ TCNs in road freight transport [p960]; more generally, posted workers are often active in construction and manufacturing [p959][p960].

81.text: In Bulgaria, 35.5% of adults had at least basic digital skills in 2023, compared with 55.6% at EU level [p548]. The same 35.5% figure is reported for Bulgaria for the population aged 16–74 with basic or above basic overall digital skills [p655].

82.text: Real statutory minimum wages rose by more than 10% between January 2022 and January 2024 in **Belgium** and **Bulgaria**, indicating real gains [p640]. By contrast, high inflation diminished these gains: real statutory minimum wages fell by more than 3% in **Czechia** and **Slovakia** over the same period [p640]; the January 2022–July 2024 data also show real declines of more than 3% in Czechia and Slovakia and 1.3% in France [p796].

83.text: High graduation rates do not guarantee adequate staffing: Ireland, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia and Romania have above-EU-average densities of medical doctor and nurse graduates but below-EU-average densities of available healthcare workers [p338]. Retention and outflow are key systemic issues—Italy faces insufficient medical school graduates and an outflow of doctors, while Latvia has the equivalent of 15% of its doctors practising in other Member States [p358]. Returnee inflows are not clearly sufficient to offset these outflows [p358].

84.text: Based on EU-SILC data, minimum wage non-compliance is estimated to affect more than 8% of the workforce in Germany, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Lithuania, Hungary, Portugal and Sweden [p797]. The workers most affected are young people, unskilled workers, women, workers in smaller firms and part-time workers; they are generally younger, less educated, more likely female, on fixed-term or part-time contracts, and employed by smaller firms [p797]. The report also notes that workers in services sectors may be particularly affected [p796].

85.text: Labour market transitions can support the green transition by moving workers out of shrinking sectors such as mining and into expanding or transforming sectors, helping avoid worsening labour shortages in affected sectors such as construction and transportation [p46]. Relatively high transitions in the sectors most affected by the green transition can facilitate a smoother labour-market adjustment to expected sectoral changes [p46]. However, training and education in some key sectors is lagging [p12], and delivering EU Green Deal wind and solar targets would require about 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU by 2030, with associated skills investment of EUR 1.1–1.4 billion [p12].

86.text: The pages attribute the high part-time rate among female EU movers—36% vs 8% for men in 2023, a 28-pp gap—to factors including inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493]. They also note the highest female-mover part-time rates in Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%), where male mover rates are much lower [p493]. Broader evidence links women’s higher part-time work to parenthood and informal long-term care responsibilities [p660].

88.text: Yes. Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a higher-than-average incidence of permanent employment, 4 percentage points above the average of 69.7% [p884].

89.text: Key factors are population ageing and decline, women’s emancipation, rising educational attainment, and migration assumptions [p1023][p1022]. By 2070, the static scenario projects a 20.2 pp/42.8 million labour-force decline; education reduces this to 15.6 pp/33.2 million, women-to-men participation to 11.0 pp/23.2 million, older-worker convergence to 11.9 pp/25.2 million, no migration to 26.7 pp/55.9 million, and convergence to Swedish rates to only 2.8 pp/5.9 million [p1011][p1012]. Proposed responses include investing in skills/human capital and activating untapped labour-force potential—8 million among ages 20-29, 12 million among ages 55-64, and 17 million women [p1023][p1017][p1022]. The brief also discusses extending working lives/retirement-age reforms and migration’s role in offsetting ageing [p1012].

90.text: Women part-time workers are less likely to be underemployed (18%; mothers 16%) than men, only about 8% of employed men work part-time and more than a quarter of male part-timers want longer hours, somewhat higher among fathers [p850]. Part-time workers living with a partner are much less likely to be underemployed (15%) than those without a partner (26%) [p850]. These patterns reflect different drivers: women’s lower underemployment is linked to structural time constraints and care responsibilities that may prevent them even considering longer hours, while men’s higher underemployment is linked to gendered primary-earner attitudes and part-time work being rarely preferred; partnered workers can rely on two-earner household income, whereas singles rely largely on their own income [p850]. Regression results show women and people living with partners have an 8 pp or more lower probability of underemployment than men and singles, respectively, and this is not explained by occupational and sectoral employment patterns [p851].

91.text: Uneven digitalisation across Europe can widen the digital divide and workplace inequalities, and digitalisation can self-reinforce social exclusion and create new categories of vulnerable workers [p924]. Platformisation and AI/robotics bring risks such as algorithmic control, physically and mentally taxing jobs, digital-skill gaps, and job displacement; in 2020, more than 28 million people worked through digital labour platforms, 5.5 million were estimated to be incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earned less than the minimum wage [p552][p924]. AI may replace routine jobs and generative AI could significantly affect high-skilled workers, while digitalisation can also increase mental stress and skilled-worker shortages [p552][p926].

92.text: In 2023, non-EU nationals accounted for **64.1%** of the total increase in the EU labour force [p755].

93.text: In 2022, EU movers had a lower AROPE rate (27%) than third-country nationals (46%), and their severe material and social deprivation rate was 8% versus 16% for TCNs [p504][p509]. Their housing cost overburden rate was also lower than TCNs’ (19% vs 26%) [p504]. The pages note that country-level disparities may reflect movers’ characteristics such as education, skills, or employment sectors interacting with national circumstances [p510], and that TCNs here include all non-EU-27 citizens, including EFTA countries [p508].

94.text: Benchlearning supports PES modernisation by systematically comparing their organisational setups and outcomes against an “ideal PES,” using quantitative performance data and self-, peer- and expert review so PES can learn from peers and improve performance [p1045]. The 4th Benchlearning cycle launched in January 2024, with 15 assessments covering Lithuania, Bulgaria, Latvia, Croatia, Austria, Portugal, Hungary, Germany, Greece, Czechia, Estonia, The Netherlands, Malta, Ireland and Cyprus; all were onsite except Portugal, which was fully online [p1045]. The 2024 Work Programme was delivered through Benchlearning, with 15 assessments in 2024 (LT, BG, LV, HR, AT, PT, HU, DE, EL, CZ, EE, NL, MT, IE and CY) [p1056]. For example, Estonia’s PES received practical tips from other PES, including Austria on quality assessment and performance management and Germany on evaluating labour market measures and decision-support tools [p1045].

95.text: In 2023, people with tertiary education had the highest EU employment rate at 86.3%, and the gap between high- and low-educated persons aged 25–64 was still 28.0 pps [p618].

96.text: The pages attribute the lower mobility of energy-intensive industry (EII) workers partly to their demographic profile, as the workforce is “relatively male dominated,” which likely contributes to lower mobility into unemployment and inactivity [p13]. They also note that EII sectors are characterised by “a high degree of labour market stability,” possibly explained by these being “relatively well-paid industries” with reported wage premiums [p13].

97.text: Career guidance has shifted toward twin-transition competencies: 51% of PES report changes in focus on digital and green skills, 48% on digital skills and 32% on green skills [p1058]. This mirrors wider labour-market change: EU ICT specialists rose 59.3% since 2013 to over 9.5 million in 2023, while 4 in 10 adults and one-third of workers lack basic digital skills [p638], and the green economy grew from 2.2% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2021, with 1.8–3.9% of EU workers switching sector annually [p638]. Training patterns also align, as workers in occupations with higher AI exposure and high digital-skills intensity are least likely to report no recent training, though one in five received some training in the preceding four weeks [p904].

98.text: Factors include women’s lag in STEM skills, which hinders participation in emerging green/digital industries, and disproportionate care responsibilities that constrain labour-market access and stable employment [p931]. Green-task jobs are also strongly gender-segregated, with women making up just 28% of such jobs, while green and digitally intensive occupations are more male-dominated [p876]. This leaves women underrepresented in “transforming sectors”: only 14% of mining workers and 26.7% of energy workers in 2023 were women [p6][p24].

99.text: In 2023, older workers (55–64) were a key driver of EU employment growth: their employment rate reached 63.9% and activity rate 67.0%, both almost 20 pps above 2009, and their share of total employment rose from 10% in 2003 to close to 20% in 2023 [p618][p819]. From 2019 to 2023, older workers remained the main driver of labour-force growth, adding about 1.2 million people yearly [p753]. By contrast, youth (15–24) employment and participation rates were much lower at 35.2% and 41.2% in 2023, though they returned to pre-2008 financial-crisis levels and the NEET rate (15–29) hit a record low of 11.2% [p618].

100.text: The projected investment in skills needed for additional wind and solar deployment to meet EU Green Deal targets is **EUR 1.1 to 1.4 billion by 2030** [p21][p138]. This is associated with about **130,000 to 145,000 additional skilled workers** in the EU [p25][p138].

101.text: Yes. The report states that older people transition from unemployment to employment at higher rates when they complete more education, and countries with high training levels (e.g. Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria) have relatively high transition rates, while low-training countries (e.g. Bulgaria, Greece, Romania, Slovakia) have rates below 10% per quarter [p828]. Graph 3.18 also presents the amount of education/training completed by people aged 55–64 alongside transition rates from unemployment to employment [p710].

102.text: Based on the PHS Employment Monitor for 2024, more than 15% of workers surveyed reported undeclared care work in **Poland** and **Spain**, and **35%** in **Italy** [p165].

103.text: The green transition transforms sectors such as mining and quarrying, manufacturing, energy, water/waste management, construction and transportation, with some expanding and others declining, which can require worker transitions [p24][p46]. EU data show average year-on-year sector-to-sector transition rates of 1.8–3.9%, and from 2018–2019 there was a net inflow of workers into all “transforming sectors” except mining and extraction [p24]. Older workers make fewer sectoral transitions, while women remain underrepresented—26.7% of energy-industry workers in 2023 and 14% in mining—and energy-intensive industries show fewer transitions to non-employment than other sectors [p24]. Delivering additional wind and solar installations would require about 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU, with skills investment of EUR 1.1–1.4 billion by 2030 [p12].

104.text: The pages highlight workers with disabilities—especially women and young people with disabilities—as particularly vulnerable, with an EU employment rate of only 50.6% for people with disabilities versus 74.8% for those without [p928]. They also identify vulnerable workers such as those in precarious employment, self-employed individuals, and people facing discrimination, as well as groups affected by disability, unpaid care work, and regional disparities [p926]. Emerging vulnerable groups include skilled workers in transition industries and workers in energy-intensive or fossil fuel-dependent industries and their regions [p946][p933].

105.text: Portugal applies a special “domestic service” regime outside the Labour Code; even formalised carers usually lack unemployment benefits because access requires a full-time monthly contract and not opting for the lower-contribution “agreed regime,” while most work for several employers and opt for that regime [p177][p269]. Hungary formally gives domestic workers employed as employees (including simplified employment) and the self-employed access to labour protection and all insurance-based benefits, but those under Act XC of 2010 are excluded and may only get basic healthcare if they pay for it [p275][p269]. Portugal has ratified ILO C189 and broader collective agreements cover domestic workers, whereas Hungary has not ratified C189 and has no collective agreements covering domestic workers [p261]. Shortfalls remain in Portugal’s unemployment/social protection for domestic service workers and in Hungary for Act XC 2010 workers and carers more broadly, who are not monitored and lack workers’ representation, collective bargaining, and social/legal protection [p177][p275][p269].

106.text: No. The Draghi report projects the EU workforce to shrink by close to 2 million workers each year by 2040 [p1023], while the activation scenarios only mitigate the decline: women’s convergence still leaves 23.2 million fewer workers by 2070, education 33.2 million fewer, and older-worker activation 25.2 million fewer [p1012]. Even convergence to Sweden’s participation levels leaves a projected decline of 5.9 million by 2070, so underutilized-group activation does not fully offset the projected losses [p1012].

108.text: Yes. Underemployment is higher among younger workers: for young people, more than a fourth of part-time workers are underemployed [p849], while older workers aged 55–64 account for about a quarter of part-timers but less than 15% of the underemployed [p846]. The probability of underemployment also drops for men aged 55–64 compared with middle-aged counterparts [p853].

109.text: Austria and France show regional income convergence: absolute disparities fell [p105], and low-income regions caught up, with beta coefficients of -0.02 for Austria (2014-2021) and -0.01 for France (2014-2021) [p106]. Czechia and Sweden differ: absolute disparities rose in both [p105], and Sweden is one of only two countries where relative median-income differences did not converge [p106]; Czechia’s absolute dispersion increased but relative dispersion declined because the increase was smaller than cross-regional average median-income growth [p106]. The pages explain this through metropolitan vs non-metropolitan income growth: in Austria growth was slow in Graz, Innsbruck, Linz-Wels, Salzburg und Umgebung, and Vienna, while in Sweden Stockholm had among the highest median income growth and Södermanland and Kronoberg the lowest [p106].

110.text: Yes. The report states that as labour demand increased over the last decade, underemployment “steadily declined both in relative and absolute terms”: around 30% of part-time workers were underemployed in 2013, compared with less than 20% by 2023, and the number of part-time workers immediately available to work longer hours fell from over 8 million to about 5 million during 2013–2023 [p847].

111.text: Undeclared care workers face “extremely poor job security” and lower wages than counterparts who declare their work [p173]. They lack legal protection and social protection, including in case of unemployment or illness [p177], whereas declared workers are entitled to labour rights such as additional compensation, overtime pay, and paid leave [p193]. Even when formalised, carers may not enjoy equal protections: in Portugal, domestic service workers have a special regime outside the Labour Code, and most lack access to unemployment benefits unless they have a full-time monthly contract and have not opted for the lower-contribution “agreed regime” [p177].

112.text: The statistical definition adds workers in ISCO categories **5152 (“butlers”), 5162 (“companions and valets”), 5322 (“home-based personal care workers”), and 9111 (“domestic cleaners and helpers”)**, in addition to all workers in NACE 97, avoiding double counting [p240][p230].

114.text: No. Although real wage growth turned positive and reached 2.4% year-on-year in Q2-2024, real wages in the EU remained below pre-pandemic levels on average and in eight Member States [p530][p715]. They were still forecast to be 1.1% below their 2019 level in 2024 [p715][p791].

115.text: According to Table 2.1, beta convergence (catching-up) was found for the AROPE rate (-0.04 in both periods), AROPE rate of children (-0.03 in both), housing cost overburden (-0.04 and -0.05), and adult participation in learning (-0.06 and -0.03) [p100]. Healthy life years at age 65 for women showed catching-up only in 2014-2023 (-0.03), while tertiary education attainment showed catching-up only in 2007-2014 (-0.06) [p100]. Healthy life years at age 65 for men showed no robust evidence of convergence [p100].

116.text: Evidence on effectiveness is mixed and mostly anecdotal: voucher impact on undeclared work is generally “quite low” in Austria, Belgium and Greece [p286], with Austria reporting vouchers are scarcely used and a 2018 Belgian study estimating that less than 10% of domestic work paid via vouchers used to be undeclared work [p286]; in Sweden, RUT evaluations suggest a probable link to low undeclared work, but this remains unsubstantiated [p287]. Tax incentives vary more: Germany reports little effect, while Spain’s 2011 introduction increased declared domestic workers over the following two years before plateauing [p287]. Coverage differs because voucher systems are implemented differently and can be inefficient when vouchers cover only up to the marginal employment threshold, as in Austria [p285], while tax deductions range from 5% in Portugal to 20% in most Member States using them and are sometimes linked to vouchers (BE, FR, HR, IT, LT, RO, SE) [p285]. Equity is a core weakness for tax incentives—German relief rises with taxable household income, and in Sweden the highest income decile received 40% of total tax deductions in a 2020 report [p287]; moreover, vouchers and tax incentives may primarily benefit higher-income households and have limited impact on formalising undeclared care work among lower-income groups, while vouchers may ensure basic social security coverage but perpetuate low wages [p194].

117.text: In 2024, the PES Network started the fourth Benchlearning cycle with 15 PES assessments and ran mutual assistance programmes for Luxembourg and Romania, alongside its Digitalisation Working Group [p1054][p1056]. Annex 2 lists the Digitalisation Working Group chaired by NL, Mutual Assistance to PES RO, and “Digital matching tools” Mutual Assistance to PES LU [p1050]. The main focuses were modernising PES service delivery, digitalisation and data-driven strategies, and digital matching tools [p1056][p1050].

118.text: Yes. EU movers’ inflow to EU/EFTA countries rose from 859,000 in 2021 to 976,000 in 2022 (+14%), an increase of 117,000, while their outflow fell from 584,000 to 543,000 (-7%), a decrease of 41,000 [p443]. Thus the inflow increase outweighed the outflow decrease.

119.text: EU movers’ EU-wide median income is higher because movers tend to go to Member States with relatively high income levels, which raises their EU-wide median even though they often earn less than nationals within each country [p524]. In 2022, EU movers’ median income was EUR 20 714 versus EUR 19 506 for nationals, while nationals’ income grew faster at 2.6% annually compared with 1.9% for EU movers [p524].

120.text: Using the 2023 figure of nearly 9.8 million ICT specialists and the 20 million 2030 target [p656], the required compound annual increase from 2023 to 2030 is approximately **10.7% per year**.

121.text: Digital transformation in PES includes online counselling and job matching, blended online/face-to-face services, digital skills training, and outreach via social media/online campaigns, especially for vulnerable jobseekers [p1037]. PES are also using or considering mixed service delivery with external partners, and AI matching was explored through a Mutual Assistance Project involving Belgium-VDAB and Sweden [p1042]. Key benefits include reaching groups furthest from the labour market and enhancing capacity/expertise [p1042], while digital public services can deliver faster services while maintaining quality and transparency, improve accessibility and efficiency, give user-friendly access, reduce corruption risk, and involve more citizens and enterprises at lower cost [p934].

122.text: The case studies on AI-powered job matching showcased approaches used in **Belgium-VDAB** and **Sweden** [p1042].

123.text: Workers in energy-intensive industries (EII) are relatively male-dominated, have high labour-market stability, and are often relatively well-paid, with less outflow into inactivity/unemployment than the total economy over 2014-2023 [p13]. Higher trade-union density and male dominance may help explain these lower transitions [p13][p25]. However, only 10.9% of EII workers received training in 2023 in the EU, versus 12.7% economy-wide [p25], while high-carbon jobs face 20% higher odds of unemployment [p14], so reskilling is needed for the green transition.

124.text: The pages show third-country nationals have higher fixed-term contract shares than nationals in Spain (34% vs 20%), France (26% vs 14%), and Italy (23% vs 16%) [p412]. The report links higher TCN temporary employment to immigration policies, employer flexibility in seasonal/project sectors, and less stringent renewal rules [p486], which could reinforce segmented labour-market integration, though the pages do not estimate an overall EU-wide effect.

125.text: Social investment, especially in early childhood education and care (ECEC), can raise parents’—particularly mothers’—labour market participation and help narrow gender employment and pay gaps [p121]. Recent estimates for eight Member States show that increasing under-3s’ ECEC participation to 50% could improve mothers’ labour participation rates by 5% to 30%, with a 9 to 21 pp increase for mothers from low-income families, potentially helping to halve the gender gap [p126].

126.text: The future-oriented occupations with the highest access to employer-funded training are less digitally intensive green new and emerging occupations (56% of workers) and green enhanced occupations (53%), including jobs such as life science professionals, physicists, astronomers and financial analysts [p903].

127.text: R&I can address the twin transitions by focusing on four streams: combining economic goals with environmental and social sustainability and reducing worker inequalities in the green transition; ensuring human-centric digital technologies that serve workers’ needs, involve workers in design, and promote well-being; and anticipating future inequalities to protect existing and emerging vulnerable groups [p953][p950]. It should also close research gaps on skills for the green and digital transitions, the widening digital divide across regions, sectors and socioeconomic groups, equitable digital access for SMEs, AI impacts, new digital vulnerabilities, labour shortages and platformisation [p936]. The report frames opportunities in upskilling and reskilling, inclusive educational pathways and human-centred technology development [p946].

128.text: Only Finland saw regional differences in tertiary education attainment decline between 2007 and 2022, though national attainment also mildly declined [p104].

129.text: Principle 17 of the European Pillar of Social Rights supports the inclusion of people with disabilities in the labour market [p514][p929].

130.text: Part-time workers living with a partner are less likely to be underemployed: about 15% vs 26% for those living without a partner [p850]. Over 2013–2023, predicted probabilities were 0.308 for living with a partner vs 0.237 for living alone [p856], and the regression finds people with partners are at least 8 pp less likely to be underemployed than singles [p851]. This effect is much stronger for women—women with partners are 9 pp less likely than women without partners—while for men having a partner has no large effect [p852].

131.text: EU movers in healthcare are consistently more female: women accounted for **90–94%** of EU movers from 2017 to 2023, compared with **79–80%** of national workers [p334][p347].

132.text: The countries with vocational education and training (VET) graduate employment rates below 70% in 2023 were Italy, Spain, Romania, and Greece [p651].

133.text: Gender disparities in AI-impacted jobs are nuanced: EU-LFS 2021 data show occupations with higher AI exposure are broadly gender-balanced, with 52% of job holders being women, but women remain underrepresented in the occupations with the highest AI exposure, which may make them more vulnerable to the digital transition and less prepared to benefit from AI [p878]. The “AI workforce” is also small and male-dominated, while gender segregation persists in certain high-AI-exposure jobs and sectors such as health, finance, and statistics [p878][p905]. These patterns imply that the digital transformation’s inclusivity depends on addressing segregation in high-AI occupations and enabling women to access AI-related opportunities [p878][p905].

134.text: Yes. The ESDE 2023 report notes that, if supported by the right employment and education policies, net-zero policies could create between 884,000, one million, and 2.5 million jobs in some sectors by 2030 [p869].

135.text: Belgium, Italy and Ireland are expected to face higher re-training costs per person in the labour force despite lower current renewable shares (26.7%–37.7%), with 2030 re-training costs around EUR 10 in Italy and EUR 13 in Belgium [p22].

136.text: Real wage growth in the EU reached 2.4% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2024 [p790][p715].

137.text: A 1 pp increase in the high-skilled share is estimated to raise GDP per capita by 0.3 pp after 50 years, or 0.15 pp after 25 years [p1016]. For the projected 2020–2045 shift—a 14.15 pp rise in the high-skilled share with equal falls in middle/low-skilled shares—the implied GDP effects are 4.24 pp by 2095 and 2.12 pp by 2070 [p1016]. The pages also note individual returns to education in the EU15 of 4.1%–9.7% for males and 3.8%–13.7% for females per additional year [p1015], and conclude that skills investment can mitigate workforce decline and provide a competitive advantage, though not compensate for demographic decline [p1017].

138.text: Among those aged 55–64, 44% have at least basic digital skills, compared with 64% of those aged 25–54 [p828]. Older people complete fewer education and training hours than younger people, but they work in jobs better matched to their skills and in less dynamic workplaces, and report less need for skills development [p840]. Older individuals wanting training cite health, age and course availability more often, and cost less often, than younger people; about 8% in both age groups cite lack of support [p828].

139.text: Yes. The pages indicate that unequal digitalisation can feed the digital divide and workplace inequalities, and that persistent unequal digitalisation threatens to exacerbate regional disparities and widen gaps between SMEs, mid-caps and larger businesses [p924]. Digital skills disparities are sizeable across countries, ranging from 28% to 83%, with slightly increasing cross-country disparities in basic digital skills [p99]. The 2025 Joint Employment Report also warns that risks to upward convergence persist regarding skills, with no signs of convergence and a best-worst gap in digital skills exceeding 55 pps [p627].

141.text: Yes. Finland’s gender employment gap was nearly non-existent at 0.2 pps [p659], while Sweden’s gap among EU movers was 2 pps and 3 pps for Swedish nationals [p492], so Finland’s gap is narrower.

142.text: The green and digital transitions intersect for vulnerable workers by combining green-sector job creation and redistribution with digital skills mismatch, digital exclusion, gig-economy job security risks, and displacement of traditional industries toward greener sectors [p928][p954]. These effects can aggravate existing disadvantages, such as job displacement in carbon-heavy industries and skills gaps as industries digitalise rapidly [p927]. For example, workers with disabilities have an EU employment rate of only 50.6%, versus 74.8% for people without disabilities, and while teleworking may help some with physical disabilities, digitalisation can create new barriers for those with visual or auditory impairments and manual green roles may be less accessible for people with physical disabilities [p928].

143.text: Yes. The table source note states that for DK and NL the figures include both posted workers and self-employed persons [p1002].

144.text: Yes. In Q2-2024, the Netherlands had a job vacancy rate of 4.3%, while Poland was among the lowest at below 1% [p635].

145.text: The share of EU movers with low education rose from 28% in 2018 to 30% in 2023, an increase of 2 percentage points [p420].

147.text: EU movers’ self-employment share was 9% in 2017, rose to 11% in 2019, fell to about 4–5% in 2020, then rebounded to 8–9% in 2021–2023, ending at 8% in 2023 [p408][p482]. Third-country nationals started higher at 11% in 2017, were 10% in 2018–2019, dropped to 6% in 2020, rose to 9% in 2021, and stabilised around 8% in 2022–2023 [p408][p482]. Thus both groups dipped in 2020 and converged near 8% by 2023, but EU movers had a sharper fall and rebound [p482].

148.text: In EFTA countries, part-time work is generally more prevalent among nationals than among EU movers [p487]. For example, in Switzerland 43% of nationals work part-time compared with 27% of EU movers and 35% of third-country nationals [p487]. Among female EU movers, Switzerland has the highest part-time rate at 47% [p493].

150.text: The EU employment rate for individuals aged 20–64 was **75.3% in 2023** [p72][p680][p582].

151.text: Slovakia’s self-employment rate among domestic workers is **28%** in Table A3 for 2023 [p321]; the report text describes it as **around 30%** [p264].

152.text: The ERA4FutureWork initiative facilitated dialogue between policymakers, social partners and stakeholders through four workshops covering the green transition and working life, the digital world of work, the twin transitions and vulnerable groups, and the future of work in EU public administrations [p949][p950]. It examined R&I gaps across these four streams and proposed actions on upskilling/reskilling, inclusive education, labour mobility, remote work, platform work and labour-market inequalities [p950][p938]. The Commission also reports Horizon Europe funding of EUR 95.5 billion for 2021-2027 and monitors 250 Horizon 2020/Horizon Europe projects, including 212 linked to the EPSR action plan and 38 from other clusters, with nearly EUR 435 million in total EU contribution for all 250 projects [p952].

153.text: In 2023, job vacancy rates remained elevated in administrative and support service activities (including temporary employment agencies), accommodation and food service activities, professional, scientific and technical activities, and information and communication [p66].

154.text: In the EU27, ageing is represented by the strong rise in labour-market participation of people aged 55–64: in 2023, 41 million participated and 39 million were employed, with activity and employment rates of 67% and 63.9%, almost 20 pps above 2009 [p819]. The statistical annex confirms older (55–64) activity at 67.0% and employment at 63.9% in 2023 [p745]. The report also projects older employment rising from 62.3% in 2022 to 72.3% in 2070, even as the EU labour force is expected to decline by 0.3% annually [p818].

155.text: Men work part-time less often largely because of gendered attitudes that identify men as primary earners and women as primary caretakers; nearly half the EU population holds attitudes that at least partly support this distribution of paid and unpaid work, which helps explain why men take up part-time work less often [p850]. Women also work part-time more frequently due to care responsibilities and parenthood: in 2023, 27.9% of women aged 20–64 worked part-time versus 7.7% of men, and among employed women with children 31.8% worked part-time versus 5.0% of men [p660].

157.text: Care allowances are typically financial benefits or payments made to either carers or care recipients; they can be “unbound,” allowing beneficiaries to spend resources freely, or “bound,” requiring documentation of how funds are spent [p185]. They are increasingly used to fight undeclared care work by formalising care relationships and providing financial incentives to declare care work [p185].

The *European Network of Public Employment Services Annual Report 2024* (January 2025) covers a network created by an EP/Council Decision in June 2014, amended in 2020, to reinforce PES capacity, effectiveness and efficiency [p1029][p1030]. Its members are the PES of all 27 EU Member States plus Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and the European Commission, governed by a Board that meets twice a year and supported by a Commission-based Secretariat [p1055].

In 2024, Caroline Mancel continued as Chair and Inga Balnanosiené began as First Vice-Chair on 1 January; the Board met in Liège on 6–7 June and Budapest on 5–6 December, with two AFEPA meetings, and the year marked the Network’s 10-year anniversary [p1056]. The 2024 Work Programme was structured around four strands—structural and labour market challenges, PES service delivery, PES performance management, and PES governance and ecosystem—delivered through Benchlearning, Mutual Learning and communication, including 15 Benchlearning site assessments in LT, BG, LV, HR, AT, PT, HU, DE, EL, CZ, EE, NL, MT, IE and CY [p1056].

The report notes EU27 unemployment at 5.9% in September 2024 while labour and skills shortages continued to grow, and it highlights the Network’s Memorandum calling for a European Decade of Skills and action on skills, activation and EU instruments [p1055]. It also describes a more volatile 2024 labour market, worsening prospects in the October 2024 European Labour Market Barometer, and pressures from the demographic, green and digital transitions [p1057].

10.text: Evidence is mixed. Yet a 2021 Belgian study found service vouchers had halved undeclared work in the activities covered [p188]. Tax incentives also vary: Germany’s had “little effect,” while Spain’s 2011 introduction increased declared domestic workers over the following two years before plateauing [p287]; France’s CESU system was associated with informal employment falling from about 50% in 1996 to 20% in 2015 [p187]. Both vouchers and tax incentives may mainly benefit higher-income households and have limited impact on formalising undeclared care work among lower-income groups [p194].

14.text: Strong gender segregation persists in digital and green occupations: women make up just 28% of green-task jobs and are underrepresented in ICT, while green occupations with increased demand are more male-dominated [p876]. Care responsibilities keep 7.7 million women outside the EU labour market versus only 450,000 men, and women’s STEM skills gap hinders participation in emerging green and digital industries [p931]. The green transition’s job displacement and creation are concentrated in traditionally male-dominated sectors such as mining, engineering, construction and energy, and the “AI workforce” is small and male-dominated [p931][p878].

15.text: In 2023, employment-rate disparities between EU movers and third-country nationals were particularly significant in Belgium (24 pps), the Netherlands (24 pps), and Germany (22 pps) [p478]. The report attributes such gaps to factors including language barriers, difficulties recognising foreign qualifications, and legal/administrative hurdles in obtaining work permits [p478].

16.text: Gender segregation persists in future-oriented technical/digital occupations: higher-digital-skills-intensity and certain green jobs are largely male-dominated, while critical labour-shortage/care occupations have a higher share of women [p905]; ICT occupations are the most digitally intensive but underrepresent women and older workers [p876]. AI-exposed occupations are broadly gender-balanced at 52% women, but women remain underrepresented in the highest-AI-exposure jobs and the “AI workforce” is small and male-dominated [p878]. This can constrain long-term adaptability because women perform more tasks prone to automation and are at higher risk of being left behind in the digital transition, requiring more digital education and training [p876][p907]. Training access is also uneven: most workers in occupations of interest have not recently trained, although higher-AI/higher-digital-intensity occupations report the highest training shares [p907], while in transforming sectors energy has the highest training rates and mining/construction are below average, with energy-intensive industries at only 10.9% trained in 2023 versus 12.7% for the whole EU economy [p25].

17.text: Gender disparities make green-transition labour-market trends uneven: women were only 20% of the workforce in “transforming sectors” (31% in Lithuania and Bulgaria), 14% in mining in 2022 and 26.7% in energy in 2023 [p6][p24]. Expected job losses are concentrated in male-dominated mining, while gains in construction and waste management are also male-represented, so raising women’s employment in clean energy is key to a gender-neutral transition [p6]. Women hold just 28% of green-task jobs and are underrepresented in future-oriented green/digital occupations, while critical shortage occupations are nearly two in three female; care responsibilities (7.7 million women outside the labour market vs 450,000 men) and STEM gaps further constrain participation [p876][p931]. Although no significant difference in sectoral transition frequency between men and women was found, these sectoral and care-related disparities shape who can access green jobs [p24][p931].

20.text: Determinants include age (older workers make fewer sectoral transitions), gender composition (women remain underrepresented in “transforming sectors,” though no significant male–female difference in sectoral transitions is observed), and sector-specific factors such as higher trade-union density and male dominance in energy-intensive industries, which are linked to lower flows out of employment [p24][p25]. Training participation also matters: energy records the highest training rates, while mining and construction lag, and only 10.9% of energy-intensive-industry workers received training in 2023 versus 12.7% economy-wide [p25][p14]. Workforce dynamics are further shaped by seasonality, cyclicality, digitisation, decarbonisation, climate/COVID-19 shocks, job upgrading, geography, skill compatibility, and labour-market rigidity [p8].

23.text: Digital-intensive future-oriented occupations show better employment conditions: job strain is lowest in occupations with higher digital skills intensity (16%) [p887], earnings predictability is highest there and in AI-exposed occupations [p906], and digitally intensive jobs are more secure than the EU average, with a majority on permanent contracts and over 90% full-time, compared with EU part-time work at 17.7% in 2021 [p884]. By contrast, green in-demand future-oriented jobs have high job strain—34% in less digitally intensive green jobs with increased demand—and only 50% of workers in green in-demand jobs can accurately predict earnings in the next three months [p887][p906]. Green-transition occupations also report long working hours, and about one in four workers in green in-demand and new/emerging/enhanced green occupations fear undesirable change; job insecurity is lower in all future-oriented occupations except green in-demand jobs with labour shortages [p887].

24.text: PES’ green-transition role is mainly strategic and skills-focused: defining “green jobs” is challenging because there is no common agreement, yet over a third of PES have a definition and a minority differentiate green skills, tasks and competencies, with pilot taxonomies/task-based approaches and researcher/training-provider partnerships [p1033]. For third-country workers, most schemes are demand- or employer-driven with a job offer as a precondition, so PES mainly handle admission, work permits, labour-market tests and working conditions, though an increasing number are active in recruitment outside the EU, often under bilateral mobility agreements [p1033]. Current initiatives reflect this split: green work includes a toolkit due early 2025 and a Sweden-led taxonomy working group, while third-country work stresses labour-market intelligence, multilingual single-source information, qualification recognition, fair/ethical recruitment and capacity-building [p1033][p1034]; the 2025 Work Programme continues both green-transition support and fair recruitment of third-country nationals [p1047].

44.text: Older workers tend to make fewer sector-to-sector transitions in the EU, while younger workers are more mobile [p7]. Younger workers also participate much more frequently in education and training across all sectors, whereas older workers receive the least training across “transforming sectors” [p10][p25]. This age pattern can make transitioning labour into green industries harder because older workers are both less mobile and less trained, and training in key sectors such as mining and construction is below average [p25].

46.text: EU labour-market resilience reflected improved matching efficiency, expected GDP growth, a shrinking working-age population and persistent labour/skills shortages that can push firms to retain workers [p764]. Labour supply also rose, with non-EU nationals contributing 1.24 million to the 2023 total labour-force increase of almost 2 million, helping alleviate shortages [p704]. Firms retained more workers than needed, and the COVID-19 policy response helped prevent unemployment scarring, while low long-term unemployment indicates improved matching [p704].

It also includes measures such as the EU Talent Pool, the European Skills Agenda, individual learning accounts and micro-credentials, and increasing participation of older workers, women and young people not in education, employment or training [p771].
