Projections show pension reforms are the main driver of the expected 8.8 million additional economically active people aged 55–68 in the EU by 2030 [p840], with retirement reforms expected to bring 6.3 million new active individuals into the labour market by 2030 [p833].

52.text: The difference is 10 percentage points: in 2023, 96% of EU movers in healthcare had permanent contracts, compared with 86% of nationals [p352][p394].

53.text: Workers in green in-demand jobs facing labour shortages report high job strain—above the EU average—and only about 50% can accurately predict their earnings in the next three months [p887][p884][p906]. In contrast, occupations with higher digital skills intensity have the lowest job strain (16%) and the highest earnings predictability [p887][p884].

54.text: Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a permanent-contract rate about 73.7%, i.e. 4 percentage points above the EU average of 69.7% [p884]. Occupations with higher digital skills intensity have the highest permanent-contract share, shown as about 79% in Figure 7, also above the EU average [p883].

55.text: In 2023, the EU employment rate for older people aged 55–64 was 63.9%, with rates above 70% in Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Latvia, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden, and below 55% in Greece, Croatia, Luxembourg, Romania and Slovenia [p659][p821]. For people over 65, employment rates were highest in Estonia (17.6%), Latvia (14.5%) and Lithuania (12.6%), and lowest in Romania (2.2%), Belgium (3.2%), Spain (3.4%), France (4.2%) and Luxembourg (4.2%) [p824]. Since 2009, the largest increases of around 30 pps were in Hungary, Poland and Slovenia for ages 55–59 and in Denmark, Hungary and Slovakia for ages 60–64 [p821].

56.text: EU movers had stronger labour-market integration than TCNs in 2023: activity was 83% vs 72%, employment 78% vs 63%, and unemployment 7% vs 12% [p474]. On part-time work, EU movers consistently had around 21–22% part-time employment from 2018 to 2023, while TCNs’ part-time share declined from 26% in 2018 to 22% in 2023 [p487].

57.text: Under the static scenario, the labour force is projected to decline by 20.2 percentage points, equivalent to around 42.8 million fewer people by 2070 [p1011].

58.text: 10% of Estonia’s nurse population is residing and working in other EU Member States or EFTA countries [p343].

60.text: No. In 2024, only 2 out of 31 PES had a supporting role in implementing Individual Learning Accounts, while 13 out of 31 were designing pilots or had plans to introduce them [p1031]. Figure 6 shows Member States divided between having implemented ILAs, having plans, having no plans, and not submitting feedback, and only a few PES had begun introducing ILA schemes by summer 2024 [p1032].

61.text: The pages point to occupational segregation and care/STEM gaps: women make up just 28% of green-task jobs and are underrepresented in ICT and male-dominated digitally intensive/green occupations, while 7.7 million EU women are outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men, and women lag in STEM skills [p876][p931]. AI-exposed occupations are broadly balanced at 52% women, but women remain underrepresented in the highest-AI-exposure jobs and the “AI workforce” is small and male-dominated [p878]. Policy actions indicated include effective lifelong learning and access for all workers, boosting upskilling/reskilling in key green sectors such as construction and energy, and treating care responsibilities as a top priority to raise women’s labour-market participation [p905][p25][p931]. Greater gender parity in these occupations can also boost labour-market participation and support more balanced, inclusive labour markets [p905].

62.text: Yes. The gap in temporary/fixed-term employment between EU movers and nationals narrowed from 5 percentage points in 2018 to 3 percentage points in 2023 [p485].

63.text: The rise was largely driven by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, which caused a significant influx of Ukrainians fleeing the conflict [p444][p446]. Third-country national inflows doubled between 2021 and 2022 to 3,324,000, a 133% increase [p444][p446].

64.text: From 2019 to 2023, Greece’s employment rate (15–64) rose from 56.5% to 61.8%, a +5.3 pps increase [p722]. Portugal’s employment rate (15–64) rose from 70.5% to 72.5%, a +2.0 pps increase [p738].

65.text: The PES Network migrated the standalone pesnetwork.eu website to a central PES Network website, creating a one-stop-shop for all Network outputs including the podcast [p1043]. It also launched a dedicated LinkedIn group in July 2024 to connect PES and share news, inspiration and best practices, reaching nearly 500 members by end-October 2024 [p1044], and used a social-media week and an anniversary PESPod podcast to share experiences [p1048].

66.text: Among returning health workers, the Netherlands’ full-time share rose from (0%) in 2018 to (38%) in 2023, with part-time falling from (100%) to (62%). Italy moved in the opposite direction: full-time fell from (100%) to (69%), while part-time rose from (0%) to (31%). These values are in parentheses, indicating low reliability [p430].

67.text: Digitalisation and AI intensify platform-work vulnerability by enabling algorithmic management and workplace surveillance that widen power imbalances between platforms and workers and create new exploitable vulnerabilities [p925]. Platform work is also marked by low wages and absent social protection, especially for vulnerable groups lacking alternative income [p925]; in the EU, more than 28 million people were estimated to work through digital labour platforms in 2020, 5.5 million were incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earned less than the minimum wage [p676]. The EU Directive aims to address bogus self-employment through a legal presumption of employment and give platform workers new rights on algorithmic management [p676].

68.text: No, not uniformly across European countries. In Austria and Germany the estimated share of undeclared workers is 90% or more in non-care domestic work, significantly lower in care-related services, and in Malta undeclared work is much more likely in non-care domestic work [p283]; EU-wide, the undeclared-work share is lowest in the care sector (34%) and highest in direct household employment (nearly 70%) [p164]. However, Italy reports an even distribution in 2022, while Bulgaria’s LTC sector and Ireland’s informal home care sector show undeclared work may be more predominant in care [p283].

69.text: Estonia reformed doctoral status by moving PhD students to employees with a €1400/month net salary and 80% research time [p1073], and its annex describes three PhD routes plus a €2446/month junior researcher wage fund with social guarantees since 2022 [p1089]. Germany’s initiative is a tenure-track programme funding up to 1,000 professorships by 2032 at 75 universities with up to €1 billion, targeting R2–R3 and reporting 971 professorships created, average appointment age 35.9, and 49.1% female [p1092]. For Slovenia, the pages only note that training is available but researcher culture is changing slowly [p1073], so no specific Slovenian recruitment/advancement initiative is detailed.

70.text: The report calls for a broad integrated policy mix: investing in active and healthy ageing, prolonging working lives, supporting adapted and flexible work arrangements, and maintaining effective and efficient pension and long-term care systems [p536]. It links this to activating underrepresented groups—especially older people, women and young people not in education, employment or training—through skills development, training, fair intra-EU mobility and attracting talent from outside the EU [p771]. It also highlights pension reforms that raise retirement ages and restrict early retirement while offering financial incentives for working beyond retirement and flexibility to combine work and retirement [p737]; projections cited show +6 million active people aged 55–64 and +2.8 million aged 65–68 in the EU by 2030 [p737], against an expected EU labour supply decline of 0.3% per year until 2070 [p726].

71.text: Between 2010 and 2019, EU sector-to-sector transition rates were 1.8%–3.9%, relatively stable with a slight upward trend around 2016 in some Member States; 2019 is the main reference year because the retrospective transition question was discontinued in 2020 [p7][p24][p3]. From 2018 to 2019, all “transforming sectors” had net inflows of workers except mining/extraction, which had a net outflow [p9][p24]. Older workers made fewer sectoral transitions than younger workers, while no significant difference was observed between men and women [p24]. Outward sectoral mobility was lower in 2015 than in 2010 or 2019, with a spike in 2019 [p38].

72.text: Future-oriented occupations accounted for 32% of EU workers in 2021 [p873].

74.text: As of October 2024, ILO Convention C189 had been ratified by nine EU Member States: Belgium, Germany, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Malta, Portugal and Sweden [p261][p310].

75.text: Nine EU Member States have ratified ILO Convention C189 [p231][p261], while eight Member States apply the same labour and social protection rules to domestic workers as to other workers [p231][p261]. Thus, ratification is slightly more common than full equal treatment under national rules.

76.text: AI-exposed occupations have below-average job strain and are among the lowest-strain groups, while labour-shortage occupations report the highest job strain at 48% [p887][p891][p906]. Access to training is highest among AI-exposed and high-digital-skills occupations, whereas only a minority of workers in residual critical labour-shortage occupations received training in the preceding four weeks [p888][p907].

77.text: Higher training completion among older people is associated with higher unemployment-to-employment transitions: Denmark, where older people complete about 20% more training hours than EU 25–64, has the highest transition rate at more than 30%, and Germany, the Netherlands and Austria also combine high training with relatively high job-finding [p828]. In contrast, Member States with low training levels—Bulgaria, Greece, Romania and Slovakia—have older people’s transition rates below 10% per quarter [p828]. In 2022, more than half of older people participated in training in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Sweden, while less than 15% did so in Bulgaria, Greece, Poland and Romania [p827]. The report concludes that education and training policies are among the most effective tools for promoting older workers’ employment, especially when combined with search assistance and counselling [p828].

78.text: Adopting Sweden’s higher labour force participation rates across EU member states would almost completely offset the projected negative impact of ageing: the EU labour force would decline by only 2.8 pp, or 5.9 million people, by 2070 [p1012]. This is far smaller than the standard “Static” scenario’s projected decline of 20.2 pp, or about 42.8 million people, by 2070 [p1011].

79.text: In 2022, EU public expenditure on education was distributed as follows: pre-primary and primary 34%, secondary 36.8%, and tertiary 16.6% [p130].

80.text: The predominant posted third-country nationals are Ukrainians: Table A1.11 shows they are the largest TCN group in several reporting states, e.g. Lithuania 78%, Austria 50%, Netherlands 45%, Belgium 32% [p997], and more than a quarter of posted TCNs are Ukrainian in Belgium, Lithuania, the Netherlands and Austria [p1008]. TCNs were most frequently sent by companies established in Poland (30%) and Lithuania (18%) [p1008]. Across Member States they are mainly employed in construction and manufacturing—e.g. Belgium construction 32% [p959], Denmark almost half in construction, France construction 31% and manufacturing 26%, Italy manufacturing 37% [p959], Lithuania construction 36% and manufacturing 24%, Netherlands construction 31% and manufacturing 28%, Sweden construction 47% and manufacturing 24% [p960]; road freight transport is also important, notably for Austria and for TCNs sent from Lithuania [p960].

81.text: In Bulgaria, 35.5% of individuals aged 16–74 had at least basic overall digital skills in 2023, compared with 55.6% in the EU [p548][p581].

82.text: Between January 2022 and January 2024, real statutory minimum wages rose by more than 10% in **Belgium** and **Bulgaria** [p640]. Over the same period, high inflation diminished these gains, with real statutory minimum wages falling by more than 3% in **Czechia** and **Slovakia** [p640].

83.text: High graduation rates do not ensure adequate staffing: Ireland, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia and Romania have above-EU densities of medical doctor and nurse graduates but below-EU densities of available healthcare workers [p338]. Projected “excess” graduates are measured only against retirement replacement, assuming current doctors/nurses per 10,000 inhabitants is sufficient and retirement is the main reason for leaving the profession, which is not always true [p340]. Retention and mobility also matter: Italy faces insufficient graduates plus doctor outflow, Latvia has the equivalent of 15% of its doctors practising in other Member States, and returnees may not offset outflows [p358].

84.text: Based on EU-SILC data, minimum wage non-compliance affects more than 8% of the workforce in Germany, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Lithuania, Hungary, Portugal and Sweden [p797]. The workers most affected are young people, unskilled workers, women, workers in smaller firms and part-time workers; they are generally younger, less educated, more likely female, on fixed-term or part-time contracts, and employed by smaller firms [p797]. Non-compliance is also relatively higher in agriculture, construction and services than in manufacturing [p797].

85.text: Labour-market transitions support the green transition by moving workers out of shrinking sectors and into expanding ones, which helps avoid worsening labour shortages in affected sectors and enables smoother sectoral adjustment [p46]. Skills investment is central: wind and solar deployment is estimated to require about 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers in the EU, with EUR 1.1–1.4 billion in associated skills investment by 2030 [p25]. However, training gaps remain—only 10.9% of workers in energy-intensive industries received training in 2023 versus 12.7% economy-wide—so upskilling and reskilling are urgently needed, especially in construction, energy production/distribution, and transport [p25].

86.text: In 2023, 36% of female EU movers worked part-time versus 8% of male EU movers, a 28-pp gap [p475][p493]. For EU movers specifically, the report attributes high female part-time employment to inequitable parental leave policies and strong labour markets with high demand for part-time work, especially in female-dominated industries [p493]. It also notes the highest female mover part-time rates in Switzerland (47%), Austria (45%) and Germany (44%), compared with much lower male mover rates of 12%, 14% and 9% [p493]. A broader analysis links women’s part-time prevalence to difficulties combining paid work with family responsibilities, unpaid care work, lack of child/long-term care services, and gendered earner/caretaker attitudes [p850].

88.text: Yes. Workers in AI-exposed occupations have a higher-than-average incidence of permanent employment, 4 percentage points above the EU average of 69.7% [p884].

89.text: Future EU labour force is projected to decline by 0.3% per year until 2070 due to population ageing [p726], with the working-age population shrinking despite the participation rate of people aged 20–64 rising from 79.4% in 2022 to 82.7% in 2070 and older workers’ employment from 62.3% to 72.3%, though this is insufficient in most Member States and the decline is concentrated by 2045 [p818]. Scenario analysis shows migration has large potential (no migration: 26.7 pp/55.9 million fewer by 2070), female participation convergence could halve ageing effects (11.0 pp/23.2 million decline), and convergence to Sweden’s subgroup rates could nearly offset the decline (2.8 pp/5.9 million) [p1012]. Proposed policies include activating underrepresented groups including older people [p726], implementing the EU Action Plan on labour and skills shortages, the EU Talent Pool, the European Skills Agenda with individual learning accounts and microcredentials, boosting participation of older workers, women and young NEETs, intra-EU mobility and attracting non-EU talent [p771]. They also include pension reforms with flexible yet fair retirement pathways, affordable childcare and long-term care, flexible working arrangements, reasonable accommodation and anti-age-discrimination policies [p787].

90.text: Gender and household status strongly shape underemployment among EU part-time workers: women are significantly less likely than men to be underemployed (by 8 pp or more), and people living with partners are less likely than singles (by 8 pp or more), differences not explained by occupational or sectoral patterns [p851]. Descriptively, 18% of women part-time workers are underemployed, including 16% of mothers of young children, while 15% of part-timers with partners are underemployed versus 26% of those without partners [p850]. In regressions, women with small children and women living with partners are 16 pp and 9 pp less likely to be underemployed than women without children or partners, whereas for men children or a partner have no large effects [p852]. These patterns reflect gendered work/care roles and working-time constraints—women’s lower underemployment can mask caring responsibilities and limited ability to consider longer hours, while male part-time work is less often preferred and more than a quarter of male part-timers want longer hours [p850][p852][p853].

91.text: Digital transformation creates labour-market risks through unequal digitalisation across European businesses and a digital divide that can hinder innovation, reduce productivity, feed workplace inequalities, and self-reinforce social exclusion and privileged positions [p924]. Platform work and AI-driven algorithmic management create unequal and exploitative dynamics, low wages, lack of social protection for vulnerable groups, wider platform–worker power imbalances, surveillance, reduced bargaining power, and “invisible” AI workers [p925]. In the EU platform economy, more than 28 million people worked through digital labour platforms in 2020, 5.5 million were estimated to be incorrectly classified as self-employed, and more than half earned less than the minimum wage [p552]. AI and automation can replace routine jobs and affect high-skilled workers, while unskilled workers are more exposed and the skilled workforce benefits, increasing polarisation [p552][p925]; women may be disproportionately affected due to overrepresentation in AI-exposed sectors and more automatable tasks, and make up just 28% of green-task jobs [p876].

92.text: In 2023, non-EU nationals accounted for **64.1%** of the total increase in the EU labour force [p755].

93.text: EU movers face lower risks and material hardship than third-country nationals: in 2022, AROPE was 27% for EU movers versus 46% for TCNs [p508], SMSD was 8% versus 16% [p509], and housing cost overburden was 19% versus 26% [p383]. The report notes that TCNs here include all non-EU countries, including EFTA countries, due to SILC data limitations [p508]. Country-level differences may also reflect movers’ characteristics such as education, skills, or employment sectors interacting with national conditions [p510].

94.text: Benchlearning supports PES modernisation by systematically comparing PES organisational set-ups and outcomes against an “ideal PES,” combining quantitative performance data with qualitative self-review, peer review and expert review [p1045]. In 2024 the 4th cycle launched with 15 assessments covering Lithuania, Bulgaria, Latvia, Croatia, Austria, Portugal, Hungary, Germany, Greece, Czechia, Estonia, The Netherlands, Malta, Ireland and Cyprus [p1045]. The findings show PES progress especially in ecosystem management, while quality management and channel strategy were most challenging; success factors included up-to-date strategies, learning from crises and uptake of technology such as e-services and automated skills-based matching [p1046]. Iceland’s example shows recommendations led to mutual learning, coaching and study visits, helping it strengthen services such as quality management [p1046].

95.text: In the EU in 2023, the employment rate for people with tertiary education was 86.3%, and the gap between high- and low-educated persons aged 25-64 was 28.0 pps, implying a low-skilled rate of about 58.3% [p618]. For persons aged 25-54, the employment rate was 64.1% for lower education and 89.7% for tertiary education [p73].

96.text: Limited mobility in energy-intensive industries is attributed to higher trade union density and a male-dominated workforce less affected by transitions into inactivity due to caring responsibilities [p12][p25]. These sectors also show high labour-market stability and are relatively well-paid, with wage premiums reported in some cases [p13].

97.text: PES career guidance has shifted toward digital and green competencies: 51% report changes covering both digital and green skills, 48% digital skills and 32% green skills [p1058]. This mirrors the digital transformation, where EU ICT specialists rose 59.3% since 2013 to over 9.5 million in 2023, yet 4 in 10 adults and one-third of workers lack basic digital skills, with shortages in Latvia, Denmark, Poland and Spain [p638]. It also mirrors the green transition: green-economy employment rose from 2.2% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2021, while skills shortages threaten upscaling of heat pumps and solar and wind technologies [p638][p921]. Training gaps remain, as EU training uptake is still below the 60% adult target for 2030 [p922].

98.text: Factors include strong gender segregation and male dominance of “transforming” and green occupations [p876][p6], women’s disproportionate care responsibilities—7.7 million women in the EU were outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men [p931], and women’s STEM skills gap [p931]. This leaves women underrepresented in green energy: they were only 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023 and 14% of mining workers in 2022 [p6], and just 28% of green-task jobs [p876]. Within renewables, women made up 40% of solar PV versus 21% of wind, while oil and gas had 22% [p6].

99.text: In 2023, the older-worker (55–64) employment rate rose by 1.7 pp to 63.9%, a much stronger increase than the 0.4 pp rise to 35.2% for young workers (15–24) [p72]. Older workers remained the main driver of labour-force growth from 2019 to 2023, adding about 1.2 million people yearly, while the youth labour force began growing from 2021 and reached 19.3 million in 2023 [p753]. Youth employment nevertheless returned to pre-2008 levels in 2023, with a 35.2% employment rate and a record-low NEET rate of 11.2% [p618].

100.text: The projected investment in skills needed for additional wind and solar deployment to meet EU Green Deal targets is **EUR 1.1 to 1.4 billion by 2030**, associated with about **130,000 to 145,000 additional skilled workers** [p21][p25]. This range is also cited in the 2024 ESDE report [p138].

102.text: Based on the PHS Employment Monitor 2024, more than 15% of workers reported undeclared care work in **Poland, Spain, and Italy** (35% in Italy) [p165]. Portugal also reports that **48% of domestic workers were not registered** in social security in 2023 [p165].

103.text: The green transition is concentrated in “transforming sectors” such as mining and quarrying, manufacturing, energy, water/waste, construction and transportation [p24][p2]. From 2018–2019 there was a net inflow of workers into all transforming sectors except mining and extraction in the EU, while older workers make fewer sectoral transitions and women remain underrepresented, at only 26.7% of energy-industry workers in 2023 and 14% in mining [p24]. Contrary to expectations, energy-intensive industries show fewer transitions to non-employment than other sectors, but training lags: only 10.9% of their workers received training in 2023 versus 12.7% economy-wide [p24][p25]. Delivering EU Green Deal renewable targets would require about 130,000–145,000 additional skilled workers and EUR 1.1–1.4 billion in skills investment by 2030 [p25][p12].

104.text: The workshop highlighted people with disabilities, unpaid care workers and regional vulnerabilities, as well as precarious workers, self-employed individuals and those facing discrimination, as vulnerable groups in the twin transitions [p926]. People with disabilities face a much lower EU employment rate, 50.6% versus 74.8% for people without disabilities [p928]. Women bear disproportionate unpaid care responsibilities, with 7.7 million women in the EU outside the labour market due to caregiving versus 450,000 men [p931]. Workers in energy-intensive/fossil-fuel-dependent industries and the regions depending on them are also flagged [p933].

105.text: In Portugal, domestic-service workers are under a special regime outside the Labour Code, and unemployment benefits require a full-time monthly written contract registered with social security; most work for several employers and opt for the lower-contribution “agreed regime,” so many lack unemployment protection [p177][p269]. Portugal also has shorter termination notice periods than for other workers—7 days for contracts under 6 months, 15 days for 6 months to 2 years, and 30 days for over 2 years [p278]. In Hungary, employees (including simplified employment) and self-employed domestic workers generally have access to all insurance-based benefits and labour protection, but those under Act XC of 2010 do not have labour protection and may only get basic healthcare if they pay for it themselves [p269][p275]. Shortfalls remain in Hungary through no collective agreements covering domestic workers and carers being unmonitored, with no access to workers’ representation or collective bargaining [p261][p177].

106.text: Not under the projections described: investing in skills “will not be able to compensate” for demographic decline, though it can mitigate the reduction in workers [p1022]. However, a hypothetical extreme positive scenario that simultaneously exploits the entire potential of labour-force activation could offset the projected adverse decline [p1022], and the most optimistic scenario—moving to Swedish participation rates—could almost fully offset the effects of ageing [p1017]. The Draghi report’s projection of a workforce shrinking by close to 2 million workers each year by 2040 is cited on [p1023].

107.text: ALMP investments are projected to produce a sustained long-term catching-up in regional GDP per capita, with lower-baseline regions growing faster, although the employment catching-up is not expected to be sustained long term [p141]. Housing allowances and social housing are found to reduce poverty in the short term and to narrow divergence in poverty risks across countries [p152][p81]. The pages do not provide a comparable long-term regional-disparity estimate for housing investment.

108.text: Yes, based on the reported age groups: younger part-time workers (20–29) are about 8 pp more likely to be underemployed than prime-aged workers, while older workers (55–64) are significantly less likely, by 8 pp or more [p851]. The 55–64 group accounts for about a quarter of part-timers but less than 15% of the underemployed [p846]. The exact 20–34 band is not reported.

109.text: Austria and France were among five countries with falling absolute regional income disparities (convergence) [p105], and show catching-up beta coefficients of -0.02 for Austria (2014–2021) and -0.01 for France (2014–2021) [p106]. By contrast, Czechia and Sweden were among four countries with rising absolute disparities (divergence) [p105]; Czechia’s standard deviation rose by 20% between 2007 and 2022 [p105], and neither Czechia nor Sweden shows robust evidence of catching-up [p106]. The difference is linked to metropolitan vs non-metropolitan income growth: in converging countries metropolitan regions had slower median income growth than non-metropolitan ones, e.g. slow growth in Austrian major metropolitan regions [p106], whereas in Sweden Stockholm had among the highest median income growth and non-metropolitan Södermanland and Kronoberg the lowest [p106]. For Czechia, absolute dispersion increased but less than the cross-regional average of median incomes, implying a decline in relative income dispersion [p106].

110.text: Yes. The report states that as labour demand increased over the last decade, underemployment “steadily declined both in relative and absolute terms” in the EU [p847]. In 2013, around 30% of part-time workers were underemployed, compared with less than 20% by 2023, and the number of underemployed part-time workers immediately available to work longer hours fell from over 8 million to about 5 million [p847].

111.text: Declared care workers are entitled to additional compensation, overtime pay, and paid leave under labour rights, while undeclared care workers lack legal protection and social protection in case of unemployment or illness [p193][p177]. Because undeclared care workers receive pay without official documentation and neither income tax nor social insurance contributions are fully paid, they are not eligible for related social insurance benefits [p161]. Care workers are also more likely to have temporary contracts and to be undeclared, depriving them of legal guarantees and social protection [p177].

112.text: The ISCO codes used to define domestic workers are 5152 (“butlers”), 5162 (“companions and valets”), 5322 (“home-based personal care workers”), and 9111 (“domestic cleaners and helpers”), added so long as they are not already included in NACE 97 [p240][p230].

113.text: Individual learning accounts enable people to accumulate funds for labour-market-relevant training, and evidence from the Netherlands and Austria suggests they can boost training participation and learning intentions among older adults [p838]. The EU treats ILAs as flagship actions that can increase adult participation in education and training and improve skills–job matching [p771]. They are intended to give individuals a personal budget for labour-market-relevant training and develop the national training offer, with 2 of 31 PES supporting access and 13 of 31 designing pilots or planning introduction [p1031]. ILAs can also make learning more accessible to underperforming groups when combined with top-ups, career guidance and targeted outreach [p654].

114.text: No. Real wage growth reached 2.4% year-on-year in Q2-2024, but real wages in the EU remained below pre-pandemic levels on average in 2024 [p530][p639]. They were still forecast to be 1.1% below their 2019 level in the EU in 2024 [p715].

115.text: Table A2.1 reports beta convergence (catching-up) for 2007-2023 in GDP per capita, employment rate, unemployment rate, NEET rate, adult participation in learning, and tertiary education attainment [p120]. For social/labour-market indicators specifically, this covers employment, unemployment, NEET, adult learning, and tertiary attainment [p120].

116.text: Voucher systems show stronger evidence of reducing undeclared domestic work: France’s CESU system was associated with informal employment falling from about 50% in 1996 to 20% in 2015 [p187], and 2021 research found Belgium’s service vouchers halved undeclared work in the covered activities [p188]. Tax incentives are more mixed: Germany’s had little effect, while Spain’s 2011 introduction increased declared domestic workers over the following two years before plateauing [p287]. On equity, tax incentives are regressive—German relief rises with household taxable income, and Sweden’s top income decile received 40% of total tax deductions [p287]—while vouchers and tax incentives may mainly benefit higher-income households and have limited formalisation impact among lower-income groups [p194]. Coverage varies: Belgium’s vouchers grew from 62,000 workers in 2006 to 150,000 by 2014, serving about one million users [p188], and France’s HR CESU distributed EUR 400 million in 2020 through 20,300 companies for 809,000 workers [p187]; vouchers could also be extended to more professions, as in Belgium [p311].

117.text: In 2024, PES modernisation collaboration included the start of the fourth Benchlearning cycle, with 15 assessments in LT, BG, LV, HR, AT, PT, HU, DE, EL, CZ, EE, NL, MT, IE and CY [p1056], plus two Mutual Assistance programmes for Luxembourg and Romania [p1054]—on digital matching tools for LU and HR strategy for RO [p1050]. The Digitalisation Working Group, chaired by NL, met twice to share IT projects/reforms, discuss AI Act implications and AI/digitalisation across customer journeys, and exchange on IT solutions and public-private partnerships [p1040]. Primary focuses included performance management, data-driven and digitalisation strategies including AI, service-delivery modernisation, support for those furthest from the labour market, and job-to-job transitions [p1056].

118.text: Yes. EU-mover inflows rose by 117,000 (859,000 to 976,000), while outflows fell by 41,000 (584,000 to 543,000) from 2021 to 2022 [p443]. Net mobility increased by 21% to 358,000 in 2022 [p449].

119.text: EU movers’ EU-wide median income was higher than nationals’ in 2022 (EUR 20 714 vs EUR 19 506), even though nationals’ median income grew faster (2.6% annually vs 1.9% for movers) [p524]. This apparent paradox reflects the migration pattern: EU movers tend to go to Member States with rather high income levels, raising their EU-wide median despite typically earning less than nationals within each Member State [p524].

120.text: Using the 2023 figure of nearly 9.8 million ICT specialists and the 20 million target for 2030 [p656][p638], the required compound annual growth rate is about **10.7% per year** over seven years.

121.text: PES are advancing digital transformation using AI to enhance service delivery and personalised support, applying it across profiling, matching and career guidance for jobseekers, employers and employees [p1039].
